children.text: prathamādhyāye prathamaḥ pādaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the first chapter, the first section.

children.text: (atra pāde spaṣṭabrahmaliṅgayuktānāṃ vākyānāṃ vicāraḥ)
children.translated_text: (In this section, there is an examination of passages possessing clear indicators of <s>Brahman</s>)

children.text: 1 jijñāsādhikaraṇam / sū. 1
children.translated_text: 1. The <s>Jijñāsādhikaraṇa</s> (Topic of the Desire to Know). <s>Sūtra</s> 1.

children.text: vedāntamīmāṃsāśāstrasya vyācikhyāsitasyedamādimaṃ sūtram-
children.translated_text: This is the opening <s>sūtra</s> of the <s>Vedānta Mīmāṃsā</s> treatise that is about to be expounded —

children.text: athāto brahmajijñāsā | BBs_1,1.1 |
children.translated_text: Then, therefore, the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>. | <s>BBs</s> 1,1.1 |

children.text:
tatrāthābda ānantaryārthaḥ parigṛhyate nādhikārārthaḥ, brahmajijñāsāyāḥ anadhikāryatvāt /
maṅgalasya ca vākyārthe samanvayābhāvāt /
arthāntaraprayukta eva śrutyā maṅgalaprayojano bhavati /
pūrvaprakṛtāpekṣāyāśca phalata ānantaryāvyatirekāt /
sati cānantaryārthatve yathā dharmajijñāsā pūrvavṛttaṃ vedādhyayanaṃ niyamenāpekṣata evaṃ brahmajijñāsāpi yatpūrvavṛttaṃ niyamenāpekṣate tadvaktavyam /
svādhyāyānantaryaṃ tu samānam /
children.translated_text: Here, the word '<s>atha</s>' (then) is taken in the sense of sequence, not in the sense of qualification, because the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> is not something that requires qualification. And because there is no syntactical connection of an auspicious [meaning] with the meaning of the sentence. For what is employed for another purpose becomes auspicious merely through the Vedic recitation. And because, when dependence on what precedes is considered, there is no distinction between sequence and its result. And when the meaning of sequence is accepted, just as the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> necessarily presupposes the prior completion of Vedic study, so too what prior completion the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> necessarily presupposes must be stated. The sequence after Vedic study, however, is common [to both].

children.text: nanviha karmāvabodhanārthaṃ viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: But is not the distinguishing factor here the understanding of ritual action?

children.text:
na /
dharmajijñāsāyāḥ prāgapyadhītavedāntasya brahmajijñāsopapatteḥ /
yathāca hṛdayādyavadānānāmānantaryaniyamaḥ, kramasya vivakṣitatvānna tatheha kramo vivakṣitaḥ, śeṣaśeṣitve 'dhikṛtādhikāre vā pramāṇābhāvāt, dharmabrahmajijñāsayoḥ phalajijñāsasyabhedācca /
abhyudayaphalaṃ dharmajñānaṃ taccānuṣṭhānāpekṣam /
niḥśreyasaphalaṃ tu brahmavijñānaṃ na cānuṣṭhānāntarāpekṣam /
bhavyaśca dharmo jijñāsyo na jñānakāle 'sti, puruṣavyāpāratantratvāt /
iha tu bhūtaṃ brahma jijñāsyaṃ nityatvānna puruṣavyāpāratantram /
codanāpravṛttibhedācca /
yā hi codanā dharmasya lakṣaṇaṃ sā svaviṣaye niyuñjānaiva puruṣamavabodhayati /
brahmacodanā tu puruṣamavabodhayatyeva kevalaṃ, avabodhasya codanājanyatvānna puruṣo 'vabodhe niyujyate /
yathākṣārthasaṃnikarṣeṇārthāvabodhe tadvat /
tasmātkimapi vaktavyaṃ yadanantaraṃ brahmajijñāsopadiśyata iti /
children.translated_text: No. Because even one who has studied the <s>Vedānta</s> before the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> can properly undertake the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>. And just as there is a fixed sequence for the <s>hṛdaya</s> and other offerings, because the sequence is intended — here, the sequence is not so intended, since there is no valid means of knowledge for [establishing] a subsidiary-principal or a qualification-qualified [relationship between them]; and because the fruits of the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> and the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> are different. The knowledge of <s>dharma</s> has worldly prosperity as its fruit, and that depends on [ritual] performance. But the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> has liberation (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) as its fruit, and does not depend on any other performance. Furthermore, <s>dharma</s>, which is to be inquired into, is something yet to be accomplished — it does not exist at the time of knowledge, since it depends on human effort. But here, <s>Brahman</s>, which is to be inquired into, is an already-existing [reality] — being eternal, it does not depend on human effort. And because of the difference in the operation of injunction: for the injunction that is the defining characteristic of <s>dharma</s> makes a person know [something] only by enjoining him to its own object. But the injunction regarding <s>Brahman</s> merely makes a person know — since knowledge arises from the injunction [directly], the person is not enjoined to know. Just as, through the contact of the senses with their objects, knowledge of objects [arises automatically] — so too here. Therefore, something must be stated as the prerequisite after which the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> is taught.

children.text:
ucyate- nityānityavastuvivekaḥ, ihāmutrārthabhogavirāgaḥ, śamadamādisādhanasaṃpat, mumukṣutvaṃ ca /
teṣu hi satsu prāgapi dharmajijñāsāyā ūrdhvaṃ ca śakyate brahmajijñāsituṃ jñātuṃ ca na viparyaye /
tasmādathābdena yathoktasādhanasaṃpattyānantaryamupadiśyate /
ataḥśabdo hetvarthaḥ /
yasmādveda evāgnihotrādīnāṃ śreyaḥsādhanānāmanityaphalatāṃ darśayati- 'tadyatheha karmacito lokaḥ kṣīyata evamevāmutra puṇyacito lokaḥ kṣīyate' (chāndo.8.1.6) ityādiḥ /
tathā brahmavijñānādapi paraṃ puruṣārthaṃ darśayati- 'brahmavidāpnoti param' ityādiḥ (taitti.2.1) tasmādyathoktasādhanasaṃpattyanantaraṃ brahmajijñāsā kartavyā /
brahmaṇo jijñāsā brahmajijñāsā /
brahma ca vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇaṃ 'janmādyasya yataḥ' iti /
ata eva na brahmaśabdasya jātyādyarthāntaramāśaṅkitavyam /
children.translated_text: It is said: the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things; dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter; the accomplishment of means such as tranquility, self-control, and the like; and the desire for liberation. For when these are present, whether before or after the inquiry into <s>dharma</s>, one is able to inquire into and know <s>Brahman</s> — but not in the reverse case. Therefore, the word '<s>atha</s>' teaches the sequence after the accomplishment of the aforesaid means. The word '<s>ataḥ</s>' (therefore) has the sense of reason. Because the <s>Veda</s> itself shows the impermanence of the fruits of means to prosperity such as the <s>Agnihotra</s> and the like: 'Just as in this world a realm built up by action perishes, so too in the other world a realm built up by merit perishes' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 8.1.6) and so forth. Likewise, it shows that from the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> comes the supreme goal of man: 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 2.1) and so forth. Therefore, after the accomplishment of the aforesaid means, the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> is to be undertaken. The desire to know <s>Brahman</s> is the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>. And <s>Brahman</s> has the characteristics to be stated [in the next sūtra]: 'that from which the origin and so on [of this world proceed].' For this very reason, no other meaning such as a class-name should be suspected for the word '<s>Brahman</s>.'

children.text: brahmaṇa iti karmaṇiṣaṣṭhī na śeṣe, jijñāsāpekṣyatvājjijñāsāyāḥ, jijñāsyāntarānirdeśācca /
children.translated_text: The genitive in '<s>brahmaṇaḥ</s>' is an objective genitive, not a genitive of relation — because the inquiry has an object to be inquired into, and because no other object of inquiry is specified.

children.text:
nanu śeṣaṣaṣṭhīparigrahe 'pi brahmaṇo jijñāsākarmatvaṃ na virudhyate, saṃbandhasāmānyasya viśeṣaniṣṭhatvāt /
evamapi pratyakṣaṃ brahmaṇaḥ karmatvamutsṛjya sāmānyadvāreṇa parokṣaṃ karmatvaṃ kalpayato vyartha prayāsaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: But even if a relational genitive is accepted, the status of <s>Brahman</s> as the object of inquiry is not contradicted, since a general relation rests on a particular [relation]. Even so, to abandon the direct objective status of <s>Brahman</s> and construe an indirect objective status through the general [relation] would be a pointless effort.

children.text:
na vyarthaḥ, brahmāśritāśeṣavicārapratijñānārthatvāditi cenna, pradhānaparigrahe tadapekṣitānāmarthākṣiptatvāt /
brahma hi jñānenāptumiṣṭatamatvātpradhānam /
tasminpradhāne jijñāsākarmaṇi parigṛhīte yairjijñāsitairvinā brahma jijñāsitaṃ na bhavati tānyarthākṣiptānyeveti na pṛthaksūtrayitavyāni /
yathā rājāsau gacchatītyukte saparivārasya rājño gamanamuktaṃ bhavati tadvat /
śrutyanugamācca /
'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante' (taitti.3.1) ityādyāḥ śrutayaḥ, 'tadvijijñāsasva tadbrahma'
children.translated_text: It is not pointless, because it serves to announce the examination of everything dependent on <s>Brahman</s> — if this is said, no; because when the principal [subject] is grasped, what depends on it is implied. For <s>Brahman</s>, being most desired as the goal to be attained through knowledge, is the principal [subject]. When that principal, as the object of inquiry, is grasped, those things without the inquiry into which <s>Brahman</s> would not be [fully] inquired into are implied — and thus need not be made the subject of separate <s>sūtras</s>. Just as when it is said 'the king goes,' the going of the king together with his retinue is understood — so too here. And because of conformity with scripture: the scriptures such as 'that from which these beings are born' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 3.1) and 'seek to know that — that is <s>Brahman</s>'

children.text: iti pratyakṣameva brahmaṇo jijñāsākarmatvaṃ darśayanti /
children.translated_text: directly show that <s>Brahman</s> is the object of the inquiry.

children.text: tacca karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhīparigrahe sūtreṇānugataṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: And that [direct objective status] conforms with the <s>sūtra</s> when the genitive is taken as objective.

children.text: tasmādbrahmaṇa iti karmaṇiṣaṣṭhī //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the genitive in '<s>brahmaṇaḥ</s>' is an objective genitive.

children.text:
jñātumicchā jijñāsā /
avagatiparyantaṃ jñānaṃ sanvācyāyā icchāyāḥ /
karmaphalaviṣayatvādicchāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Because the desire has as its object the fruit of action [i.e., knowledge leading to the result].

children.text: jñānena hi pramāṇenāvagantumiṣṭaṃ brahma /
children.translated_text: For <s>Brahman</s> is desired to be known through knowledge, which is the valid means of cognition.

children.text: brahmāvagatirhi puruṣārthaḥ, niḥśeṣasaṃsārabījāvidyādyanarthanibarhaṇāt /
children.translated_text: For the realization of <s>Brahman</s> is the supreme goal of man, because it eradicates the entirety of evil such as ignorance, which is the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s>.

children.text: tasmādbrahma vijijñāsitavyam //
children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is to be inquired into.
The desire to know is inquiry (<s>jijñāsā</s>). The knowledge in question is that which culminates in realization (<s>avagati</s>), belonging to the desire that is to be expressed.

children.text:
tatpunarbrahma prasiddhamaprasddhaṃ vā syāt /
yadi prasiddhaṃ na jijñāsitavyam /
athāprasiddhaṃ naiva śakyaṃ jijñāsitumiti /
children.translated_text: Now, that <s>Brahman</s> would be either well-known or not well-known. If well-known, it need not be inquired into. If not well-known, it simply cannot be inquired into.

children.text:
ucyate- asti tāvadbrahma nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaṃ, sarvajñaṃ, sarvaśaktisamanvitam /
brahmaśabdasya hi vyutpādyamānasya nityaśuddhatvādayor'thāḥ pratīyante, bṛhaterdhātorarthānugamāt /
sarvasyātmatvācca brahmāstitvaprasiddhiḥ /
sarvo hyātmāstitvaṃ pratyeti, na nāhamasmīti /
yadi hi nātmāstitvaprasiddhiḥ syāt sarvo loko nāhamasmīti pratīyāt /
ātmā ca brahma /
children.translated_text: It is said: <s>Brahman</s> indeed exists, having the nature of eternal purity, consciousness, and freedom, omniscient, endowed with all powers. For when the word '<s>Brahman</s>' is etymologically derived, meanings such as eternal purity and the rest are understood, following the meaning of the root '<s>bṛh</s>' (to be great). And because it is the Self of all, the existence of <s>Brahman</s> is well-known. For everyone is aware that the Self exists — no one thinks 'I do not exist.' If the existence of the Self were not well-known, everyone would think 'I do not exist.' And the Self is <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text: yadi tarhi loke brahmātmatvena prasiddhamasti tato jñātamevetyajijñāsyatvaṃ punarāpannam /
children.translated_text: If, then, <s>Brahman</s> is well-known in the world as the Self, then since it is already known, the objection of there being nothing to inquire into returns.

children.text:
na /
tadviśeṣaṃ prati vipratipatteḥ /
dehamātraṃ caitanyaviśiṣṭamātmeti prakṛtā janā laukāyatikāśca pratipannāḥ /
indriyāṇyeva cetanānyātmetyapare /
mana ityanye /
vijñānamātraṃ kṣaṇikamityeke /
śūnyamityapare /
asti dehādivyatiriktaḥ saṃsārī kartā, bhoktetyapare /
bhoktaiva kevalaṃ na kartetyeke /
asti tadvyatirikta īśvaraḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvāktiriti kecit /
ātmā sa bhokturityapare /
children.translated_text: Others [hold] that the Self is that experiencer [alone, identical with the Lord].

children.text: evaṃ bahavo vipratipannā yuktivākyatadābhāsasamāśrayāḥ santaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, there are many who hold conflicting views, relying on reasoning, scriptural statements, and their semblances.

children.text: tatrāvicārya yatkiñcitpratipadyamāno niḥśreyasātpratihanyetānarthaṃ ceyāt /
children.translated_text: Among these, one who, without examination, accepts any one [view] whatsoever, would be barred from the supreme good and would come to harm.

children.text: tasmātbrahmajijñāsopanyāsamukhena vedāntavākyamīmāṃsā tadavirodhitarkopakaraṇā niḥśreyasaprayojanā prastūyate // 1 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, with the introduction of the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> as the opening, the examination of the <s>Vedānta</s> passages — aided by reasoning that does not conflict with them — having liberation as its purpose, is commenced. // 1 //

No. Because there are conflicting views regarding its specific nature. Ordinary people and the <s>Lokāyatas</s> (materialists) hold that the Self is merely the body qualified by consciousness. Others [hold] that the sense organs themselves are the conscious Self. Yet others, that it is the mind. Some [say] it is momentary consciousness alone. Others, that it is the void. Some [hold] that there exists a transmigrating [soul] distinct from the body — an agent and experiencer. Others, that it is merely an experiencer, not an agent. Some [hold] that there exists a Lord distinct from that [soul] — omniscient, omnipotent.

children.text:
FN: adhikaraṇamiti- viṣayaḥ saṃdehaḥ saṃgatiḥ pūrvapakṣaḥ siddhānta ityekaikamadhikaraṇaṃ pañcāvayavaṃ jñeyam /
tataśca jñānajanyacikīrṣayā yatnesati yāgādidharmo bhavati /
brahmaṇo hi nivṛttāvaraṇatvena phalarūpatvaṃ tajjñānopayogitayā caturthisamāsa eṣitavyaḥ 'caturthī tadarthe' ityādineti kecit /
yaccāpnoti yadādatte yaccātti viṣayāniha /
yaccāsya saṃtato bhāvastasmādātmeti bhaṇyate /
vipratipattṛparigaṇanam-śūnyavādo mādhyamikānāṃ, kṣaṇikijñānavādo yogācārāṇāṃ, jñānākārānumeyakṣaṇikabāhyārthavādaḥ sautrāntikānāṃ, kṣaṇikabāhyārthavādo vaibhāṣikāṇāṃ, dehārthavādaścārvākāṇāṃ, dehātiriktadehapariṇāmavādo digambarāṇāmityādyūhyam /
children.translated_text: NOTE: '<s>Adhikaraṇa</s>' (topic) is to be understood as having five components: subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view, and conclusion. And when there is effort born of the desire to act produced by knowledge, <s>dharma</s> such as sacrifice and the like comes about. Since <s>Brahman</s> has the nature of fruit through the removal of obstruction, the fourth-case compound should be sought through the rule '<s>caturthī tadarthe</s>' (the dative is used for its purpose), on account of its being serviceable to the knowledge of it — so say some. 'That which pervades, that which absorbs, that which enjoys objects here, and that whose existence is continuous — therefore it is called <s>ātman</s> (Self).' Enumeration of conflicting views: the doctrine of the void belongs to the <s>Mādhyamikas</s>; the doctrine of momentary consciousness belongs to the <s>Yogācāras</s>; the doctrine of momentary external objects inferred from the form of cognition belongs to the <s>Sautrāntikas</s>; the doctrine of momentary external objects belongs to the <s>Vaibhāṣikas</s>; the doctrine that the Self is the body belongs to the <s>Cārvākas</s>; the doctrine that the Self is distinct from the body yet a transformation of the body belongs to the <s>Digambaras</s> — and so on, this should be understood.

children.text: 2 janmādyādhikaraṇam / sū. 2.
children.translated_text: 2. The <s>Janmādi Adhikaraṇa</s> (Topic of Origin and So Forth). <s>Sūtra</s> 2.

children.text:
brahmajijñāsitavyamityuktam /
kiṃlakṣaṇaṃ punastadbrahmetyata āha bhagavānsūtrakāraḥ-
children.translated_text: It has been stated that <s>Brahman</s> is to be inquired into. What, then, are the defining characteristics of that <s>Brahman</s>? To this, the blessed <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the <s>sūtras</s>) says —

children.text: janmādyasya yataḥ | BBs_1,1.2 |
children.translated_text: That from which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed]. | <s>BBs</s> 1,1.2 |

children.text:
janmotpattirādirasyeti tadguṇasaṃvijñāno bahuvrīhiḥ /
janmasthitibhaṅgaṃ samāsārthaḥ /
janmanaścāditvaṃ śrutinirdeśāpekṣaṃ vastuvṛttāpekṣaṃ ca /
śrutinirdeśastāvat 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante' (taitti.3.1) ityasminvākye janmasthitipralayānāṃ kramadarśanāt /
vastuvṛttamapi, janmanā labdhasattākasya dharmiṇaḥ sthitiprayasaṃbhavāt /
asyeti pratyakṣādisaṃnidhāpitasya dharmiṇa idamā nirdeśaḥ /
ṣaṣṭhī janmādidharmasaṃbandhārthā /
children.translated_text: The genitive is for expressing the relation of the qualities — origin and so forth — [to their substrate].

children.text: yata iti kāraṇanirdeśaḥ asya jagato nāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākṛtasyānekakartṛbhoktṛsaṃyuktasya pratiniyatadeśakālanimittakriyāphalāśrayasya manasāpyacintyaracanārūpasya janmasthitibhaṅgaṃ yataḥ sarvajñātsarvaśakteḥ kāraṇādbhavati tadbrahmeti vākyaśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'From which' (<s>yataḥ</s>) is the indication of the cause. Of this world — which is differentiated by names and forms, conjoined with numerous agents and experiencers, which serves as the locus of actions, fruits, and their fixed times, places, and occasions, and whose arrangement is inconceivable even by the mind — the origin, continuance, and dissolution proceed from the omniscient, omnipotent cause — that is <s>Brahman</s>: this is the completion of the sentence.

children.text: anyeṣāmapi bhāvavikārāṇāṃ triṣvevāntarbhāva iti janmasthitināśānāmiha grahaṇam /
children.translated_text: Since all other modifications of existence are included within these three, origin, continuance, and destruction are taken here [as representative].

children.text: yāskaparipaṭhitānāṃ tu 'jāyate 'sti' ityādīnāṃ grahaṇe teṣāṃ jagataḥ sthitkāle saṃbhāvyamānatvānmūlakāraṇādutpattisthitināśāṃ jagato na gṛhītāḥ syurityāśaṅkyeta, tanmā śaṅkīti yotpattirbrahmastatraiva sthitiḥ pralayaśca ta eva gṛhyante //
children.translated_text: But if the [six modifications] enumerated by <s>Yāska</s> — 'is born,' 'exists,' and so forth — were taken, then since those [such as growth, transformation, and decay] are conceivable during the period of the world's continuance, one might suspect that the origin, continuance, and destruction of the world from the root cause are not grasped — lest this be suspected: the very [modifications of] origin from <s>Brahman</s>, continuance in it, and dissolution into it are what is grasped.

'<s>Janma</s>' (origin, birth) is the beginning (<s>ādi</s>) of this — this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound expressing the quality of the referent. The meaning of the compound is: origin, continuance, and dissolution. And the primacy of 'origin' is based both on scriptural indication and on the nature of things. The scriptural indication is that in the passage 'that from which these beings are born' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 3.1), origin, continuance, and dissolution are seen in sequence. The nature of things [shows it] too, because continuance and dissolution are possible only for a thing that has acquired existence through origin. 'Of this' (<s>asya</s>) is a demonstrative reference to the entity made present through perception and other [means of knowledge].

children.text:
na yathoktaviśeṣaṇasya jagato yathoktaviśeṣaṇamīśvaraṃ muktvānyataḥ pradhānādacetanādaṇubhyo 'bhāvātsaṃsāriṇo vā utpattyādi saṃbhāvayituṃ śakyam /
naca svabhāvataḥ, viśiṣṭadeśakālanimittānāmihopādānāt /
etadevānumānaṃ saṃsārivyatirikteśvarāstitvādisādhanaṃ manyanta īśvarakāraṇinaḥ /
children.translated_text: It is not possible to attribute the origin and so on of a world possessing the aforesaid characteristics to anything other than a Lord possessing the aforesaid characteristics — not to the <s>Pradhāna</s>, which is unconscious, nor to atoms, nor to non-existence, nor to a transmigrating soul. Nor [can it arise] from its own nature, because specific conditions of place, time, and cause are here accepted [as necessary]. The proponents of God as the cause consider this very inference to be the means of establishing the existence of a Lord distinct from the transmigrating soul.

children.text: nanvihāpi tadevopanyastaṃ janmādisūtre /
children.translated_text: But is not this very [inference] presented here too, in the <s>Janmādi Sūtra</s>?

children.text:
na /
vedāntavākyakusumagrathanārthatvātsūtrāṇām /
vedāntavākyāni hi sūtrairudāhṛtya vicāryante /
vākyārthavicāraṇādhyavasānanivṛttā /
satsu tu vedāntavākyeṣu jagato janmādikāraṇavādiṣu tadarthagrahaṇadārḍhāyānumānamapi vedāntavākyāvirodhi pramāṇaṃ bhavanna nivāryate, śrutyaiva ca sahāyatvena tarkasyābhyupetatvāt /
tathāhi- 'śrotavyo mantavyaḥ' (bṛha. 2.4.5) iti śrutiḥ 'paṇḍito medhāvī gandhārānevopasaṃpadyetaivamevehācāryavānpuruṣo veda' (chāndo.6.14.2) iti ca puruṣabuddhisāhāyyamātmanor dāyati /
na dharmajijñāsāyāmiva śrutyādayo 'nubhavādayaśca yathāsaṃbhavamiha pramāṇaṃ anubhavāvasānatvādbhūtavastuviṣayatvācca brahmajñānasya /
kartavye hi viṣaye nānubhavāpekṣāstīti śrutyādīnāmeva prāmāṇyaṃ syātpuruṣādhīnātmalābhatvācca kartavyasya /
kartumakartumanyathā vā kartuṃ śakyaṃ laukikaṃ vaidikaṃ ca karma, yathāśvena gacchati, padbhyāmanyathā vā, na vā gacchatīti /
tathā 'atirātre ṣoḍaśinaṃ gṛhṇāti, nātirātre ṣoḍaśinaṃ gṛhṇāti', 'udite juhoti, anudite juhoti' iti vidhipratiṣedhāścātrārthavantaḥ syuḥ, vikalpotsargāpavādāśca /
natu vastvevaṃ naivamasti nāstīti vā vikalpyate /
vikalpanāstu puruṣabuddhyapekṣāḥ /
na vastuyāthātmyajñānaṃ puruṣabuddhyapekṣam /
kiṃ tarhi vastutantrameva tat /
nahi sthāṇāvekasmisthāṇurvā puruṣo 'nyo veti tattvajñānaṃ bhavati /
tatra puruṣo 'nyo veti mithyājñānam /
sthāṇureveti tattvajñānaṃ,vastutantratvāt /
evaṃ bhūtavastuviṣayāṇāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ vastutantram /
tatraivaṃ sati brahmajñānamapi vastutantrameva, bhūtavastu viṣayatvāt /
children.translated_text: No. Because the <s>sūtras</s> have the purpose of stringing together the flowers of <s>Vedānta</s> statements. For the <s>Vedānta</s> statements are cited by the <s>sūtras</s> and examined. The investigation of the meaning of statements comes to a conclusion. But when there are <s>Vedānta</s> statements declaring that the cause of the world's origination and such [is <s>Brahman</s>], inference too — being a valid means of knowledge not contradicting the <s>Vedānta</s> statements — is not barred for the purpose of strengthening the grasp of their meaning, since reasoning is accepted by scripture itself as an aid. For thus: 'It should be heard, it should be reflected upon' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.5) — this is the scripture; and 'A wise, intelligent person would reach <s>Gandhāra</s>; just so, a person who has a teacher knows' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.14.2) — this shows the assistance of human reasoning regarding the self. It is not the case that scripture and such, along with experience and such, are the valid means of knowledge here as they are in the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> — each according to its applicability — because the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> culminates in experience and has as its object an existing reality. For in matters that are to be done, there is no dependence on experience, so only scripture and such would have validity, since what is to be done depends on human will for its accomplishment. Worldly and Vedic action can be done, not done, or done otherwise — just as one may go by horse, on foot, by other means, or not go at all. Similarly, 'At the <s>Atirātra</s> one takes the <s>ṣoḍaśin</s> cup; at the <s>Atirātra</s> one does not take the <s>ṣoḍaśin</s> cup'; 'One offers when the sun has risen; one offers when the sun has not risen' — injunctions and prohibitions, options, general rules and exceptions would be meaningful here. But a real thing is not subject to the alternative 'it is thus or not thus, it exists or does not exist.' Alternatives depend on human cognition. The knowledge of the true nature of a thing does not depend on human cognition. Rather, it depends entirely on the thing itself. For regarding a single post, the true knowledge is not 'it is a post, or a person, or something else.' Therein, 'it is a person or something else' is false knowledge. 'It is a post itself' is true knowledge, because it depends on the thing. Thus, the validity of means of knowledge regarding existing realities depends on the thing itself. This being so, the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> too depends entirely on the thing, because it has an existing reality as its object.

children.text: nanu bhūtavastutve brahmaṇaḥ pramāṇāntaraviṣayatvameveti vedāntavākyavicāraṇānarthikaiva prāptā /
children.translated_text: But if <s>Brahman</s> is an existing reality, then it would be an object of other means of knowledge — so the examination of <s>Vedānta</s> statements would be purposeless. This is the objection raised.

children.text:
na /
indriyāviṣayatvena saṃbandhāgrahaṇāt /
svabhāvato viṣayaviṣayāṇīndriyāṇi, na brahmaviṣayāṇi /
sati hīndriyaviṣayatve brahmaṇa-, idaṃ brahmaṇā saṃbaddhaṃ kāryamiti gṛhyeta /
kāryamātrameva tu gṛhyamāṇaṃ kiṃ brahmaṇā saṃbaddhaṃ kimanyena kenacidvā saṃbaddhamiti na śakyaṃ niścetum /
tasmājanmādisūtraṃ nānumānopanyāsārthaṃ, kiṃ tarhi vedāntavākyaprardānārtham /
kiṃ punastadvedāntavākyaṃ yatsūtreṇaiha lilakṣayiṣitam /
'bhṛgurvai vāruṇiḥ /
varuṇaṃ pitaramupasasāra /
adhīhi bhagavo brahmeti' /
ityupakramya- 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante /
yena jātāni jīvanti /
yatprayantyabhisaṃviśanti /
tadvijijñāsasva /
tadbrahmeti' /
(taitti. 3.1) /
tasya ca nirṇayavākyam- 'ānandāddhyeva khalvimāni bhūtāni jāyante /
children.translated_text: And the concluding statement of that [passage] is: 'From <s>Ānanda</s> (bliss) indeed are these beings born;

children.text: ānandena jātāni jīvanti /
children.translated_text: by <s>Ānanda</s>, once born, they live;

children.text: ānandaṃ prayantyabhisaṃviśanti' /
children.translated_text: into <s>Ānanda</s>, departing, they enter'

children.text: (taitti. 3.6) anyānyāpyevañjātīyakāni vākyāni nityāśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvasarvajñasvarūpakāraṇaviṣayāṇyudāhartavyāni // 2 //
children.translated_text: (<s>Taittirīya</s> 3.6). Other statements of this kind, whose subject is the cause that is by nature eternally pure, awakened, and free, and whose essential nature is omniscience, should also be cited. // 2 //

No. Because, since [<s>Brahman</s>] is not an object of the senses, the relation [between <s>Brahman</s> and the world] cannot be grasped. The senses by nature have [their own] sense-objects as objects, not <s>Brahman</s> as their object. For if <s>Brahman</s> were an object of the senses, one could grasp: 'This effect is connected with <s>Brahman</s>.' But when only the effect is grasped, it cannot be determined whether it is connected with <s>Brahman</s> or with something else. Therefore, the <s>sūtra</s> on origination and such is not for the purpose of presenting an inference, but rather for indicating the <s>Vedānta</s> statement. What then is that <s>Vedānta</s> statement that the <s>sūtra</s> wished to indicate here? '<s>Bhṛgu</s>, the son of <s>Varuṇa</s>, approached his father <s>Varuṇa</s> [and said]: "Teach me, revered sir, <s>Brahman</s>."' Having thus begun — 'That from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, that into which, departing, they enter — seek to know that; that is <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 3.1).

children.text: FN: 'idaṃ sarvamasṛjata yadidaṃ kiñca' iti pratyakṣam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: 'He created all this, whatever there is' — this is direct [evidence].

children.text: 3 śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇam / sū. 3
children.translated_text: 3. The <s>Śāstrayonitva</s> (Scripture as Source) Section / <s>Sūtra</s> 3

children.text: jagatkāraṇatvaprardānena sarvajñaṃ brahmetyupakṣiptaṃ tadeva draḍhayannāha-
children.translated_text: Having introduced [the thesis] that <s>Brahman</s> is omniscient, through the indication that it is the cause of the world, he now reinforces that very [point] —

children.text: śāstrayonitvāt | BBs_1,1.3 |
children.translated_text: <s>Śāstrayonitvāt</s> — Because [<s>Brahman</s>] is the source of scripture. | <s>BBs</s> 1.1.3 |

children.text:
mahata ṛgvedādeḥ śāstrasyānekavidyāsthānopabṛṃhitasya pradīpavatsarvārthāvadyotinaḥ sarvajñakalpasya yoniḥ kāraṇaṃbrahma /
nahīdṛśasya śāstrasyargvedādikṣaṇasya sarvajñaguṇānvitasya sarvajñādanyataḥ saṃbhavo 'sti /
yadyadvistarārthaṃ śāstraṃ yasmātpuruṣaviśeṣātsaṃbhavati, yathā vyākaraṇādi pāṇinyāderjñeyaikadeśārthamapi sa tato 'pyadhikataravijñāna iti prasiddhaṃ loke /
kimu vaktavyamanekaśākhābhedabhinnasya devatiryaṅmanuṣyavarṇāśramadipravibhāgahetor ṛgvedādyākhyasya sarvajñānākarasyāprayatnenaiva līlānyayena puruṣaniḥśvāsavadyasmānmahato bhūtādyoneḥ saṃbhavaḥ, 'asya mahato bhūtasya niḥśvasitametadyadṛgvedaḥ' (bṛha. 2.4.10) ityādiśruteḥ /
tasya mahato bhūtasya niratiśayaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ sarvaśaktimattvaṃ ceti /
athavā yathokta ṛgvedādiśāstraṃ yoniḥ kāraṇaṃ pramāṇamasya brahmaṇo yathāvatsvarūpādhigame /
śāstrādeva praṇāṇājjagato janmādikāraṇaṃ brahmādhigamyata ityabhiprāyaḥ /
śāstramudāhṛtaṃ pūrvasūtre- 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante' ityādi /
children.translated_text: The source (<s>yoni</s>), the cause, of the great scripture beginning with the <s>Ṛgveda</s> — which is enriched by numerous branches of knowledge, which illuminates all things like a lamp, and which is virtually omniscient — is <s>Brahman</s>. For such a scripture as the <s>Ṛgveda</s> and so forth, endowed with the qualities of omniscience, cannot possibly originate from anyone other than the omniscient. Whatever extensive scripture originates from whatever particular person — as grammar and such originate from <s>Pāṇini</s> and others, even though dealing with only a portion of what is to be known — it is well-known in the world that he possesses even greater knowledge than that. What then need be said of the great being from whom, effortlessly, as if in sport, like the breathing of a person, originates the scripture called <s>Ṛgveda</s> and so forth — which is divided into many branches, which is the basis for distinguishing gods, animals, humans, <s>varṇas</s>, <s>āśramas</s>, and such — this being the treasury of all knowledge? As scripture states: 'The <s>Ṛgveda</s> is the breath of this great being' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.10), and so forth. Of that great being, there is unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence. Alternatively: the scripture of the <s>Ṛgveda</s> and such, as described, is the source (<s>yoni</s>), the cause, the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for the proper ascertainment of the true nature of this <s>Brahman</s>. The purport is that <s>Brahman</s>, the cause of the world's origination and such, is ascertained from scripture alone as the means of valid knowledge. The scripture was cited in the previous <s>sūtra</s>: 'That from which these beings are born,' and so forth.

children.text: kimarthaṃ tarhīdaṃ sūtraṃ, yāvatā pūrvasūtra evaivañjātīyakaṃ śāstramudāharatā śāstrayonitvaṃ brahmaṇo darśitam /
children.translated_text: What then is the purpose of this <s>sūtra</s>, when the scripture-source-nature of <s>Brahman</s> was already shown in the previous <s>sūtra</s> itself by citing such a scripture?

children.text: ucyate- tatra pūrvasūtrākṣareṇa spaṣṭaṃ śāstrasyānupādānājjanmādi kevalamanumānamupanyastamityāśaṅkyeta tāmāśaṅkāṃ nirvartayitumidaṃ sūtraṃ pravavṛte śāstrayonitvāditi // 3 //
children.translated_text: The answer: Since in the previous <s>sūtra</s>, because scripture was not explicitly taken up in its wording, it might be suspected that only bare inference about origination and such was being presented — to remove that doubt, this <s>sūtra</s> was introduced: '<s>śāstrayonitvāt</s>' (because of being the source of scripture). // 3 //

children.text:
FN: upabṛṃhaṇīyāścatvāro vedāḥ tatra /
purāṇāni sṛṣṭyādipratipādakavākyāni parakṛtipurākalparūpānarthavādāṃśca prādhānyenopabṛṃhayanti prasaṅgādadvaitabhāgaṃ karmabhāgaṃ ca /
nyāyaśāstraṃ tu pramāṇaprameyalakṣaṇānirūpaṇena padārthānvivicya jñāpayadupabṛṃhayati /
pūrvottaramīmāṃse tu tātparyanirṇayadvāropayukte /
dharmaśāstraṃ śrutamanusmṛtiṃ vā vidhibhāgamupabṛṃhayati /
śikṣā sthānakaraṇādinirūpaṇadvārā svādhyāyo 'dhyetavya iti vidhyarthamupabṛṃhayati /
kalpāstu prayoganirūpaṇārthamupayuktāḥ /
vyākaraṇaṃ tāvadasminnarthe idaṃ padaṃ sādhviti padārthānvyākaroti /
niruktaṃ teṣu teṣu padeṣu yaugikamarthaṃ pradarśayati /
chandaḥśāstraṃ vedagatāngāyatryādichandān lakṣaṇamukhena viśadayati /
jyotiṣaṃ paurṇamāsyāṃ jayeddetāmāvāsyāyāmamāvāsyayā yajetetyādinopāttaṃ kālaviśeṣaṃ vyavasthāpayati /
tathāca tattaddeśavyākhyānāya bahavo maharṣayaḥ purāṇādinibandhapraṇetāro yatra pravṛttāstasya mahattvaṃ vyaktameva /
children.translated_text: Footnote: The four <s>Vedas</s> are to be supplemented in this context. The <s>Purāṇas</s> supplement primarily the statements teaching creation and such, and the <s>arthavāda</s> portions dealing with ancient events of others' doings, and incidentally the non-dualism section and the ritual section. The science of logic (<s>Nyāya</s>) supplements by discriminating and revealing categories through the determination of the characteristics of means and objects of knowledge. The prior and later <s>Mīmāṃsās</s> are useful as means for determining the purport. <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> supplements the injunctive portion — whether heard [directly] or recalled through <s>smṛti</s>. <s>Śikṣā</s> (phonetics) supplements the injunction 'one's own study should be recited' through the determination of places of articulation and such. The <s>Kalpas</s> (ritual manuals) are useful for determining the application of rituals. Grammar discriminates word-meanings as correct in this or that sense. <s>Nirukta</s> (etymology) shows the etymological meaning of various words. The science of prosody (<s>Chandas</s>) clarifies the meters found in the <s>Vedas</s> — <s>Gāyatrī</s> and such — through their characteristics. <s>Jyotiṣa</s> (astronomy) determines the specific times taken up in statements like 'one should sacrifice on the full moon' and 'one should sacrifice on the new moon with the <s>amāvāsyā</s> rite.' And that many great sages — composers of <s>Purāṇas</s> and treatises — have engaged in explaining those respective topics clearly shows its greatness.

children.text:
vistararūpor'tho dharmo yasyeti vigrahaḥ /
vistṛtamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The analysis is: [<s>Brahman</s>] is that whose meaning — namely <s>dharma</s> — has an extensive form. The meaning is: it is extensive.

children.text: 4 samanvayādhikaraṇam / sū. 4
children.translated_text: 4. The <s>Samanvaya</s> (Harmony) Section / <s>Sūtra</s> 4

children.text:
kathaṃ punarbrahmaṇaḥ sāstrapramāṇakatvamucyate, yāvatā, ' āmnāyasya kriyārthatvādānarthakyamatadarthānām' /
(jai.sū. 1.2.1) iti kriyāparatvaṃ śāstrasya pradarśitim /
ato vedāntānāmānarthakyaṃ, akriyārthatvāt /
children.translated_text: But how can it be said that <s>Brahman</s> is known through scripture as a means of valid knowledge, when [the <s>Pūrva Mīmāṃsā</s> states]: 'Because the <s>Āmnāya</s> (Veda) has action as its purpose, those statements not serving that purpose are meaningless' (<s>Jaimini Sūtra</s> 1.2.1) — thus showing that scripture is directed toward action? Therefore, <s>Vedānta</s> statements would be meaningless, since they do not have action as their purpose.

children.text:
kartṛdevatādiprakāśanārthatvena vā kriyāvidhiśeṣatvaṃ, upāsanādikriyāntavidhānārthatvaṃ vā /
nahi pariniṣṭhitavastupratipādanaṃ saṃbhavati, pratyakṣādiviṣayatvātpariniṣṭhitavastunaḥ /
tatpratipādane ca heyopādeyarahite puruṣārthābhāvāt /
ata eva 'so 'rodīt' ityevamādināmānarthakyaṃ mā bhūditi 'vidhinā tvekavākyatvātstutyarthena vidhinā syuḥ' /
(jai.sū. 1.2.7) iti stāvakatvenārthavattvamuktam /
mantrāṇāṃ ca 'iṣe tvā' ityādīnāṃ kriyātatsādhanābhidhāyitvena karmasamavāyitvamuktam /
na Dvacidapi vedavākyānāṃ vidhisaṃsparśamantareṇārthavattā dṛṣṭopapannā vā /
na ca pariniṣṭhite vastusvarūpe vidhiḥ saṃbhavati, kriyāviṣayatvādvidheḥ /
tasmātkarmāpekṣitakartṛsvarūpadevatādiprakāśanena kriyāvidhiśeṣatvaṃ vedāntānām /
atha prakaraṇāntarabhayānnaitadabhyupagamyate tathāpi svavākyagatopāsanādikarmaparatvam /
tasāmānna brahmaṇaḥ śāstrayonitvamiti prāpte ucyate-
children.translated_text: [They might be meaningful] either as subsidiary to injunctions of action, by illuminating the agent, deity, and such; or as having the purpose of enjoining actions such as meditation and the like. For the communication of an established reality is not possible, since an established reality is the object of perception and such [direct means of knowledge]. And in communicating that, since it is devoid of what is to be accepted or rejected, there would be no human purpose. For this very reason, lest statements like 'He wept' and such be meaningless, it was stated: 'But by virtue of forming a single sentence with an injunction, they would serve as praise for the injunction' (<s>Jaimini Sūtra</s> 1.2.7) — thus their meaningfulness is stated as being laudatory. And of <s>mantras</s> beginning with '<s>iṣe tvā</s>' and so forth, their connection with ritual action was stated through their designation of the action and its means. Nowhere is the meaningfulness of any Vedic statement seen or established without connection to an injunction. And an injunction is not possible regarding the established nature of a thing, because an injunction has action as its object. Therefore, <s>Vedānta</s> statements are subsidiary to injunctions of action, through illuminating the nature of the agent, deity, and such that are required by ritual. Or, if this is not accepted for fear of [the topic] belonging to another context, then at least they are directed toward actions such as meditation contained in their own statements. Therefore, the scripture-source-nature of <s>Brahman</s> is not established — this is the position reached. The reply is —

children.text:
FN: āmnāyasyeti pūrvapakṣam /
asyārthaḥ - āmnāyasya vedasya kriyāpratipādanaparatvādatadarthānāmakriyārthānāṃ 'so 'rodī' dityādivākyānāmānarthakatvaṃ /
tasmādanityamaniyataṃ vedānāṃ prāmāṇyamucyate /
tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthena samanvaya iti siddhāntaḥ /
tatteṣu vedavākyeṣu bhūtānāṃ siddārthapratipādakavākyānāṃ kriyārthena kriyāpratipādakavākyena 'barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyaṃ, paśunā yajete' tyādinā sahānvayaḥ /
tathāca nindyatvādyarthapūraṇenānvaye kṛte kriyāparatvasiddhyā prāmāṇyaṃ siddham /
siddhavastujñānātphalabhāvādevetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Āmnāyasya</s>' and so on is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (objection). Its meaning is: because the <s>Āmnāya</s> (Veda) is directed toward teaching action, the statements not serving that purpose — the non-action-oriented statements like 'He wept' and such — are meaningless. Therefore it is said that the authority of the <s>Vedas</s> is non-eternal and indeterminate. 'Their connection with action-purpose is the established conclusion' — of those Vedic statements, the statements that teach established facts have their connection (<s>anvaya</s>) with statements that teach action, such as 'Silver should not be given on the sacrificial grass' and 'One should sacrifice with an animal.' And thus, when the connection is made through supplying the purpose of censure and such, the authority [of such statements] is established through establishing their orientation toward action. The meaning is: precisely because there is no result from the knowledge of an established fact [alone].

children.text: tat tu samanvayāt | BBs_1,1.4 |
children.translated_text: <s>Tat tu samanvayāt</s> — But that [is known from scripture], because of consistent harmonization. | <s>BBs</s> 1.1.4 |

children.text:
tu śabdaḥ pūrvapakṣavyāvṛttyarthaḥ /
tadbrahma sarvajñaṃ sarvaśakti jagadutpatti sthitilayakāraṇaṃ vedāntaśāstrādevāvagamyate /
katham, samanvayāt /
sarveṣu hi vedānteṣu vākyāni tātparyeṇaitasyārthasya pratipādakatvena samanugatāni /
'sadeva somyedamagra āsīt' /
'ekamevādvitāyam' /
(chāndo. 6.2.1) 'ātmāvā idameka evāgra āsīt' /
(aita. 2.1.1.1) 'tadetadbrahmāpūrvamanaparamanantaramabāhyam' /
children.translated_text: The word '<s>tu</s>' (but) is for distinguishing from the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (opponent's position). That <s>Brahman</s> — omniscient, omnipotent, the cause of the origination, sustenance, and dissolution of the world — is known from the <s>Vedānta</s> scripture alone. How? Because of <s>samanvaya</s> (consistent harmonization). For in all <s>Vedānta</s> texts, the statements are consistently directed toward teaching this very meaning as their purport. 'Being alone, O dear one, this was in the beginning' — 'one only, without a second' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.2.1); '<s>Ātman</s> alone was this, one only, in the beginning' (<s>Aitareya</s> 2.1.1.1); 'That is <s>Brahman</s>, without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior.'

kuta etat /

children.translated_text: 'This Self is <s>Brahman</s>, the experiencer of all' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.5.19); 'This immortal <s>Brahman</s> is in front' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.2.11) — and so forth. And when the words occurring in those [passages] have an ascertained, consistent meaning (<s>samanvaya</s>) regarding the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, it is not proper to imagine some other meaning, because that would lead to the abandonment of what is heard and the fabrication of what is not heard. Nor can it be determined that their purport is to teach the nature of an agent, because of scriptural passages such as 'then by what would one see what?' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.13), which negate action, instrument, and result. Nor is <s>Brahman</s>, though of the nature of an established reality, an object of perception and such means of knowledge, because the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and the Self — as in 'You are That' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.7) — cannot be known without scripture. As for the objection that instruction would be purposeless because [<s>Brahman</s>] is devoid of what is to be rejected and accepted — this is no fault, because the purpose of human life is accomplished through the elimination of all afflictions that comes from the very knowledge of the identity of the Self with <s>Brahman</s>, which is devoid of what is to be rejected and accepted. And there is no contradiction in the teaching of deities and such having the purpose of meditation prescribed in their own [textual] context. But it is not possible for <s>Brahman</s> to be subsidiary to an injunction of meditation in the same way, because in [the realization of] oneness, since it is devoid of what is to be rejected and accepted, the destruction of the dualistic cognition of action, agent, and such follows. For the dualistic cognition, once overthrown by the cognition of oneness, cannot arise again, so that <s>Brahman</s> could be regarded as subsidiary to an injunction of meditation. Even though elsewhere the validity of Vedic statements is not seen without connection with injunction, nevertheless, since the knowledge of the Self culminates in its own result, the authority of scripture concerning that [<s>Brahman</s>] cannot be denied. And the authority of scripture is not something to be known through inference, such that it would require an example seen elsewhere. Therefore, it is established that <s>Brahman</s> is knowable through scriptural authority. Here, others object in turn: even though <s>Brahman</s> is knowable through scriptural authority, nevertheless, scripture presents <s>Brahman</s> only as the object of an injunction of apprehension (<s>pratipattividhi</s>). Just as the sacrificial post, the <s>Āhavanīya</s> fire, and such, though not of ordinary experience, are presented by scripture as subsidiary to injunctions — so too [with <s>Brahman</s>]. How so? Because scripture has the purpose of [directing] activity and cessation. Thus, those who know the purport of scripture say: 'For it is seen that its purpose is the knowledge of action'; 'An injunction (<s>codanā</s>) is a statement that impels to action'; 'Instruction is the knowledge of that' (<s>Jaiminisūtra</s> 1.1.5); 'The scriptural tradition of those [substances] is for the purpose of action' (<s>Jaiminisūtra</s> 1.1.25); 'Because scripture has the purpose of action, what does not serve that purpose is meaningless' —

children.text:
(jai.sū. 1.2.1) itica /
ataḥ puruṣaṃ Dvacidviṣayaviśeṣe pravartayatkutaścidviṣayaviśeṣānnivartayaccārthavacchāstram /
taccheṣatayā cānyadupayuktam /
tatsāmānyādvedāntānāmapi tathaivārthavattvaṃ syāt /
sati ca vidhiparatve yathā svargādikāmasyāgnihotrādisādhanaṃ vidhīyata evamamṛtatvakāmasya brahmajñānaṃ vidhīyata iti yuktam /
children.translated_text: (<s>Jaiminisūtra</s> 1.2.1) — and so forth. Therefore, scripture is meaningful when it impels a person to engage in some particular object or restrains [him] from some particular object. And anything else is useful as subsidiary to that. By analogy with that general [principle], the <s>Vedānta</s> passages too would have their meaningfulness in the same way. And given that their purport is injunctive, just as for one who desires heaven, <s>Agnihotra</s> and such are enjoined as means — so too it is reasonable that for one who desires immortality, the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is enjoined.

children.text:
nanviha jijñāsyavailakṣaṇyamuktam- karmakāṇḍe bhavyo dharmo jijñāsya iha tu bhūtaṃ nityanivṛttaṃ brahma jijñāsyamiti /
tatra dharmajñānaphalādanuṣṭhānāpekṣādvilakṣaṇaṃ brahmajñānaphalaṃ bhavitumarhati /
nārhatyevaṃ bhavitum /
kāryavidhiprayukttasyaiva brahmaṇaḥ pratipādyamānatvāt /
'ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ' (bṛha. 2.4.5) iti /
'ya ātmāpahatapāpmā-so 'nvevyaḥ sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ' (chāndo. 8.7.1) 'ātmetyovopāsīta' (bṛha.1.4.7) 'ātmānameva lokamupāsata' (bṛha. 1.4.15) /
'brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati' (muṇḍa. 3.2.9) ityādividhāneṣu satsu ko 'sāvātmā kiṃ tadbrahma ityākāṅkṣāyāṃ tatsvarūpasamarpaṇena sarve vedāntā upayuktāḥ- 'nityaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvagato nityatṛpto nityāśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvo vijñānamānandaṃ brahma. ityevamādayaḥ /
tadupāsanācca śāstradṛṣṭo 'pi mokṣaḥ phalaṃ bhaviṣyatīti /
kartavyavidhyananupraveśe vastumātrakathane hānopādānasaṃbhavāt, saptadvīpā vasumatī, rājāsau gacchatītyādivākyavadvedāntavākyānāmānarthakyameva syāt /
children.translated_text: But here, the difference in what is to be inquired into has been stated: in the <s>Karmakāṇḍa</s>, <s>dharma</s> — which is yet to come into being — is to be inquired into; but here, <s>Brahman</s> — which is already existent and eternally accomplished — is to be inquired into. Given that, the result of the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> should be different from the result of the knowledge of <s>dharma</s>, which requires [subsequent] performance. [Objection:] It cannot be so different, because <s>Brahman</s> is taught only as what is enjoined through an injunction of action. [They cite:] 'The Self indeed is to be seen' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.5); 'The Self that is free from evil — He is to be sought, He is to be inquired into' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 8.7.1); 'One should meditate on [It] as the Self' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 1.4.7); 'One should meditate on the Self alone as the world' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 1.4.15). Given these injunctions such as 'He who knows <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 3.2.9), when the desire arises — 'Who is this Self? What is this <s>Brahman</s>?' — all the <s>Vedānta</s> passages are useful by presenting its nature: 'Eternal, omniscient, all-pervading, ever-satisfied, of the nature of eternal purity, awareness, and freedom — <s>Brahman</s> is knowledge and bliss' — and such passages. And from meditation on that, liberation too, which is seen in scripture, will be the result. [But we reply:] if there is no entry of an injunction of duty and it is merely a statement of fact, then since there would be no possibility of rejection or acceptance, the <s>Vedānta</s> statements would be entirely purposeless — like the statements 'the earth has seven continents' or 'the king is going.'

children.text:
nanu vastumātrakathane 'pi rajuriyaṃ nāyaṃ sarpa ityādau bhrāntijanitabhītinivartanenārthavattvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ tathehāpyasaṃsāryātmavastukathanena saṃsāritvabhrāntinivartanenārthavattvaṃ syāt /
syādetadevaṃ, yadi rajusvarūpaśravaṇa iva sarpabhrāntiḥ, saṃsāritvabhrāntirbrahmasvarūpaśravaṇamātreṇa nivarteta /
natu nivartate, śrutabrahmaṇo 'pi yathāpūrvaṃ sukhaduḥkhādisaṃsāridharmadarśanāt, 'śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ' (bṛha. 2.4.5) iti ca śravaṇottarakālayormanananididhyāsanayorvidhirdarśanāt /
tasmātpratipattividhiviṣayatayaiva śāstrapramāṇakaṃ brahmābhyupagantavyamiti /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But even in mere statements of fact, meaningfulness is seen — as in 'This is a rope, not a snake,' where the fear born of delusion is removed. Similarly here too, there would be meaningfulness through the removal of the delusion of being a <s>saṃsārin</s> by the statement of the reality of the Self as non-<s>saṃsārin</s>. [Reply:] This would be so if the delusion of being a <s>saṃsārin</s> were removed merely by hearing about the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, just as the delusion about the snake is removed upon hearing about the nature of the rope. But it is not so removed, because even one who has heard about <s>Brahman</s> is seen to experience the properties of <s>saṃsāra</s> — pleasure, pain, and so forth — just as before; and because injunctions of reflection (<s>manana</s>) and meditation (<s>nididhyāsana</s>) after hearing are seen: 'It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.5). Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> must be accepted as knowable through scriptural authority only as the object of an injunction of apprehension — [so they argue].

children.text:
atrābhidhīyate- na /
karmabrahmavidyāphalayorvailakṣaṇyāt /
śārīraṃ vācikaṃ mānasaṃ ca karma śrutismṛtisiddhaṃ dharmākhyaṃ, yadviṣayā jijñāsā 'athāto dharmajijñāsā' (jai.sū. 1.1.1) iti sūtritā, adharmo 'pi hiṃsādiḥ pratiṣedhacodanālakṣaṇatvājjijñāsyaḥ parihārāya /
tayoścodanālakṣaṇayorarthānarthayordharmādharmayoḥ phale pratyakṣe sukhaduḥkhe śarīravāṅmanobhirevopabhujyamāne viṣayendriyasaṃyogajanye brahmādiṣu sthāvarānteṣu prasiddhe /
manuṣyatvādārabhya brahmānteṣu dehavatsu sukhatāratamyamanuśrūyate /
tataśca taddhetordharmasya tāratamyaṃ gamyate /
dharmatāratamyādadhikāritāratamyam /
prasiddhaṃ cārthitvasārmathyādikṛtamadhikāritāratamyam /
tathāca yāgādyanuṣṭhāyināmeva vidyāsamādhiviśeṣāduttareṇa pathā gamanaṃ, kevalairiṣṭāpūrtadattasādhanairdhūmādikrameṇa dakṣiṇena pathā gamanaṃ, tatrāpi sukhatāratamyaṃ tatsādhanatāratamyaṃ ca śāstrāt 'yāvatsaṃpātamuṣitvā' (chāndo. 5.10.5)
children.translated_text: To this we say: No. Because the results of ritual action and the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> are different. Bodily, vocal, and mental action, established by <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>, called <s>dharma</s> — concerning which the inquiry was formulated in the <s>sūtra</s> 'Then, therefore, the inquiry into <s>dharma</s>' (<s>Jaiminisūtra</s> 1.1.1) — and <s>adharma</s> too, such as violence, since it is characterized by prohibitory injunction, is to be inquired into for the sake of avoidance. Of those two — <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — which are characterized by injunction and which are beneficial and harmful respectively, the results are pleasure and pain, which are directly experienced, enjoyed through body, speech, and mind, produced by the contact of senses and objects, and well-known in beings from <s>Brahmā</s> down to stationary beings. A gradation of happiness is heard of in embodied beings from humans up to <s>Brahmā</s>. From that, a gradation in <s>dharma</s>, which is its cause, is understood. From the gradation of <s>dharma</s>, a gradation of qualification [of the agent] is understood. And a gradation of qualification based on desire and capacity is well known. And thus, for those who perform sacrifices and such, going by the northern path is [attained] through the distinction of knowledge and meditation; going by the southern path through the smoke and so forth is [attained] by mere <s>iṣṭāpūrta</s> and gifts as means; and even there, the gradation of happiness and the gradation of its means are understood from scripture: 'having dwelt [there] until [the merit is] exhausted' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 5.10.5) —

children.text:

tathordhvagateṣvadhogateṣu ca dehavatsu duḥkhatāratamyardānāttaddhetoradharmasya pratiṣedhacodanākṣaṇasya tadanuṣṭhāyināṃ ca tāratamye gamyate /

aśarīraṃ vāva santaṃ na priyāpriye spṛśataḥ' (chāndo. 8.12.1) iti priyāpriyasparśanapratiṣedhāccodanālakṣaṇadharmakāryatvaṃ mokṣākhyasyāśarīratvasya pratiṣidhyata iti gamyate /
dharmakāryatve hi priyāpriyasparśanapratiṣedho nopapadyate /
aśarīratvameva dharmakāryamiticenna, tasya svābhāvikatvāt /
'aśarīraṃ śarīreśvanavastheṣvavasthitam /
mahāntaṃ vibhumātmānaṃ matvā dhīro na śocati' (kāṭha. 1.2.21) 'aprāṇo hyamanāḥ śubhraḥ' (muṇḍa. 2.1.2) 'asaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣaḥ' (bṛha. 4.3.15) ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
ata evānuṣṭheyakarmaphalavilakṣaṇaṃ mokṣākhyamaśarīratvaṃ nityamiti siddham /

yathā pṛthivyādijagannityatvavādinām /

yatra dharmādharmī saha kāryeṇa kālatrayaṃ ca nopāvartete /
tadedārīratvaṃ mokṣākhyam /
'anyatra dharmādanyatrādharmādanyatrāsmātkṛtākṛtāt /
anyatra bhūtācca bhavyācca' (ka. 2.14)
children.translated_text: — from this it is understood. Likewise, it is understood that even in human beings and such down to hell-dwellers and stationary beings, the traces of happiness are accomplished only through <s>dharma</s> characterized by injunction, existing in gradation. And similarly, in embodied beings going upward and downward, from the gradation of suffering, a gradation in <s>adharma</s> — which is its cause and is characterized by prohibitory injunction — and in those who practice it, is understood. Thus, for those possessed of defects such as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the cycle of <s>saṃsāra</s>, involving the taking up of bodies caused by the gradation of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, and occasioned by the gradation of pleasure and pain, is well established through <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, and reasoning. And thus the <s>Smṛti</s> confirms: 'For one who is embodied, there is no escape from the pleasant and unpleasant' — this describes the nature of <s>saṃsāra</s> as characterized [above]. 'But when one is bodiless, the pleasant and unpleasant do not touch [one]' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 8.12.1) — from the negation of being touched by the pleasant and unpleasant, it is understood that the state of bodilessness called <s>mokṣa</s> is negated as being an effect of <s>dharma</s>. For if it were an effect of <s>dharma</s>, the negation of being touched by the pleasant and unpleasant would not be justified. [Objection:] But bodilessness itself is the effect of <s>dharma</s>. [Reply:] No, because it is [the Self's] own nature. [This is known] from scriptures such as: 'The bodiless [Self], established in bodies that are unstable — the wise one, knowing the great, all-pervading Self, does not grieve' (<s>Kaṭha</s> 1.2.21); 'Without breath, without mind, pure' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.1.2); 'For this <s>Puruṣa</s> is unattached' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.3.15) — and such. For this very reason, it is established that the bodilessness called <s>mokṣa</s>, being different from the result of action to be performed, is eternal. Now, there is a kind of permanence involving transformation, where even when something undergoes modification, the cognition 'this is still that same thing' is not contradicted — as for those who hold the earth and such world to be permanent, and as the <s>guṇas</s> of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>. But this [permanence of <s>Brahman</s>] is ultimate — immutably eternal, all-pervading like space, devoid of all modifications, ever-satisfied, without parts, self-luminous by nature — where <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, together with their effects and the three times, do not return. That bodilessness is what is called <s>mokṣa</s>. 'Other than <s>dharma</s>, other than <s>adharma</s>, other than what is done and not done here, other than what has been and what will be' (<s>Kaṭha</s> 2.14) —

children.text:

tatraivaṃ sati yathoktakarmaphaleṣveva tāratamyāvasthiteṣvanityeṣu kaścidatiśayo mokṣa iti prasajyeta, nityaśca mokṣaḥ sarvairmokṣavādibhirabhyupagamyate, ato na kartavyaśeṣatvena brahmopadeśo yuktaḥ /

'ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān /
na bibheti kutaścayana' (taitti. 2.9) /
'abhayaṃ vai janaka prāpto 'si' (bṛha. 4.2.4) 'tadātmānamevāvedehaṃ brahmāsmīti tasmāttatsarvamabhavat' /
(vājasaneyabrāhmaṇopa. 1.4.10) 'tatra ko mohaḥ kaḥ śoka ekatvamanupayataḥ' (ī(?). 7) ityevamādyāḥ śrutayo brahmavidyānantaraṃ mokṣaṃ darśayantyo madhye kāryāntaraṃ vārayanti /
tathā 'tadvaitatpaśayannṛṣirvāmadevaḥ pratipede 'haṃ manurabhavaṃ sūryaśca' (bṛha. 1.4.10)iti brahmadarśanasarvātmabhāvayormadhye kartavyāntaravāraṇāyodāhāryam /
yathā tiṣṭhangāyatīti tiṣṭhatigāyatyayormadhye tatkartṛkaṃ kāryāntaraṃ nāstīti gamyate /
'tvaṃ hi naḥ pitā yo 'smākamavidyāyāḥ paraṃ pāraṃ tārayasi' (pra. 6.8) 'śrutaṃ hyeva me bhagavaddṛśebhyastarati śokamātmaviditi so 'haṃ bhagavaḥ śocāmi tvaṃ mā bhagavacchokasya pāraṃ tārayatu' (chāndo. 7.1.3) 'tasmai mṛditakaṣāyāya tamasaḥ pāraṃ darśayati bhagavānsanatkumāraḥ' (chāndo. 7.26.2) iti caivamādyāḥ śrutayo mokṣapratibandhanivṛttimātramevātmajñānasya phalaṃ darśayanti /
tathācāryapraṇītaṃ nyāyopabṛṃhitaṃ sūtram- 'duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣamithyājñānānāmuttarottarāpāye tadanantarāpāyādapavargaḥ' (nyā. sū. 1.1.2) iti /
mithyājñānāpāyaśca brahmātmaikatvavijñānādbhavati /

ato na puruṣavyāpāratantrā brahmavidyā /

tathopāstikriyākarmatvapratiṣedho 'pi bhavati- yadvācānabhyuditaṃ yena vāgabhyudyate ityaviṣayatvaṃ brahmaṇa upanyasya, 'tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate' (kena. 1.4) iti /

na /
avidyākalpitabhedanivṛttiparatvācchāstrasya /

avijñātaṃ vijānatāṃ vijñātamavijānatām' (kena. 2.3) 'na dṛṣṭerdraṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ', 'na vijñātervijñātāraṃ vijānīyāḥ' (bṛha. 3.4.2) iti caivamādi /

svātmadharma eva saṃsthirobhīto mokṣaḥ kriyayātmani saṃskriyamāṇe 'bhivyajyate, yathā'darśe nigharṣaṇakriyayā saṃskrayamāṇe bhāsvaratvaṃ dharma iticet /
na /
children.translated_text: — from such <s>śruti</s> passages. Therefore, that <s>Brahman</s> regarding which this inquiry has been undertaken — if it were taught as something to be accomplished through action, and if liberation were admitted as achievable through that action, it would be impermanent. In that case, since it would follow that liberation is merely some degree of superiority within the already hierarchically arranged and impermanent fruits of action as described, it would be impermanent. But liberation is accepted as permanent by all proponents of liberation. Therefore, it is not proper to teach <s>Brahman</s> as something that requires further action. Moreover: 'One who knows <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 3.2.9); 'And his actions are destroyed when that Supreme, both higher and lower, is seen' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.2.8); 'The knower of the bliss of <s>Brahman</s> fears nothing whatsoever' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 2.9); 'O <s>Janaka</s>, you have indeed attained fearlessness' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.2.4); 'He knew the Self: "I am <s>Brahman</s>" — therefore he became everything' (<s>Vājasaneyabrāhmaṇopaniṣad</s> 1.4.10); 'Therein what delusion, what sorrow, for one who perceives oneness?' (<s>Īśā</s> 7) — such <s>śruti</s> passages, showing liberation immediately following knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, preclude any intervening action. Similarly, 'Seeing this, the seer <s>Vāmadeva</s> realized: "I was <s>Manu</s>, and I was <s>Sūrya</s>"' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 1.4.10) — this is cited to preclude any intervening action between the vision of <s>Brahman</s> and the state of being all selves. Just as in 'He sings while standing,' it is understood that between standing and singing there is no other action performed by the same agent. 'For you are our father who carries us across to the far shore of ignorance' (<s>Praśna</s> 6.8); 'I have heard from those like yourself that the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow — I, sir, am in sorrow; please carry me across to the far shore of sorrow' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 7.1.3); 'To him whose impurities have been crushed, the venerable <s>Sanatkumāra</s> shows the far shore of darkness' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 7.26.2) — such <s>śruti</s> passages show that the fruit of Self-knowledge is merely the removal of the obstruction to liberation. And the <s>sūtra</s> composed by the <s>Ācārya</s> [<s>Gautama</s>], supported by reasoning, states: 'From the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defect, and false knowledge, there results <s>apavarga</s> (liberation)' (<s>Nyāya Sūtra</s> 1.1.2). And the removal of false knowledge arises from the realization of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s>. And this realization of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s> is not of the nature of a meditation (<s>saṃpad</s>). As in: 'The mind is indeed infinite, the <s>Viśvedevas</s> are infinite — by that he conquers an infinite world' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 3.1.9). Nor is it of the nature of superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>), as in: 'One should meditate on the mind as <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 3.18.1) and 'The sun is <s>Brahman</s> — this is the instruction' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 3.19.1), where there is a superimposition of the vision of <s>Brahman</s> upon the mind, sun, and such. Nor is it caused by connection with a specific ritual action, as in '<s>Vāyu</s> indeed is the absorber' and '<s>Prāṇa</s> indeed is the absorber' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 4.3.1). Nor is it of the nature of a subsidiary ritual purification (<s>saṃskāra</s>), like the inspection of ghee for a horse sacrifice. For if the realization of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s> were admitted to be of the nature of meditation (<s>saṃpad</s>) and such, the syntactical connection of the words in passages such as 'You are That' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.7), 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 1.4.10), and 'This Self is <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.5.19), which are aimed at establishing the reality of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s>, would be compromised. And passages revealing the fruit as the removal of ignorance, such as 'The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are dissolved' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.2.8), would be obstructed. And statements declaring the attainment of that state, such as 'One who knows <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 3.2.9), would not be consistently explicable on the view of meditation (<s>saṃpad</s>) and such. Therefore, the realization of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s> is not of the nature of meditation and such. Hence, knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is not dependent on human effort. What then? It is dependent on the reality of its object, just like knowledge of objects that are the domain of perception and other valid means of knowledge. For <s>Brahman</s> of such a nature, and for knowledge of it, no involvement of action can be conceived by any reasoning. Nor does <s>Brahman</s> become involved in action by being the object of the act of knowing, because of the denial of its being the object of the act of knowing: 'It is indeed other than the known and also beyond the unknown' (<s>Kena</s> 1.3); and 'By what means should one know that by which all this is known?' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.13). Similarly, there is also a denial of its being the object of the act of meditation — having presented the non-objectivity of <s>Brahman</s> with 'That which is not expressed by speech, by which speech is expressed,' the text states: 'Know that alone as <s>Brahman</s>, not this which people meditate upon' (<s>Kena</s> 1.4). If it be objected that the non-objectivity of <s>Brahman</s> makes the statement 'whose source is scripture' (<s>śāstrayonitva</s>) untenable — no, because scripture aims at removing the distinctions superimposed by ignorance. For scripture does not seek to teach <s>Brahman</s> as an object, as a 'this.' Rather, by presenting it as the inner Self, as non-object, it removes the distinctions of known, knower, knowledge, and so forth, which are superimposed by ignorance. And thus scripture states: 'To whomever it is not known, to him it is known; to whomever it is known, he does not know. It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know' (<s>Kena</s> 2.3); 'You cannot see the seer of seeing,' 'You cannot know the knower of knowing' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 3.4.2) — and so on. Therefore, by removing the state of being a transmigrator superimposed by ignorance and revealing the eternally liberated nature of the Self, there is no defect of impermanence in liberation. But for one for whom liberation is something to be produced, it is reasonable that it would require mental, verbal, or physical action. And in both alternatives — whether liberation is something to be modified or produced — it is certainly impermanent. For nothing that is modified, like curds, or produced, like a pot, is seen to be permanent in the world. Nor is there a need for action [to attain <s>Brahman</s>] as something to be reached, because when <s>Brahman</s> is one's own nature, it is already attained. Even if <s>Brahman</s> were different from one's own nature, it would not be something to be reached, because, being all-pervading, <s>Brahman</s> is eternally attained by everyone, like space. Nor is liberation something to be purified, requiring effort. For purification (<s>saṃskāra</s>) means either adding a quality or removing a defect. It cannot be through adding a quality, because liberation, being of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, which admits no additional excellence, [cannot be improved]. Nor through removing a defect, because liberation, being of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, which is eternally pure, [has no defect to remove]. If it be objected that liberation is a quality inherent in the Self that becomes manifest when the Self is purified through action — just as the quality of brightness becomes manifest in a mirror when it is purified through the action of polishing — no.

children.text:
kriyāśrayatvānupapatterātmanaḥ /
yadāśrayā kriyā tamavikurvatī naivātmānaṃ labhate /
yadyātmā kriyayā vikriyetānityatvamātmanaḥ prasajyeta /
'avikāryo 'yamucyate' iti caivamādīni vākyāni bādhyeran /
taccāniṣṭam /
tasmānna svāśrayā kriyā'tmānaḥ saṃbhavati /
anyāśrayāyāstu kriyāyā aviṣayatvānna tayātmā saṃskriyate /
children.translated_text: Because the Self cannot be the locus of action. Action, being based in a locus, does not find the Self when it does not modify it. If the Self were modified by action, the impermanence of the Self would follow. And passages such as 'It is called immutable' would be contradicted. And that is undesirable. Therefore, no action whose locus is the Self itself is possible. And with regard to action whose locus is something other [than the Self], since the Self is not its object, the Self is not purified by it.

children.text: nanu dehāśrayayā snānācamanayajñopavītādikayā kriyayā dehī saṃskriyamāṇo dṛṣṭaḥ /
children.translated_text: But is it not observed that the embodied self is purified by action whose locus is the body, such as bathing, sipping water, wearing the sacred thread, and sacrificial rites?

children.text:
na /
dehādisaṃhatasyaivāvidyāgṛhītasyātmānaḥ saṃskriyamāṇatvāt /
pratyakṣaṃ hi snānācamanāderdehasamavāyitvam /
tayā dehāśrayayā tatsaṃhata eva kaścidavidyayātmatvena parigṛhītaḥ saṃskriyata iti yuktam /
yathā dehāśrayacikitsānimittena dhātusāmyena tatsaṃhatasya tadabhimānina ārogyaphalaṃ, ahamaroga iti yatra buddhirutpadyate /
evaṃ snānācamanayajñopavītādinā ahaṃ śuddhaḥ saṃskṛta iti yatra buddhirutpadyate sa saṃskriyate /
sa ca dehena saṃhata eva /
tenaiva hyahaṅkartrāhaṃpratyayaviṣayeṇa pratyayinā sarvāḥ kriyā nirvartyante /
tatphalaṃ ca sa evāśnāti, 'tayoranyaḥ pippalaṃ svādvattyanāśnannanyo abhicākāśīti' (muṇḍa. 3.1.1) iti mantravarṇāt /
'ātmendriyamanoyuktaṃ bhoktetyāhurmanīṣiṇaḥ' (kāṭha. 1.3.4) iti ca /
tathāca 'eko devaḥsarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ sarvavyāpī sarvabhūtāntarātmā /
karmādhyakṣaḥ sarvabhūtādhivāsaḥ sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaśca' (śvetā. 6.11) iti /
sa paryagācchukramakāyamantraṇamastrāviraṃśuddhamapāpaviddham /
(ī(?). 8) iti ca /
etau mantrāvanādheyātiśayatāṃ nityaśuddhatāṃ ca brahmaṇo darśayataḥ /
brahmabhāvaśca mokṣaḥ /
tasmānna saṃskāryo 'pi mokṣaḥ /
ato 'nyanmokṣaṃ prati kriyānupraveśadvāraṃ na śakyaṃ kenaciddarśayitum /
tasmāt jñānamekaṃ muktvā kriyāyā gandhamātrasyāpyanupraveśa iha nopapadyate /
children.translated_text: No. Because it is only the self that is conjoined with the body and such, apprehended through ignorance, that is purified. For it is evident that bathing, sipping water, and such belong to the body. It is reasonable that by such body-based action, some entity conjoined with the body and apprehended as the self through ignorance is purified. Just as through the equilibrium of bodily humors caused by treatment based in the body, the fruit of health accrues to one conjoined with the body who identifies with it — [the one] in whom the cognition 'I am healthy' arises. Similarly, through bathing, sipping water, wearing the sacred thread, and such, the one in whom the cognition 'I am pure, I am purified' arises — he is purified. And he is indeed conjoined with the body. For it is by that very ego-maker, that subject of the 'I'-cognition who is the object of the 'I'-notion, that all actions are accomplished. And he alone enjoys their fruits — as stated in the <s>mantra</s>: 'Of these two, one eats the sweet <s>pippala</s> berry, while the other looks on without eating' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 3.1.1); and 'The wise call the enjoyer that which is united with the Self, senses, and mind' (<s>Kaṭha</s> 1.3.4). And likewise: 'The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings, the overseer of actions, dwelling in all beings, the witness, the consciousness, alone, and without qualities' (<s>Śvetāśvatara</s> 6.11); and 'He pervaded — the pure, the bodiless, the unwounded, the sinewless, the bright, the unpierced by evil' (<s>Īśā</s> 8). These two <s>mantras</s> show that <s>Brahman</s> admits no additional excellence and is eternally pure. And the state of <s>Brahman</s> is liberation. Therefore, liberation too is not something to be purified. Hence no one can point to any door of entry for action with respect to liberation other [than knowledge]. Therefore, setting aside knowledge alone, there is no entry here of even a trace of action.

children.text: nanu jñānaṃ nāma mānasī kriyā /
children.translated_text: But is not knowledge a mental action?

children.text:
na /
vailakṣaṇyāt /
kriyā hi nāma sā yatra vastusvarūpanirapekṣaiva codyate, puruṣacittavyāpārādhīnā ca /
yathā yasyai devatāyai havirgṛhītaṃ syāttāṃ manasā dhyāyedvṣaṭkariṣyan iti /
'saṃdhyāṃ manasā dyāyet' (ai.brā. 3.8.1) iti caivamādiṣu /
dhyānaṃ cintanaṃ yadyapi mānasaṃ tathāpi puruṣeṇa kartumakartumanyathā vā kartuṃ śakyaṃ, puruṣatantratvāt /
children.translated_text: Although contemplation and thinking are mental, they can be done or not done or done otherwise by a person, because they are subject to the person's will.

children.text: jñānaṃ tu pramāṇajanyam /
children.translated_text: But knowledge is born of valid means of cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>).

children.text: pramāṇaṃ ca yathābhūtavastuviṣayamato jñānaṃ kartumakartumanyathā vā kartumaśakyaṃ, kevalaṃ vastutantrameva tat /
children.translated_text: And a valid means of cognition has for its object a thing as it really is; therefore knowledge cannot be done or not done or done otherwise — it is entirely dependent on the object alone.

children.text: na codanātantram //
children.translated_text: It is not dependent on injunction,

No. Because of the difference in character. For what is called 'action' is that which is enjoined entirely independently of the nature of the real object, and which depends on the mental effort of the person. As in: 'He should mentally contemplate the deity for whom the oblation has been taken up, while about to pronounce the <s>vaṣaṭ</s> call'; and '<s>Sandhyā</s> should be contemplated mentally' (<s>Aitareya Brāhmaṇa</s> 3.8.1) — in such cases.

children.text:
nāpi puruṣatantram /
tasmānmānasatve 'pi jñānasya mahadvailakṣaṇyam /
yathāca 'puruṣo vāva gautamāgniḥ', 'yoṣā vāva gautamāgniḥ (chāndo. 5.7,8.1) ityatra yoṣitpuruṣayoragnibuddhirmānasī bhavati /
kevacodanājanyatvātkriyaiva sā puruṣatantrā ca /
yā tu prasiddhe 'gnāvagnibuddhirna sā codanātantrā /
nāpi puruṣatantrā /
kiṃ tarhi pratyakṣavastutantraiveti jñānamevaitanna kriyā /
evaṃ sarvapramāṇaviṣayavastuṣu veditavyam /
tatraivaṃ sati yathābhūtabrahmātmaviṣayamapi jñānaṃ na codanātantram /
tadviṣaye liṅāgādayaḥ śrūyamāṇā apyaniyojyaviṣayatvātkuṇṭhībhavantyupalādiṣu prayuktakṣurataikṣṇyādivat, aheyānupādeyavastuviṣayatvāt /
kimarthāni tarhi 'ātmā vāre draṣyavyaḥ śrotavyaḥ' ityādīni vidhicchāyāni vacanāni /
svābhāvikapravṛttiviṣayavimukhīkaraṇārthānīti brūmaḥ /
yo hi bahirmukhaḥ pravartate puruṣaḥ iṣṭaṃ me bhūyādadaniṣṭaṃ mābhūditi, naca tatrātyantikaṃ puruṣīrthaṃ labhate, tamātyantikapuruṣārthavāñchinaṃ svābhāvikakāryakaraṇasaṃghātapravṛttigocarādvimukhīkṛtya pratyagātmasrotastayā pravartayanti 'ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ'
children.translated_text: nor is it dependent on the person. Therefore, even though knowledge is mental, there is a great difference in its character. Just as in 'A person indeed, O <s>Gautama</s>, is a fire' and 'A woman indeed, O <s>Gautama</s>, is a fire' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 5.7-8.1), the notion of fire in a woman and a man is mental. Yet because it is generated solely by injunction, it is indeed an action and is subject to the person's will. But the notion of fire with respect to a commonly known fire is not dependent on injunction, nor is it subject to the person's will. Rather, it is dependent solely on the perceptible object — therefore it is knowledge, not action. The same should be understood regarding the objects of all valid means of cognition. This being so, the knowledge concerning the true nature of <s>Brahman</s> as the Self is also not dependent on injunction. With regard to that subject matter, even though injunctive verbal forms and such are heard, since there is no one to be enjoined, they become blunted — like the sharpness of a razor applied to stones — because the object is one that is neither to be avoided nor adopted. Then for what purpose are the injunction-like statements such as 'The Self indeed is to be seen, to be heard'? We say they serve the purpose of turning [the mind] away from the objects of its natural outward activity. For the person who turns outward, thinking 'May what is desired happen to me, may what is undesired not happen' — he does not obtain the ultimate purpose of a person. Desiring the ultimate purpose of a person, these [texts] turn him away from the sphere of natural outward activity of the aggregate of body and senses, and direct him inward toward the current of the inner Self: 'The Self indeed is to be seen.'

children.text:
ityādīni /
tasyātmānveṣaṇāya pravṛttasyāheyamanupādeyaṃ cātmatattvamupadiśyate /
'idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā' (bṛha. 2.4.6) 'yatra tvasya sarvamātmaivābhūttatkena kaṃ paśyet kena kaṃ vijānīyāt vījñātāramare kena vijānīyāt' (bṛha. 4.5.15) 'ayamātmā brahma' (bṛha. 2.5.19) ityādibhiḥ /
yadapyakartavyapradhānamātmajñānaṃ hānāyopādānāya vā na bhavatīti, tattathaivetyabhyupagamyate /
children.translated_text: And as for the [objection] that knowledge of the Self, being primarily about what is not to be done, does not serve abandonment or adoption — that is accepted as being just so.

children.text: alaṅkāro hyayamasmākaṃ yadbrahmātmāvagatau satyāṃ sarvakartavyatāhāniḥ kṛtakṛtyatā ceti /
children.translated_text: For this is our ornament: that when the realization of <s>Brahman</s> as the Self has occurred, there is the cessation of all obligation and the state of having accomplished all that is to be accomplished.

children.text: tathāca śrutiḥ- 'ātmānaṃ cedvijānīyādayamastīti pūruṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus also the <s>śruti</s>: 'If a person should know the Self, [thinking] "I am this" —

children.text: kimicchankasya kāmāya śarīramanusaṃjvaret' //
children.translated_text: desiring what, for whose sake would he worry about the body?'

And such others.
For one who has undertaken the search for the Self, the reality of the Self — which is neither to be abandoned nor adopted — is taught:
'All this is the Self' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.6); 'But when to him all has become the Self alone, then what would he see and by what? What would he know and by what? The knower — by what would one know him?' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.5.15); 'This Self is <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.5.19) — and through such [passages].

children.text:
(bṛha. 4.4.12) iti /
'etadbuddhvā buddhimānsyātkṛtakṛtyaśca bhārata' /
(bha.gī. 15.20) iti smṛtiḥ /
tasmānna pratipattividhiviṣayatayā brahmaṇaḥ samarpaṇam /
yadapi kecidāhuḥ- 'pravṛttinivṛttividhitaccheṣavyatirekeṇa kevalavastuvādī vedabhāgo nāsti' iti tanna, aupaniṣadasya puruṣasya puruṣasyānanyaśeṣatvāt /
yo 'sāvupaniṣatsvevādhigataḥ puruṣo 'saṃsārī brahma utpādyādicaturvidhadravyavilakṣaṇaḥ svaprakaraṇastho 'nanyośeṣaḥ, nāsau nāsti nādhigamyata iti vā śakyaṃ vaditum, 'sa eṣa neti netyātmā' (bṛha. 3.9.26) ityāmaśabdāt, ātmanaśca pratyākhyātumaśakyatvāt, ya eva nirākartā tasyaivātmatvāt /
children.translated_text:
(<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.12). And the <s>smṛti</s>: 'Having known this, one would become wise and one who has accomplished all that is to be done, O <s>Bhārata</s>' (<s>Bhagavad Gītā</s> 15.20).
Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is not presented as the object of an injunction of practice.
As for what some say — 'Apart from being subsidiary to injunctions of activity and cessation, there is no portion of the <s>Veda</s> that merely teaches an established reality' — that is not so, because the person [taught] in the <s>Upaniṣads</s> is not subsidiary to anything else.
That person who is ascertained in the <s>Upaniṣads</s> themselves — the non-transmigrating <s>Brahman</s>, distinct from the four types of substance beginning with what is produced, standing in its own section, not subsidiary to anything else — of that one, it cannot be said either that it does not exist or that it is not ascertained, because of the culminating expression 'This Self is "not this, not this"' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 3.9.26), and because the Self cannot be denied, since the very one who would deny it is itself the Self.

children.text: nanvātmāhaṃpratyayaviṣayatvādupaniṣatsveva vijñāyata ityanupapannam /
