but in the reality of things, no modification whatsoever exists.
This is merely a name, unreal — 'clay alone is the reality.'
This illustration pertains to <s>Brahman</s> and is taught in scripture.
Therein, from the scriptural word '<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>' (a mere verbal handle for origination), it is understood that in the thing illustrated as well, the entire class of effects has no existence apart from <s>Brahman</s>.
And again, having stated that fire, water, and food are effects of <s>Brahman</s>, [the text] states the non-existence of the effects of fire, water, and food apart from fire, water, and food: 'The nature of fire as fire has departed; the modification is merely a name, a verbal handle; the three forms alone are the reality' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.4.1), and so forth.
By the word '<s>ādi</s>' (and such) in 'from the word <s>ārambhaṇa</s> and such,' [we should cite]: 'All this has that as its Self; that is the truth; that is the Self; you are that' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.7), 'All this is nothing but the Self' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.6), '<s>Brahman</s> alone is all this' (<s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.2.11), 'The Self alone is all this' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 7.25.2), 'There is no multiplicity whatsoever here' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.19) — statements of this kind, which are devoted to establishing the oneness of the Self, should also be cited.
And in no other way does knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing succeed.
Therefore, just as the space in pots, jars, and such is not other than the great space, and just as the water of a mirage and such is not other than the desert and such — because its apparent form is seen to perish, because in its true nature it is unnameable — so too, this entire manifold of experienced objects, experiencer, and such has no existence apart from <s>Brahman</s>: thus it should be understood.

children.text:
nanvanekātmakaṃ brahma, yathā vṛkṣo 'nekaśākha evamanekaśaktipravṛttiyuktaṃ brahma /
ata ekatvaṃ nānātvaṃ cobhayamapi satyameva /
yathā vṛkṣa ityanekatvaṃ śākhā iti nānātvam /
yathāca samudrātmanaikatvaṃ phenataraṅgādyātmanā nānātvam /
yathāca mṛdātmanaikatvaṃ ghaṭaśarāvādyātmanā nānātvam /
tatraikatvāṃśena jñānānmokṣavyavahāraḥ setsyati /
nānātvāṃśena tu karmakāṇḍāśrayau laukikavaidikavyavahārau setsyata iti /
evañca mṛdādidṛṣṭāntā anurūpā bhaviṣyantīti /
children.translated_text:
Objection: <s>Brahman</s> has many aspects — just as a tree has many branches, so <s>Brahman</s> is endowed with many powers and activities.
Therefore, both oneness and multiplicity are equally real.
Just as 'tree' [denotes] unity, and 'branches' [denote] multiplicity.
And just as there is unity as the ocean and multiplicity as foam, waves, and such.
And just as there is unity as clay and multiplicity as pots, saucers, and such.
Therein, by the aspect of unity, the practice of liberation through knowledge will succeed.
And by the aspect of multiplicity, worldly and Vedic practices, which are based on the section on action (<s>karmakāṇḍa</s>), will succeed.
And in this way, the illustrations of clay and such will be fitting.

children.text:
naivaṃ syāt /
'mṛttiketyeva satyam' iti prakṛtimātrasya dṛṣṭānte satyatvāvadhāraṇāt /
vācārambhaṇaśabdena ca vikārajātasyānṛtatvābhidhānāt /
dārṣṭāntike 'pi 'aitadātmyamidaṃ sarvaṃ tatsatyam' iti ca paramakāraṇasyaivaikasya satyatvāvadhāraṇāt 'sa ātmā tattvamasi śvetaketo' iti ca śārīrasya brahmabhāvopadeśāt /
svayaṃ prasiddhaṃ hyetaccharīrasya brahmātmatvamupadiśyate na yatnāntaraprasādhyam /
ataścedaṃ śāstrīyaṃ brahmātmatvamavagamyamānaṃ svābhāvikasya śārīrātmatvasya bādhakaṃ saṃpadyate, rajjvādibuddhaya iva sarpādibuddhīnām /
bādhite ca śārīrātmatvasya tadāśrayaḥ samastaḥ svābhāviko vyavahāro bādhito bhavati yatprasiddhaye nānātvāṃśo 'paro brahmaṇaḥ kalpyeta /
darśayati ca-
children.translated_text: This should not be so. Because in the illustration, the reality of the material cause alone is ascertained by 'clay alone is real' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.1.4). And by the word '<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>' (a mere verbal handle), the entire class of modifications is declared to be unreal. And in the illustrated case too, the reality of the one ultimate cause alone is ascertained by 'all this has That as its Self; That is the Real' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.7). And by 'That Self — thou art that, O <s>Śvetaketu</s>' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.7), the identity of the embodied soul with <s>Brahman</s> is taught. For this identity of the embodied soul with <s>Brahman</s> is taught as something self-evident — it is not something to be accomplished by another effort. And therefore this scriptural knowledge of the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s>, when comprehended, turns out to sublate the natural [sense of] embodied selfhood — just as the cognition of the rope sublates the cognition of the snake. And when the embodied selfhood is sublated, the entire natural conventional activity that depends on it — for whose establishment a separate aspect of plurality in <s>Brahman</s> would have to be imagined — is also sublated. And [the <s>śruti</s>] demonstrates —

children.text:
'yatra tvasya sarvamātmaivābhūttatkena kaṃ paśyet' (bṛ. 4.5.15) ityādinā brahmātmatvadarśinaṃ prati samastasya kriyākārakaphalalakṣaṇasya vyavahārasyābhāvam /
nacāyaṃ vyavahārābhāvoṣa'vasthāviśeṣanibaddho 'bhidhīyata iti yuktaṃ vaktum, 'tattvamasi' iti brahmātmabhāvasyānavasthāviśeṣanibandhanatvāt /
taskaradṛṣṭāntena cānṛtābhisaṃdhasya bandhanaṃ satyābhisaṃdhasya ca mokṣaṃ darśayannekatvamevaikaṃ pāramārthikaṃ darśayati (chā. 6.16) /
mithyājñānavijṛmbhitaṃ ca nānātvam /
ubhayasatyatāyāṃ hi kathaṃ vyavahāragocaro 'pi janturanṛtābhisaṃdha ityucyeta /
'mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati' (bṛ. 4.4.19) iti ca bhedadṛṣṭimapavadannevaitaddarśayati /
nacāsmindarśane jñānānmokṣa ityupapadyate, samyagjñanāpanodyasya kasyacinmithyājñānasya saṃsārakāraṇatvenānabhyupagamāt /
ubhayasatyatāyāṃ hi kathamekatvavijñānena nānātvajñānamapanudyata ityucyate /
children.translated_text: 'But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom would one see?' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.5.15) — by such passages [the <s>śruti</s>] shows the absence of all conventional activity characterized by action, agent, and result for one who has realized the identity of the Self with <s>Brahman</s>. And it is not proper to say that this absence of conventional activity is tied to a particular state, because the identity of the Self with <s>Brahman</s> [taught by] 'Thou art That' is not tied to any particular state. And by the illustration of the thief — showing the bondage of one who declares falsely, and the liberation of one who declares truly — [the scripture] shows oneness alone as the sole ultimate reality (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.16). And plurality is a manifestation of false knowledge. For if both [oneness and plurality] were real, how could a being who is within the range of conventional activity be called 'one who declares falsely'? And 'He who sees plurality here, as it were, goes from death to death' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.19) — by censuring the vision of difference, [the <s>śruti</s>] demonstrates precisely this. And in this [Advaita] view, liberation through knowledge is logically established — because some false knowledge is accepted as the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is to be removed by right knowledge. For if both [oneness and plurality] were real, how could it be said that the knowledge of plurality is removed by the knowledge of oneness?

children.text:
nanvekatvaikāntābhyupagame nānātvābhāvatpratyakṣādīni laukikāni pramāṇāni vyāhanyerannirviṣayatvāt, sthāṇvādiṣviva puruṣādijñānāni /
tathā vidhipratiṣedhaśāstramapi bhedāpekṣatvāttadabhāve vyāhanyeta, mokṣaśāstrasyāpi śiṣyaśāsitrādibhedāpekṣatvāttadabhāve vyāghātaḥ syāt /
kathaṃ cānṛtena mokṣaśāstreṇa pratipāditasyātmaikatvasya satyatvamupapadyeteti /
children.translated_text: Objection: If absolute oneness were accepted, then — because of the absence of plurality — worldly means of knowledge such as perception and the like would be contradicted, being without objects, like the cognitions of persons and such in tree-stumps and the like. Likewise, the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions, being dependent on difference, would also be contradicted in the absence of that [difference]. Even the scripture of liberation, being dependent on the distinction of student, teacher, and such, would be contradicted in the absence of that [difference]. And how could the oneness of the Self, established through an unreal scripture of liberation, be real?

children.text:
atrocyate- naiṣa doṣaḥ /
sarvavyavahārāṇāmeva prāgbrahmātmatāvijñānātsatyatvopapatteḥ /
svapnavyavahārasyeva prākprabodhāt /
yāvaddhi na satyātmaikatvapratipattistāvatpramāṇaprameyaphalalakṣaṇeṣu vikāreṣvanṛtatvabuddhirna kasyacidutpadyate /
vikārāneva tvahaṃ mametyavidyāyāmātmīyena bhāvena sarvo jantuḥ pratipadyate svābhāvikīṃ brahmātmatāṃ hitvā /
tasmātprāgbrahmātmatāpratibodhādupapannaḥ sarvo laukiko vaidikaśca vyavahāraḥ /
yathā suptasya prākṛtasya janasya svapna uccāvacānbhāvānpaśyato niścitameva pratyakṣābhimataṃ vijñānaṃ bhavati prākprabodhāt, naca pratyakṣābhāsābhiprāyastatkāle bhavati, tadvat /
children.translated_text: To this we say: This is not a fault. Because the reality of all conventional activities is tenable prior to the knowledge of the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s> — just as dream-activity [is real] prior to waking. For as long as the realization of the true Self's oneness has not arisen, the notion of unreality does not arise for anyone with respect to the modifications characterized by means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and their results. Rather, every being, abandoning the natural identity with <s>Brahman</s>, through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) apprehends the modifications as 'I' and 'mine' with a sense of ownership. Therefore, prior to the awakening to the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s>, all conventional activity — both worldly and Vedic — is well established. Just as for an ordinary person who is asleep, seeing various high and low things in a dream, there is certainly a cognition regarded as perception before awakening, and the thought 'this is a mere semblance of perception' does not arise at that time — so too here.

children.text:
kathaṃ tvasatyena vedāntavākyena satyasya brahmātmatvasya pratipattirupapadyeta /
nahi rajjusarpeṇa dṛṣṭo mriyate /
nāpi mṛgatṛṣṇikāmbhasā pānāvagāhanādiprayojanaṃ kriyata iti /
children.translated_text: But how could the realization of the Self's true identity with <s>Brahman</s> be established through an unreal <s>Vedānta</s> statement? For indeed, one who sees a rope-snake does not die from it. Nor can the purpose of drinking, bathing, and such be accomplished with the water of a mirage.

children.text:
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
śaṅkāviṣādinimittamaraṇādikāryopalabdheḥ /
svapnadarśanāvasthasya ca sarpadaṃśanodakasnānādikāryadarśanāt /
tatkāryamapyanṛtameveti cedbrūyāt /
children.translated_text: This is not a fault. Because effects such as death are observed to result from causes like apprehension, fear, poison, and such [regardless of their reality]. And because for one in the state of dream-experience, effects such as snakebite, bathing in water, and the like are observed. If one were to say: those effects too are unreal —

children.text:
tatra brūmaḥ- yadyapi svapnadarśanāvasthasya sarpadaṃśanodakasnānādikāryamanṛtaṃ tathāpi tadavagatiḥ satyameva phalaṃ, pratibuddhasyāpyabādhyamānatvāt /
nahi svapnādutthitaḥ svapnadṛṣṭaṃ sarpadaṃśanodakasnānādikāryaṃ mithyeti manyamānastadavagatimapi mithyeti manyate kaścit /
etena svapnadṛśo 'vagatyabādhanena dehamātrātmavādo dūṣito veditavyaḥ /
tathāca śrutiḥ - 'yadā karmasu kāmyeṣu striyaṃ svapneṣu paśyati /
samṛddhiṃ tatra jānīyāttasminsvapnanidarśane' (chā. 5.2.9) ityasatyena svapnadarśanena satyāyāḥ samṛddheḥ pratipattiṃ darśayati /
tathā pratyakṣadarśaneṣu keṣucidariṣṭeṣu jāteṣu 'na ciramiva jīviṣyatīti vidyāt' ityuktvā 'atha svapnāḥ puruṣaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ kṛṣṇadantaṃ paśyati sa enaṃ hanti' ityādinā tena tenāsatyenaiva svapnadarśanena satyaṃ maraṇaṃ sūcyata iti darśayati /
prasiddhaṃ cedaṃ loke 'nvayavyatirekakuśalānāmīdṛśena svapnadarśanena sādhvāgamaḥ sūcyata īdṛśenāsādhvāgama iti /
tathākārādisatyākṣarapratipattirddaṣṭā rekhānṛtākṣarapratipatteḥ /
apicāntyamidaṃ pramāṇamātmaikatvasya pratipādakaṃ nātaḥ paraṃ kiñcidākāṅkṣyamasti /
yathāhi loke yajetetyukte kiṃ kena kathamityākāṅkṣyate naivaṃ 'tattvamasi' 'ahaṃ brahmāsmi' ityukte kiñcidanyadākāṅkṣyamasti, sarvātmaikatvaviṣayatvāvagateḥ /
sati hyasminnavaśiṣyamāṇer'the ākāṅkṣā syāt /
natvātmaikatvavyatirekeṇāvaśiṣyamāṇo 'nyor'tho 'sti ya ākāṅkṣyeta /
na ceyamavagatirnopapadyata iti śakyaṃ vaktum, 'taddhāsya vijajñau' (chā. 6.16.3) ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
avagatisādhanānāṃ ca śravaṇādīnāṃ vedānuvacanādīnāṃ ca vidhānāt /
naceyamavagatiranarthikā bhrāntirveti śakyaṃ vaktum /
avidyānivṛttiphaladarśanāt, bādhakajñānāntarābhāvācca /
prākcātmaikatvāvagateravyāhataḥ sarvaḥ satyānṛtavyavahāro laukiko vaidikaścetyavocāma /
tasmādantyena pramāṇena pratipādita ātmaikatve samastasya prācīnasya bhedavyavahārasya bādhitatvānnānekātmakabrahmakalpanāvakāśo 'sti /
children.translated_text: To that we say: Even though for one in the state of dream-experience, the effects such as snakebite, bathing in water, and the like are unreal, nevertheless the cognition thereof is truly a real result — because it is not sublated even upon awakening. For no one, having arisen from sleep and thinking that the snakebite, bathing in water, and other effects seen in the dream are false, also thinks that the cognition of those [effects] is false. By this [argument] — through the non-sublation of cognition in dream — the doctrine that the Self is merely the body is refuted; this should be understood. And thus the <s>śruti</s>: 'When, among the rites performed for the sake of desires, one sees a woman in dreams — one should know prosperity in that dream-vision' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 5.2.9) — shows the realization of real prosperity through an unreal dream-vision. Likewise, after mentioning certain omens that have appeared in waking perception, [the <s>śruti</s>] says: 'One should know that he will not live long,' and then — 'In dreams, he sees a dark person with dark teeth — that one kills him' — thus showing by various unreal dream-visions that real death is indicated. And it is well-known in the world among those skilled in positive and negative correlation that such-and-such a dream-vision indicates a fortunate occurrence, and such-and-such indicates an unfortunate one. Similarly, the apprehension of real letters from drawn unreal letters is observed. Moreover, this is the final valid means of knowledge that establishes the oneness of the Self; nothing further is to be expected beyond it. For just as in the world, when [the injunction] 'One should sacrifice' is stated, there is the expectation of 'what, by what means, how?' — [but] when 'Thou art That' or 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' is stated, nothing else remains to be expected, because it is understood to pertain to the oneness of all selves. For expectation would arise only if there remained some further object [to be known]. But apart from the oneness of the Self, there is no remaining object that could be expected. Nor can it be said that this cognition does not arise — because of <s>śruti</s> passages such as 'He understood that' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.16.3). And because the means to this cognition — hearing, and so forth, and recitation of the <s>Vedas</s> — are enjoined. Nor can it be said that this cognition is a purposeless delusion — because the result of the cessation of <s>avidyā</s> is observed, and because there is no other sublating knowledge. And we have already said that prior to the realization of the oneness of the Self, all conventional activity — both true-and-false, worldly and Vedic — remains uncontradicted. Therefore, since the oneness of the Self has been established by the final valid means of knowledge, and since the entirety of prior conventional activity based on difference has been sublated, there is no room for imagining <s>Brahman</s> to have a manifold nature.

children.text:
nanu mṛdādidṛṣṭāntapraṇayanātpariṇāmavadbrahma śāstrasyābhimatamiti gamyate /
pariṇāmino hi mṛdādayor'thā loke samadhigatā iti /
children.translated_text: Objection: From the employment of the illustration of clay and such, it is understood that the scripture intends <s>Brahman</s> to undergo real transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>). For the meanings of [the illustrations of] clay and such are understood in the world as involving [real] transformation.

children.text:
netyucyate /
'sa vā eṣa mahājana ātmājaro 'maro 'mṛto 'bhayo brahma' (bṛ. 4.4.25) 'sa eṣa neti netyātmā' (bṛ. 3.9.23), 'asthūlamanaṇu' (bṛ. 3.8.8) ityādyābhyaḥ sarvavikriyāpratiṣedhaśrutibhyo brahmaṇaḥ kūṭasthatvāvagamāt /
nahyekasya brahmaṇaḥ pariṇāmadharmatvaṃ tadrahitatvaṃ ca śkyaṃ pratipattum /
children.translated_text: No, it is said. Because from <s>śruti</s> passages that negate all modification — 'This great being, the Self, is unaging, undying, immortal, fearless — <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.25), 'This Self is "not this, not this"' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 3.9.26), 'Neither gross nor subtle' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 3.8.8), and the like — <s>Brahman</s> is understood to be immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>). For one cannot understand the same <s>Brahman</s> as both possessing the property of transformation and as being free from it.

children.text: sthitigativatsyāditi cet /
children.translated_text: If it be said: it could be like rest and motion [coexisting in the same entity] —

children.text:
na /
kūṭasthasyeti viśeṣaṇāt /
nahi kūṭasthasya brahmaṇaḥ sthitigativadanekadharmāśrayatvaṃ saṃbhavati /
kūṭasthaṃ ca nityaṃ brahma sarvavikriyāpratiṣedhādityavocāma /
naca yathā brahmaṇa ātmaikatvadarśanaṃ mokṣasādhanamevaṃ jagadākārapariṇāmitvadarśanamapi svatantrameva kasmaicitphalāyābhipreyate /
pramāṇābhāvāt /
kūṭasthabrahmātmavijñānādeva hi phalaṃ darśayati śāstram- 'sa eṣa neti netyātmā' ityupakramya 'abhayaṃ vai janaka prāpto 'si' (bṛ. 4.2.4)
children.translated_text: No. Because of the qualifying term 'immutable' (<s>kūṭastha</s>). For it is not possible for immutable <s>Brahman</s> to be the substratum of multiple properties, like rest and motion. And we have said that <s>Brahman</s> is immutable and eternal, because of the negation of all modifications. Nor is the vision of <s>Brahman</s> as transforming into the form of the world independently intended for any result, in the way that the vision of the Self's oneness with <s>Brahman</s> is a means to liberation. Because there is no valid means of knowledge [for that]. For the scripture shows the result [to follow] from the knowledge of the immutable <s>Brahman</s> as the Self alone — having begun with 'This Self is "not this, not this"' [and then saying] 'O <s>Janaka</s>, you have attained fearlessness' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.2.4) —

children.text:
ityevañjātīyakam /
tatraitatsiddhaṃ bhavati- brahmaprakaraṇe sarvadharmaviśeṣarahitabrahmadarśanādeva phalasiddhau satyāṃ yattatrāphalaṃ śrūyate brahmaṇo jagadākārapariṇāmitvādi tadbrahmadarśanopāyatvenaiva viniyujyate, phalavatsaṃnidhāvaphalaṃ tadaṅgamitivat /
natu svatantraṃ phalāya kalpyata iti /
nahi pariṇāmavattvavijñānātpariṇāmavattvamātmanaḥ phalaṃ syāditi vaktuṃ yuktaṃ, kūṭasthanityatvānmokṣasya /
children.translated_text: and similar [passages]. Therein, this is established: In the context of <s>Brahman</s>, when the result is accomplished through the vision of <s>Brahman</s> as devoid of all distinguishing properties, whatever is heard there that is without [independent] result — such as <s>Brahman</s>'s transformation into the form of the world — that is employed only as a means to the vision of <s>Brahman</s>, just as what is without [independent] result in the vicinity of what has a result is [regarded as] an auxiliary of it. But it is not imagined as independently [serving] a result. For it would not be proper to say that from the knowledge of [<s>Brahman</s>'s] being subject to transformation, the transformation of the Self would be the result — because liberation is immutable and eternal.

children.text: kūṭasthabrahmātmavādina ekatvaikāntyādīśitrīśitavyābhāva īśvarakāraṇapratijñāvirodha iti cet /
children.translated_text: Objection: For one who holds the doctrine of the immutable <s>Brahman</s> as the Self — because of the absolute commitment to oneness — the distinction of ruler and ruled would be absent, [leading to] a contradiction with the thesis that the Lord is the cause.

children.text:
na /
avidyātmakanāmarūpabījavyākaraṇāpekṣatvātsarvajñatvasya /
'tasmādvā etasmādātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ' (tai. 2.1) ityādivākyebhyo nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvarūpātsarvajñātsarvaśakterīśvarājjagajjanisthi tipralayā nācetanātpradhānādanyasmādvetyeṣor'thaḥ pratijñātaḥ 'janmādyasya yataḥ' (bra.sū. 1.1.4) iti /
sā pratijñā tadavasthaiva na tadviruddhor'thaḥ punarihocyate /
kathaṃ nocyate 'tyantamātmana ekatvamadvitīyatvaṃ ca bruvatā /
śruṇu yathā nocyate /
sarvajñasyeśvarasyātmabhūta ivāvidyākalpite nāmarūpe tattvānyatvābhyāmanirvacanīye saṃsāraprapañcabījabhūte sarvajñasyeśvarasya māyāśaktiḥ prakṛtiriti ca śrutismṛtyorabhilapyete /
tābhyāmanyaḥ sarvajña īśvaraḥ 'ākāśo vai nāma nāmarūpayornirvahitā te yadantarā tadbrahma' (chā. 8.14.1) iti śruteḥ /
'nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi' (chā. 6.3.2), 'sarvāṇi rūpāṇi vicitya dhīro nāmāni kṛtvābhivadanyadāste' (tai. ā. 3.12.7), 'ekaṃ bījaṃ bahudhā yaḥ karoti' (śvaṃ. 6.12) ityādiśrutibhyaśca /
evamavidyākṛtanāmarūpopādhyanurodhīśvaro bhavati, vyomeva ghaṭakarakādyupādhyanurodhi /
sa ca svātmabhūtāneva ghaṭākāśasthānīyānavidyāpratyupasthāpitanāmarūpakṛtakāryakaraṇasaṃghātānurodhino jīvākhyānvijñānātmanaḥ pratīṣṭe vyavahāraviṣaye /
tadevamavidyātmakopādhiparicchedāpekṣameveśvarasyeśvaratvaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ sarvaśaktitvaṃ ca na paramārthato vidyāyāpāstasarvopādhisvarūpa ātmanīśitrīśitavyasarvajñatvādivyavahāra upapadyate /
tathācoktam- 'yatra nānyatpaśyati nānyacchṛṇoti nānyadvijānāti sa bhūmā' (chā. 7.24.1) iti 'yatra tvasya sarvamātmaivābhūttatkena paśyet' (bṛ. 4.5.15) ityādinā ca /
children.translated_text: And thus it is said: 'Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else — that is the <s>Bhūmā</s> (the Infinite)' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 7.24.1), and 'But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom would one see?' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.5.15), and so forth.

children.text: evaṃ paramārthāvasthāyāṃ sarvavyavahārābhāvaṃ vadanti vedāntāḥ sarve /
children.translated_text: Thus, all the <s>Vedānta</s> texts declare the absence of all conventional activity in the state of ultimate reality.

children.text: tatheśvaragītāsvapi- 'na kartṛtvaṃ na karmāṇi lokasya sṛjati prabhuḥ /
children.translated_text: And in the <s>Īśvaragītā</s> too: 'The Lord does not create agenthood or actions for the world,

children.text: na karmaphalasaṃyogaṃ svabhāvastu pravartate //
children.translated_text: nor the connection of action and result — but inherent nature proceeds [of its own accord]. //

No. Because the omniscience [of the Lord] is dependent on the differentiation of the seed of name and form, which is of the nature of <s>avidyā</s>. From passages such as 'From that very Self, space was born' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 2.1) and the like — [the thesis is that] the origination, sustenance, and dissolution of the world are from the Lord who is omniscient, omnipotent, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and free — and not from the insentient <s>Pradhāna</s> or from anything else. This meaning was proposed in 'That from which the origin and so forth [of this world proceed]' (<s>BBs</s> 1.1.2). That thesis remains as it is; no meaning contradicting it is stated here. How is it not stated, when you assert the absolute oneness and non-duality of the Self? Hear how it is not stated. The omniscient Lord's name and form — as though constituting His own nature, imagined through <s>avidyā</s>, indeterminable as either identical with or different from [Him], being the seed of the phenomenal world of <s>saṃsāra</s>, being the <s>māyā</s>-power of the omniscient Lord — are spoken of in <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> as His <s>prakṛti</s> (nature). The omniscient Lord is other than those two [name and form] — as the <s>śruti</s> says: 'Space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is indeed the accomplisher of name and form; that which is other than these two — that is <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 8.14.1). And from <s>śruti</s> passages such as: 'Let me differentiate names and forms' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.3.2), 'The wise one, having fashioned all forms and created the names, sits uttering them' (<s>Taittirīya Āraṇyaka</s> 3.12.7), 'He who makes the one seed manifold' (<s>Śvetāśvatara</s> 6.12), and the like. Thus, the Lord is [called Lord] in accordance with the limiting adjuncts of name and form created by <s>avidyā</s> — just as space [is designated variously] in accordance with the limiting adjuncts of pot, water-jar, and the like. And He regards, within the domain of conventional activity, the <s>jīvas</s> — called <s>vijñānātmans</s> (cognitive selves) — who, like the space-within-a-pot, are conforming to the aggregate of body-and-organs constituted by name and form presented through <s>avidyā</s>, and who are as it were His own nature. Thus, the Lord's lordship, omniscience, and omnipotence are only relative to the delimitation by the limiting adjuncts that are of the nature of <s>avidyā</s>, and not in the ultimate sense. In the true nature of the Self, where all limiting adjuncts have been removed through <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), the conventional usage of ruler, ruled, omniscience, and such is not tenable.

children.text:
nādatte kasyacitpāpaṃ na caiva sukṛtaṃ vibhuḥ /
ajñānenāvṛtaṃ jñānaṃ tena muhyanti jantavaḥ' (gī. 5.14.-15) iti paramārthāvasthāyāmīśitrīśitavyādivyavahārābhāvaḥ pradarśyate /
vyavahārāvasthāyāṃ tūktaḥ śrutāvapīśvarādivyavahāraḥ 'eṣa sarveśvara eṣa bhūtādhipatireṣa bhūtapāla eṣa seturvidhāraṇa eṣāṃ lokānāmasaṃbhedāya' (bṛ. 4.4.22) iti /
tathāceśvaragītāsvapi- 'īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ hṛddeśer'juna tiṣṭhati /
bhrāmayansarvabhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā' (gī. 18.61) iti /
children.translated_text: causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine, through <s>māyā</s>' (<s>Gītā</s> 18.61).

children.text: sūtrakāro 'pi paramārthābhiprāyeṇa tadanyatvamityāha /
children.translated_text: The author of the <s>sūtras</s> too, with the intention of [expressing] the ultimate reality, says 'Its otherness' [i.e., the non-difference of cause and effect].

children.text: vyavahārābhiprāyeṇa tu syāllokavaditi mahāsamudrasthānīyatāṃ brahmaṇaḥ kathayati /
children.translated_text: But with the intention of [expressing] the transactional [reality], [he says] 'As in the world, [so should it be]' — thereby describing the status of <s>Brahman</s> as being like the great ocean.

children.text: apratyākhyāyaiva kāryaprapañcaṃ pariṇāmaprakriyāṃ cāśrayati saguṇopāsaneṣūpayokṣyata iti // 14 //
children.translated_text: Without rejecting the phenomenal elaboration and the doctrine of transformation, [the <s>sūtrakāra</s>] adopts [them] as they will be useful in meditations on <s>Brahman</s> with attributes (<s>saguṇa upāsanas</s>). // 14 //

'He does not take on anyone's sin, nor indeed anyone's merit — the all-pervading one. Knowledge is covered by ignorance; thereby beings are deluded' (<s>Gītā</s> 5.14-15) — in the absolutely real state, the absence of transactions such as ruler and ruled is demonstrated. But in the transactional state, the transaction of the Lord and such is stated even in <s>śruti</s>: 'He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge that holds apart these worlds so they do not collapse' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.22). And likewise in the <s>Bhagavad Gītā</s>: 'The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O <s>Arjuna</s>,

children.text:
FN: dṛṣṭaṃ prātītikaṃ naṣṭhamanityaṃ yatsvarūpaṃ tadrūpeṇānupākhyatvātsattāsphūrtiśūnyatvādananyatvamiti saṃbandhaḥ /
svabhāvo 'trāvidyā tayā kṛtaḥ svābhāvikaḥ /
ekatvasyaikāntaḥ kaivalyam /
vyāhanyerannapramāṇāni syuḥ /
satyatvaṃ bādhā bhāvaḥ /
bādho mityātvaniścayaḥ /
rekhāsvakāratvādibhrāntyā satyā akārādayo jñāyanta iti prasiddham /
children.translated_text: NOTE: That which is perceived, phenomenal, perishable, and impermanent — because it cannot be described as having [independent] reality, because it is devoid of [independent] existence and manifestation — its non-otherness [from the cause] is the connection. 'Nature' (<s>svabhāva</s>) here means <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance); 'made by it' means natural. The culmination of oneness is <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute aloneness). '[The means of knowledge] would be contradicted' means they would not be valid means. 'Reality' (<s>satyatva</s>) means the state of non-sublation. 'Sublation' (<s>bādha</s>) means the ascertainment of unreality. It is well known that through the illusion of seeing the letter 'a' and such in drawn lines, the real [letters] 'a' and such are cognized.

children.text: bhāve copalabdheḥ | BBs_2,1.15 |
children.translated_text: And because of apprehension only when [the cause] exists. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.15 |

children.text:
itaśca kāraṇādananyatvaṃ kāryasya, yatkāraṇaṃ bhāva eva kāraṇasya kāryamupalabhyate, nābhāve /
tadyathā satyāṃ mṛdi ghaṭa upalabhyate satsu ca tantuṣu paṭaḥ /
naca niyamenānyabhāve 'nyasyopalabdhirdṛṣṭā /
nahyaśvo goranyaḥ san gorbhāva evopalabhyate /
naca kulālabhāva eva ghaṭa upalabhyate /
satyapi nimittanaimittikabhāve 'nyatvāt /
children.translated_text: For this further reason the effect is non-different from the cause: the effect is apprehended only when the cause exists, and not in the absence [of the cause]. For example, the pot is apprehended only when clay exists, and cloth only when threads exist. And no instance is seen where one thing is invariably apprehended only in the existence of something else [that is genuinely different from it]. For a horse, being different from a cow, is not apprehended only in the existence of a cow. And a pot is not apprehended only in the existence of a potter — even though there is a relationship of efficient cause and effect, because they are different.

children.text: nanvanyasya bhāve 'pyanyasyopalabdhirniyatā dṛśyate, yathāgnibhāve dhūmasyeti /
children.translated_text: But is not the apprehension of one thing invariably seen in the existence of another — as smoke in the existence of fire?

children.text:
netyucyate /
uddhāpite 'pyagnau gopālaghuṭikādidhāritasya dhūmasya dṛśyamānatvāt /
atha dhūmaṃ kayācidavasthayā viśiṃṣyādīdṛśo dhūmo nāsatyāgnau bhavatīti /
naivamapi kaściddoṣaḥ tadbhāvānuraktāṃ hi buddhiṃ kāryakāraṇayorananyatve hetuṃ vayaṃ vadāmaḥ /
nacāsāvagnidhūmayorvidyate /
bhāvāccopalabdheriti vā sūtram /
na kevalaṃ śabdādeva kāryakāraṇayorananyatvaṃ,
children.translated_text: No, it is replied. Because smoke is seen to persist even when fire has been extinguished, being sustained by cow-dung balls and such. And if one were to qualify the smoke by some specific condition — 'such-and-such smoke does not occur without fire' — even so, there is no fault, for we declare [as the ground of non-difference] the cognition that follows the existence [of the cause] with respect to cause and effect. And such [cognition] does not exist between fire and smoke. Alternatively, the <s>sūtra</s> [may be read as]: 'And because of apprehension [only] when [the cause] exists.' Not merely from scripture alone is the non-difference of cause and effect [established],

children.text:
pratyakṣopalabdhibhāvācca tayorananyatvamityarthaḥ /
bhavatihi pratyakṣopalabdhiḥ kāryakāraṇayorananyatve /
tadyathā-
children.translated_text: but also from the fact of perceptual apprehension, their non-difference [is established] — this is the meaning. For there is indeed perceptual apprehension [establishing] the non-difference of cause and effect. For example:

children.text: tantusaṃsthāne paṭe tantuvyatirekeṇa paṭo nāma kāryaṃ naivopalabhyate kevalāstu tantava ātānavitānavantaḥ pratyakṣamupalabhyante, tathā tantuṣvaṃśavoṃ'śuṣu tadavayavāḥ /
children.translated_text: In the arrangement of threads that constitutes a cloth, no effect called 'cloth' is ever apprehended apart from the threads — only the threads themselves, extending lengthwise and crosswise, are directly perceived. Similarly, in the threads [one sees only] the fibers, and in the fibers their component parts.

children.text: anayā pratyakṣopalabdhyā lohitaśuklakṛṣṇāni trīṇi tato rūpāṇi vāyumātramākāśamātraṃ cetyanumeyam /
children.translated_text: Through this perceptual apprehension, the three forms — red, white, and black — are inferred, and beyond them mere air, mere space.

children.text: (chā. 6.4) tataḥ paraṃ brahmaikamevādvitīyaṃ, tatra sarvapramāṇānāṃ niṣṭhāmavocāma // 15 //
children.translated_text: (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.4). Beyond that, <s>Brahman</s> alone, one without a second — there we have stated that all means of knowledge find their culmination. // 15 //

children.text: FN: kāraṇasya bhāve sattve upalabdhau ca kāryasya sattvādupalabdheścānanyatvamiti sūtrārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: NOTE: The meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is: because of the existence of the cause, i.e., its being, and because of the apprehension of the effect, i.e., from its being and apprehension, the non-difference [of the effect from the cause is established].

children.text: satvāc cāparasya | BBs_2,1.16 |
children.translated_text: And because the subsequent [effect] exists [in the cause prior to origination]. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.16 |

children.text:
itaśca kāraṇātkāryasyānanyatvaṃ, yatkāraṇaṃ prāgutpatteḥ kāraṇātmanaiva kāraṇe sattvamavarakālīnasya kāryasya śrūyate /
'sadeva somyedamagra āsīt' (chā. 6.2.1), 'ātmā vā idameka evāgra āsīt' (ai.ā. 2.4.1.1) ityādāvidaṃśabdagṛhītasya kāryasya kāraṇena sāmānādhikaraṇyāt /
yacca yadātmanā yatra na vartate na tattata utpadyate, yathā sikatābhyastailam /
children.translated_text: And that which does not exist in something in the form of that thing does not originate from it — just as oil [does not originate] from sand.

children.text: tasmātprāgutpatterananyatvādutpannamapyananyadeva kāraṇātkāryamityavagamyate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, since [the effect] is non-different prior to origination, it is understood that even after origination the effect is nothing but non-different from the cause.

children.text: yathāca kāraṇaṃ brahma triṣu kāleṣu sattvaṃ na vyabhicaratyevaṃ kāryamapi jagattriṣu kāleṣu sattvaṃ na vyabhicarati /
children.translated_text: And just as <s>Brahman</s>, the cause, does not deviate from existence in the three times, so too the world, the effect, does not deviate from existence in the three times.

children.text: ekaṃ ca punaḥ sattvamato 'pyananyatvaṃ kāraṇātkāryasya // 16 //
children.translated_text: And existence is one — hence, for this reason too, the effect is non-different from the cause. // 16 //

For this further reason the effect is non-different from the cause: because the <s>śruti</s> declares that the effect, which comes into being at a later time, exists in the cause in the very form of the cause prior to origination. 'Being alone, dear one, was this in the beginning' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.2.1), 'The Self alone was this, one only, in the beginning' (<s>Aitareya Āraṇyaka</s> 2.4.1.1) — in such [texts], the effect, referred to by the word 'this,' is placed in co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with the cause.

children.text: asadvyapadeśān neti cen na dharmāntareṇa vākyaśeṣāt | BBs_2,1.17 |
children.translated_text: If [you say] no, because of the designation as non-existent — [we say] no, because [it is] in a different sense, from the remainder of the sentence. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.17 |

children.text:
nanu kvacidasattvamapi prāgutpatteḥ kāryasya vyapadiśati śrutiḥ - 'asadevedamagra āsīt (chā. 3.19.1) iti, 'asadvā idamagra āsīt' (tai. 2.7.1) iti ca /
tasmādasadvyapadeśānna prāgutpatteḥ kāryasya sattvamiti cet /
children.translated_text: But the <s>śruti</s> somewhere designates the effect as non-existent prior to origination: 'Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 3.19.1), and 'Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 2.7.1). Therefore, because of the designation as non-existent, the effect does not exist prior to origination — if this is the objection,

children.text:
neti brūmaḥ /
nahyayamatyantāsatvābhiprāyeṇa prāgutpatteḥ kāryasyāsadvyapadeśaḥ,kiṃ tarhi vyākṛtanāmarūpatvāddharmādavyākṛtanāmarūpatvaṃ dharmāntaraṃ tena dharmāntareṇāyamasadvyapadeśaḥ prāgutpatteḥ sata eva kāryasya kāraṇarūpeṇānanyasya /
kathametadavagamyate /
vākyaśeṣāt /
yadupakrame saṃdigdhārthaṃ vākyaṃ taccheṣānniścīyate /
iha ca tāvat 'asadevedamagra āsīt' ityasacchabdenopakrame nirdiṣṭaṃ yattadeva punastacchabdena parāmṛśya saditi viśinaṣṭi 'tatsadāsīt' iti /
asataśca pūrvāparakālāsaṃbandhādāsīcchabdānupapatteśca /
'asadvā idamagra āsīt' ityatrāpi 'tadātmānaṃ svayamakuruta' iti vākyaśeṣe viśeṣaṇānnātyantāsattvam /
children.translated_text: In 'Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning' [of the <s>Taittirīya</s>] too, from the qualification in the remainder of the sentence — 'It made itself by itself' — [it follows that] there is no absolute non-existence.

children.text: tasmāddharmāntareṇaivāyamasadvyapadeśaḥ prāgutpatteḥ kāryasya /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the designation as non-existent pertains to the effect prior to origination only in a different sense [than absolute non-existence].

children.text: nāmarūpavyākṛtaṃ hi vastu sacchabdārhaṃ loke prasiddham /
children.translated_text: For a thing that has its names and forms manifested is well known in the world as deserving the designation 'existent.'

children.text: ataḥ prāṅnāmarūpavyākaraṇādasadivāsīdivāsīdityupacaryate // 17 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, prior to the manifestation of names and forms, it is figuratively spoken of as 'it was as if non-existent, it was as if non-existent.' // 17 //

we say: No. For this designation of the effect as non-existent prior to origination is not with the intention of absolute non-existence. Rather — from the property of having manifest names and forms, [the effect passes to] a different property, namely having unmanifest names and forms. It is by this different property that the designation as 'non-existent' is made — of the effect that in fact exists prior to origination, in the form of the cause, non-different [from it]. How is this understood? From the remainder of the sentence. For a sentence whose meaning is doubtful at the beginning is determined by its remainder. And here, that which is referred to at the opening by the word 'non-existent' in 'Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning' — that very same thing, being referred to again by the pronoun 'that,' is qualified as 'existent': 'That was existent' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 3.19.1). And because the word 'was' (<s>āsīt</s>) is inapplicable to the absolutely non-existent, which has no connection with any earlier or later time.

children.text:
FN: agre śūnyamāsīcchūnyādeva jagatabhūditi pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ /
rāddhānte tu idaṃ jagadagre sṛṣṭeḥ prāgasadavyākṛtanāmarūpatvādasattulyamatisūkṣmaṃ brahmaivāsīt /
tato brahmaṇaḥ sat vyākṛtanāmarūpaṃ jagadajāyateti /
children.translated_text: NOTE: The prima facie view is: In the beginning there was a void; from that very void the world arose. But in the established conclusion: this world, in the beginning — prior to creation — was 'non-existent' in the sense of having unmanifest names and forms, i.e., equivalent to non-existence, exceedingly subtle, [and was] <s>Brahman</s> alone. From that <s>Brahman</s>, the existent world with manifest names and forms was born.

children.text: yukteḥ śabdāntarāc ca | BBs_2,1.18 |
children.translated_text: And because of reasoning and another scriptural text. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.18 |

children.text:
yukteśca prāgutpatteḥ kāryasya sattvamananyatvaṃ ca kāraṇādavagamyate, śabdāntarācca /
yuktistāvadvarṇyate- dadhighaṭarucakādyarthibhiḥ pratiniyatāni kāraṇāni kṣīramṛttikāsuvarṇādīnyupādīyamānāni loke dṛśyante /
nahi dadhyarthibhirmṛttikopādīyate na ghaṭārthibhiḥ kṣīraṃ tadasatkāryavāde nopapadyeta /
aviśiṣṭe hi prāgutpatteḥ sarvasya sarvatrāsatve kasmātkṣīrādeva dadhyutpadyate na mṛttikāyāḥ mṛttikāyā eva ca ghaṭa utpadyate na kṣīrāt /
athāviśiṣṭe 'pi prāgasattve kṣīra eva dadhnaḥ kaścidatiśayo na mṛttikāyāṃ, mṛttikāyāmeva ca ghaṭasya kaścidatiśayo na kṣīra ityucyeta, tarhyatiśayavattvātprāgavasthāyā asatkāryavādahāniḥ satkāryavādasiddhiśca /
śaktiśca kāraṇasya kāryaniyamārthā kalpamānā nānyāsatī vā kāryaṃ niyacchet /
asattvāviśeṣādanyatvāviśeṣācca /
tasmātkāraṇasyātmabhūtā śaktiḥ śakteścātmabhūtaṃ kāryam /
apica kāryakāraṇayordravyaguṇādīnāṃ cāśvamahiṣavadbhedabuddhyabhāvāttādātmyamabhyupagantavyam /
samavāyakalpanāyāmapi samavāyasya samavāyibhiḥ saṃbandhe 'bhyupagamyamāne tasya tasyānyonyaḥ saṃbandhaḥ kalpayitavya ityanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ /
anabhyupagamyamāne ca vicchedaprasaṅgaḥ /
atha samavāyaḥ svayaṃ saṃbandharūpatvādanapekṣyaivāparaṃ saṃbandhaṃ saṃbadhyate, saṃyogo 'pi tarhi svayaṃ saṃbandharūpatvādanapekṣyaiva samavāyaṃ saṃbadhyeta /
tādātmyapratīteśca dravyaguṇādīnāṃ samavāyakalpanānarthakyam /
kathaṃ ca kāryamavayavidravyaṃ kāraṇeṣvavayavadravyeṣu vartamānaṃ vartate /
kiṃ samasteṣvavayaveṣu vartetota pratyavayavam /
yadi tāvatsamasteṣu varteta tato 'vayavyanupalabdhiḥ prasajyeta, samastāvayavasamanikarṣasyāśakyatvāt /
nahi bahutvaṃ samasteṣvāśrayeṣu vartamānaṃ vyastāśrayagrahaṇena gṛhyate /
athāvayavaśaḥ samasteṣu varteta tadāpyarambhakāvayavavyatirekeṇāvayavino 'vayavāḥ kalpyeran yairārambhakeṣvavayaveṣvavayavaśo 'vayavī varteta kośāvayavavyatiriktairhyavayavairasiḥ kośaṃ vyāpnoti /
anavasthā caivaṃ prasajyeta /
teṣu teṣvayavayaveṣu vartayitumanyeṣāmavayavānāṃ kalpanīyatvāt /
atha pratyavayavaṃ varteta tadaikatra vyāpāre.'nyatrāvyāpāraḥ syāt /
nahi devadattaḥ snughne saṃnidhīyamānastadahareva pāṭaliputre 'pi saṃnidhīyeta /
yugapadanekatra vṛttāvanekatvaprasaṅgaḥ syāt /
devadattayajñadattayoriva srughnāpāṭaliputranivāsinoḥ /
gotvādivatpratyekaṃ parisamāpterna doṣa iti cet /
na /
tathā pratītyabhāvāt /
yadi gotvādivatpratyekaṃ parisamāpto 'vayavī syādyathā gotvaṃ prativyakti pratyakṣaṃ gṛhyata evamavayavyapi pratyavayavaṃ pratyakṣaṃ gṛhyeta /
nacaivaṃ niyataṃ gṛhyate /
pratyekaparisamāptau cāvayavinaḥ kāryeṇādhikārāttasya caikatvācchṛṅgeṇāpi stanakāryaṃ kuryādurasā ca pṛṣṭhakāryam /
nacaivaṃ dṛśyate /
prāgutpatteśca kāryasyāsattva utpattirakartṛkā nirātmikā ca syāt /
utpacattiśca nāma kriyā, sā sakartṛkaiva bhavitumarhati gatyādivat /
kriyā ca nāma syādakartṛkā ceti vipratiṣidhyeta /
ghaṭasya cetpattirucyamānā na ghaṭakartṛkā kiṃ tarihyanyakartṛketi kalpyā syāt /
tathā kapālādīnāmapyutpattirucyamānānyakartṛkaiva kalpyeta /
tathāca sati ghaṭa utpadyata ityukte kulālādīnāmapyutpadyamānatā pratīyate /
utpannatāpratīteśca /
atha svakāraṇasattāsaṃbandha evotpattirātmalābhaśca kāryasyeti cet, kathamalabdhātmakaṃ saṃbadhyeteti vaktavyam /
satorhi dvayoḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃbhavati na sadasatorasatorvā /
abhāvasya ca nirupākhyatvātprāgutpatteriti maryādākaraṇamanupapannam /
satāṃ hi loke kṣetragṛhādīnāṃ maryādā dṛṣṭā nābhāvasya /
nahi vandhyāputro rājā babhūva prākpūrṇavarmaṇo 'bhiṣekādityevañjātīyakena maryādākāraṇena nirupākhyo vandhyāputro rājā babhūva prākpūrṇavarmaṇo 'bhiṣekādityevañjātīyakena maryādākaraṇena nirupākhyo vandhyaputro rājā babhūva bhavati bhaviṣyatīti vā viśeṣyate /
yadi ca vandyāputro 'pi kārakavyāpārādūrdhvamabhaviṣyattata idamapyupātsyata kāryābhāvo 'pi kārakavyāpārādūrdhvaṃ bhaviṣyatīti /
vayaṃ tu paśyāmo vandyāputrasya kāryābhāvasya cābhāvatvāviśeṣādyathā vandhyāputraḥ kārakavyāpārādūrdhvaṃ na bhaviṣyatyevaṃ kāryābhāvo 'pi kārakavyāpārādūrdhvaṃ na bhaviṣyatīti /
children.translated_text: And from reasoning and from another scripture, the existence of the effect prior to origination and its non-difference from the cause are apprehended. The reasoning is first described: it is seen in the world that those desiring curds, pots, gold ornaments, and such employ specifically determined causes — milk, clay, gold, and such. For those desiring curds do not employ clay, nor do those desiring pots employ milk. This would not be possible on the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect prior to origination (<s>asatkāryavāda</s>). For if everything were equally non-existent everywhere prior to origination, why should curds arise from milk alone and not from clay, and a pot from clay alone and not from milk? If it be said that even though the prior non-existence is undifferentiated, there is some special capacity (<s>atiśaya</s>) in milk alone for curds and not in clay, and in clay alone for a pot and not in milk — then, because the prior state possesses such a special capacity, the <s>asatkāryavāda</s> is abandoned and the <s>satkāryavāda</s> is established. And the capacity (<s>śakti</s>) of the cause, posited for the purpose of determining a particular effect, could not determine the effect if it were different [from the cause] or non-existent. Because there is no distinction in non-existence and no distinction in otherness [that could ground such determination]. Therefore, the capacity is of the nature of the cause, and the effect is of the nature of the capacity. Moreover, because there is no apprehension of difference — as between a horse and a buffalo — between cause and effect, or between substance and quality and such, identity must be accepted. And even if <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) is posited [as the relation between them], if a relation between <s>samavāya</s> and the things inhering is accepted, then for each [such relation] another mutual relation would have to be posited — resulting in an infinite regress. And if [a relation between <s>samavāya</s> and its relata] is not accepted, there would be a contingency of disconnection. And if it is said that <s>samavāya</s>, being itself of the nature of a relation, connects without depending on another relation — then <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) too, being itself of the nature of a relation, would connect without depending on <s>samavāya</s>. And because of the apprehension of identity among substance, quality, and such, the positing of <s>samavāya</s> is purposeless. Moreover, how does the composite substance (<s>avayavin</s>) — the effect — subsist in the component substances (<s>avayava</s>) — the causes? Does it subsist in all the parts collectively, or in each part individually? If it subsists in all collectively, then the composite would become imperceptible, because simultaneous contact with all parts is impossible. For plurality, subsisting in all its substrates collectively, is not apprehended by grasping individual substrates. And if it subsists part-by-part in the collective, then additional parts of the composite — distinct from the originating parts — would have to be posited, by which the composite would subsist part-by-part in the originating parts; for a sword pervades a scabbard through parts distinct from the scabbard's parts. And an infinite regress would follow — because for subsistence in each successive set of parts, further parts would have to be posited. And if it subsists in each part individually, then being active in one place, it would be inactive in another. For <s>Devadatta</s>, being present in <s>Srughna</s>, cannot be present in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> on that same day. If it subsisted simultaneously in many places, then multiplicity would follow — as in the case of <s>Devadatta</s> and <s>Yajñadatta</s> residing in <s>Srughna</s> and <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> [respectively]. If it be said: 'There is no fault, because like <s>gotva</s> (cowness) and such universals, [the composite] is completely present in each [part]' — no. Because there is no such apprehension. If the composite were completely present in each part, like <s>gotva</s> in each individual [cow], then just as <s>gotva</s> is directly perceived in each individual, so too the composite should be directly perceived in each part. But it is not invariably so perceived. And if the composite were completely present in each part, then since the composite would have functional capacity in each part, and since it is one [entity], a horn could perform the function of an udder, and a chest could perform the function of a back. But this is not seen. And if the effect were non-existent prior to origination, then origination would be without an agent and without a self. But origination is indeed an action, and an action must have an agent — like going and such. And [to say] 'it is an action' and 'it is without an agent' would be self-contradictory. And if the origination of a pot is said to be not accomplished by the pot [itself as agent], then it would have to be posited as accomplished by another agent. Similarly, the origination of potsherds and such would also have to be posited as accomplished by another agent. And in that case, when it is said 'the pot originates,' the origination of the potter and others would also be understood. And [that would imply] the understanding that they too have originated. If it be said that origination of the effect is [nothing but] the connection with the existence of its own cause, and that this is the self-attainment of the effect — then one must ask: how can that which has not attained its own being enter into a relation? For a relation is possible between two existing entities, not between an existent and a non-existent, nor between two non-existents. And since non-being is indeterminate (<s>nirupākhya</s>), the setting of a boundary 'prior to origination' is unjustified. For in the world, boundaries are seen for existing things — fields, houses, and such — not for non-being. For a barren woman's son is not delimited as 'a barren woman's son was a king before the coronation of <s>Pūrṇavarman</s>' — [the application of] such boundary-setting to the indeterminate barren woman's son, as 'was, is, or will be a king,' is impossible. And if a barren woman's son too could come into being after the operation of instrumental causes, then this too would follow — that the non-existence of the effect could come into being after the operation of instrumental causes. But we observe that since a barren woman's son and the non-existence of an effect are equally non-existent, just as a barren woman's son will not come into being after the operation of instrumental causes, so too the non-existence of an effect will not come into being after the operation of instrumental causes.

children.text:
nanvevaṃ sati kārakavyāpāro 'narthakaḥ prasajyeta /
yathaiva hi prāksiddhatvātkāraṇasvarūpasiddhaye na kaścidvyāpriyate /
evaṃ prāksiddhatvāttadananyatvācca kāryasya svarūpasiddhaye 'pi na kaścidvyāpriyeta /
vyāpriyate ca /
ataḥ kārakavyāpārārthavattvāya manyāmahe prāgutpatterabhāva /
kāryasyeti /
children.translated_text: But if this is so, the operation of instrumental causes would become purposeless. For just as no one exerts effort to establish the intrinsic nature of the cause, since it is already established beforehand — so too, since the effect is already established beforehand and is non-different from the cause, no one would exert effort to establish its intrinsic nature either. And yet effort is exerted. Therefore, we hold that the effect is non-existent prior to origination — in order to give purpose to the operation of instrumental causes.

children.text:
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
yataḥ kāryākāreṇa kāraṇaṃ vyavastāpayataḥ kārakavyāpārasyārthavattvamapapadyate /
kāryākāro 'pi kāraṇasyātmabhūta evānātmabhūtasyānārabhyatvādityabhāṇi /
naca viśeṣadarśanamātreṇa vastvanyatvaṃ bhavati /
nahi devadattaḥ saṃkocitahastapādaḥ prasāritahastapādaśca viśeṣaṇa dṛśyamāno 'pi vastvanyatvaṃ gacchati, sa eveti pratyabhijñānāt /
tathā pratidinamanekasaṃsthānānāmapi pitrādīnāṃ na vastvanyatvaṃ bhavati, mama pitā mama bhrātā mama putra iti pratyabhijñānāt /
janmocchedānantaritatvāttatra yuktaṃ nānyatreti cet /
children.translated_text: This is not a fault. Because the operation of instrumental causes does have purpose — since it establishes the cause in the form of the effect. And even the form of the effect is of the very nature of the cause — because what is not of the nature [of the cause] cannot be originated. This has been stated. And the mere perception of a distinction does not make something a different entity. For <s>Devadatta</s>, even though seen with a distinction when his hands and feet are contracted versus extended, does not become a different entity — because of recognition [as the same person]. Likewise, even though parents and others assume many different configurations day after day, they do not become different entities — because of recognition: 'my father, my brother, my son.' If one objects: '[Recognition is justified there] because birth and destruction intervene [in other cases], but not here' —

children.text:
na /
kṣīrādīnāmapi dadhyādyākārasaṃsthānasya pratyakṣatvāt /
adṛśyamānānāmapi vaṭadhānādīnāṃ samānajātīyāvayavāntaropacitānāmaṅ kurādibhāvena darśanagocaratāpattau janmasaṃjñā /
teṣāmevāyavānāmapacayavaśādadarśanāpattāvucchedasaṃjñā /
tatredṛgjanmocchedāntaritatvāccedasataḥ sattvapattistathā sati garbhavāsina uttānaśāyinaśca bhedaprasaṅgaḥ /
tathāca bālyayauvanasthāvireṣvapi bhedaprasaṅgaḥ, pitrādivyavahāralopaprasaṅgaśca /
etena kṣaṇabhaṅgavādaḥ prativaditavyaḥ /
yasyapunaḥ prāgutpatterasatkāryaṃ tasya nirviṣayaḥ kārakavyāpāraḥ syāt /
abhāvasya viṣayatvānupapatterākāśahananaprayojanakhaḍgādyanekāyudhaprayuktivat /
children.translated_text: No. Because even for milk and such, the configuration in the form of curds and such is directly perceptible. And for fig seeds and such that are not [initially] visible — when they have accumulated additional parts of the same kind and come within the range of vision in the form of sprouts and such — this is called 'birth.' And when those very parts diminish and fall below the range of vision — this is called 'destruction.' Therein, if from such birth and destruction as these, being (<s>sattva</s>) were to arise from non-being — then there would be the contingency of difference between a fetus in the womb and a newborn lying on its back. And likewise, there would be the contingency of difference between [the same person in] childhood, youth, and old age — and the contingency of the loss of [relational] transactions such as 'father' and such. By this, the doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda</s>) is also answered. But for one who holds that the effect is non-existent prior to origination, the operation of instrumental causes would be without an object. Because non-being cannot serve as an object — like the employment of numerous weapons such as a sword for the purpose of striking space.

children.text: samavāyikāraṇaviṣayaḥ kārakavyāpāraḥ syāditi cet /
children.translated_text: If it be said that the operation of instrumental causes is directed at the material cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) —

children.text:
na /
anyaviṣayeṇa kārakavyāpāreṇānyaniṣpatteratiprasaṅgāt /
samavāyikāraṇasyaivātmātiśayaḥ kāryamiti cet /
children.translated_text: No. Because if an operation directed at one thing were to produce another, there would be over-extension [of the principle]. If it be said that the effect is nothing but a special modification of the material cause itself —

children.text:
na /
satkāryatāpatteḥ /
tasmātkṣīrādīnyeva dravyāṇi dadhyādibhāvenāvatiṣṭhamānāni kāryākhyāṃ labhanta iti na kāraṇādanyatkāryaṃ varṣaśatenāpi śakyaṃ niścetum /
tathā mūlakāraṇamevāntyātkāryāttena tena kāryākāreṇa naṭavatsarvavyavahārāspadatvaṃ pratipadyate /
evaṃ yukteḥ kāryasya prāgutpatteḥ sattvamananyatvaṃ ca kāraṇādavagamyate /
śabdāntarāccaitadavagamyate /
pūrvasūtre 'sadvyapadeśinaḥ śabdasyodāhṛtatvāttato 'nyaḥ sadvyapadeśī śabdaḥ śabdāntaram- 'sadeva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyam' ityādi /
'taddhaika āhurasadevedamagra āsīt' iti cāsatpakṣamupakṣipya 'kathamasataḥ sajjāyeta' ityākṣipya 'sadeva somyedamagra āsīt' (chā. 6.2.1) ityavadhārayati /
tatredaṃśabdavācyasya kāryasya prāgutpatteḥ sacchabdavācyena kāraṇena sāmānādhikaraṇyasya śrūyamāṇatvātsattvānanyatve prasiddhyataḥ /
children.translated_text: Therein, because the co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of the effect — denoted by the word 'this' — with the cause — denoted by the word 'Being' (<s>sat</s>) — prior to origination is heard, its existence and non-difference [from the cause] are established.

children.text: yadi tu prāgutpatterasatkāryaṃ syātpaścāccotpadyamānaṃ kāraṇe samaveyāttadānyakāraṇātsyāt /
children.translated_text: But if the effect were non-existent prior to origination, and if [only] after origination it were to inhere in the cause, then it would be different from the cause.

children.text: tatra 'yenāśrutaṃ śrutaṃ bhavati' (chā. 6.1.3) itīyaṃ pratijñā pīḍyeta /
children.translated_text: In that case, the promise 'By which the unheard becomes heard' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.1.3) would be violated.

children.text: sattvānanyatvāvagatestviyaṃ pratijñā samarthyate // 18 //
children.translated_text: But by the apprehension of [the effect's] existence and non-difference [from the cause], this promise is vindicated. // 18 //

No. Because [that] amounts to the <s>satkāryavāda</s>. Therefore, the substances milk and such, subsisting in the form of curds and such, receive the designation 'effect' — and no effect different from the cause can be determined even in a hundred years. Similarly, the root cause itself, through each successive form of effect, attains the status of being the locus of all transactions — like an actor. Thus from reasoning, the existence of the effect prior to origination and its non-difference from the cause are apprehended. And this is also apprehended from another scripture. Since the scripture that designates [the effect] as existent (<s>sat</s>) was cited in the previous <s>sūtra</s>, another scripture designating it as existent is cited here: 'Being alone, O dear one, this was in the beginning — one only, without a second' and such. And having introduced the position of non-existence — 'Some say: Non-being alone was this in the beginning' — and having rejected it — 'How could Being arise from Non-being?' — [the text] determines: 'Being alone, O dear one, this was in the beginning' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.2.1).

children.text:
FN: atiśayaḥ kāryadharmaḥ kāraṇadharmo vā /
kāryābhāvo 'satkāryamityarthaḥ upāpatsyata upapannamabhaviṣyadityanvayaḥ /
vastvantaratvaṃ paramārthato bhinnatvam /
etena kāraṇasya sarvakāryeṣvanvayakathanena /
vivartavādaṃ vyaktīkartuṃ naṭavadityudāharaṇam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Atiśaya</s>' means a property of the effect or a property of the cause. 'The non-existence of the effect' (<s>kāryābhāva</s>) means <s>asatkārya</s> — this is the meaning. '[It] would have been justified' (<s>upāpatsyata</s>) — the construction is: it would have been established. 'Being a different entity' (<s>vastvantaratva</s>) means being truly distinct. By this — i.e., by describing the continuity of the cause in all effects — the example of the actor is given to make the <s>vivartavāda</s> (doctrine of apparent transformation) explicit.

children.text: paṭavac ca | BBs_2,1.19 |
children.translated_text: And like a cloth. | <s>BBs</s> 2.1.19 |

children.text: yathā ca saṃveṣṭitaḥ paṭo na vyaktaṃ gṛhyate kimayaṃ paṭaḥ kiṃ vānyaddravyamiti /
sa eva prasārito yatsaṃveṣṭitaṃ dravyaṃ tatpaṭa eveti prasāraṇenābhivyakto gṛhyate /
children.translated_text: that very [substance], when spread out — 'what was rolled up is indeed a cloth' — is apprehended as manifested by the spreading out.

children.text: yathāca saṃveṣṭanasamaye paṭa iti gṛhyamāṇe 'pi na viśiṣṭāyāmavistāro gṛhyate sa eva prasāraṇasamaye viśiṣṭāyāmavistāro gṛhyate na saṃveṣṭitarūpādanyo 'yaṃ bhinnaḥ paṭa iti /
children.translated_text: And just as at the time of rolling up, even though it is apprehended as 'a cloth,' the specific dimensions of length and breadth are not apprehended — the same [cloth] at the time of spreading out is apprehended in its specific dimensions of length and breadth, [and it is known:] 'this cloth is not different from and separate from its rolled-up form.'

children.text: evaṃ tantvādikāraṇāvasthaṃ paṭādikāryamaspaṣṭaṃ sat turīvemakuvindādikārakavyāpāradibhirvyaktaṃ spaṣṭaṃ gṛhyate /
children.translated_text: Similarly, the effect — such as cloth — in its causal state as threads and such, being indistinct, becomes distinct and clearly apprehended through the operation of instrumental causes such as the weaver, the spindle, and such.

children.text: ataḥ saṃveṣṭitaprasīritapaṭanyāyenaivānanyatkāraṇātkāryamityarthaḥ // 19 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, by the analogy of the rolled-up and spread-out cloth, the effect is non-different from the cause — this is the meaning. // 19 //
Just as a rolled-up cloth is not clearly apprehended — 'Is this a cloth, or some other substance?' —

children.text: FN: āyāmo dairghyam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Āyāma</s>' means length.

children.text: yathā ca prāṇādiḥ | BBs_2,1.20 |
children.translated_text: And as in the case of <s>Prāṇa</s> and such. | <s>BBs</s> 2.1.20 |

children.text: yathā ca loke prāṇāpānādiṣu prāṇabhedeṣu prāṇāyāmena niruddheṣu kāraṇamātreṇa rūpeṇa vartamāneṣu jīvanamātraṃ kāryaṃ nivartyate nākuñcanaprasāraṇādikaṃ kāryāntaram /
teṣveva prāṇabhedeṣu punaḥ pravṛtteṣu jīvanādadhikamākuñcanaprāsāraṇādikamapi kāryāntaraṃ nirvartyate /
children.translated_text: When those very modifications of <s>Prāṇa</s> resume their activity, then effects beyond mere living — such as contraction, extension, and such — are also produced.

children.text: naca prāṇabhedānāṃ prabhedavataḥ prāṇādanyatvaṃ, samīraṇasvabhāvāviśeṣāt /
children.translated_text: And the modifications of <s>Prāṇa</s>, being differentiated, are not different from <s>Prāṇa</s> — because of no distinction in their nature as air.

children.text: evaṃ kāryasya kāraṇādananyatvam /
children.translated_text: Thus the non-difference of the effect from the cause [is established].

children.text: ataśca kṛtsnasya jagato brahmakāryatvāttadananyatvācca siddhaiṣā śrautī pratijñā 'yenāśrutaṃ śrutaṃ bhavatyamataṃ matamavijñātaṃ vijñātam' (chā. 6.1.1) iti // 20 //
children.translated_text: And since the entire world is an effect of <s>Brahman</s> and is non-different from it, this scriptural promise is established: 'By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.1.1). // 20 //

Just as in the world, when the various modifications of <s>Prāṇa</s> — <s>Prāṇa</s>, <s>Apāna</s>, and such — are restrained through <s>Prāṇāyāma</s> and subsist in the form of the cause alone, only the effect [called] 'mere living' is produced, but not any other effect such as contraction, extension, and such.

children.text: 7 itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇam / sū. 21-23
children.translated_text: 7. The <s>Itaravyapadeśa Adhikaraṇa</s> (Topic of Designation as Other) / <s>Sūtras</s> 21-23

children.text: itaravyapadeśād dhitākaraṇādidoṣaprasaktiḥ | BBs_2,1.21 |
children.translated_text: Because of the designation as other, there would be the contingency of faults such as failure to act for [the world's] benefit. | <s>BBs</s> 2.1.21 |

children.text:
anyathā punaścetanakāraṇavāda ākṣipyate /
cetanāddhi jagatprakriyāyāmāśrīyamāṇāyāṃ hitākaraṇādayo doṣāḥ prasajyante /
kutaḥ /
itaravyapadeśāt /
itarasya śārīrasya brahmātmatvaṃ vyapadiśati śrutiḥ - 'sa ātmā tattvamasi śvetaketo' (chā. 6.8.7) iti prabodhanāt /
yadvā /
itarasya ca brahmaṇaḥ śārīrātmatvaṃ vyapadiśati 'tatsṛṣṭvā tadevānuprāviśat' (tai. 2.6) iti sraṣṭurevāvikṛtasya brahmaṇaḥ kāryānupraveśena śārīrātmatvapradarśanāt /
'anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi' (chā. 6.3.2) iti ca parā devatā jīvamātmaśabdena vyapadiśantī na brahmaṇo bhinnaḥ śārīra iti darśayati /
tasmādyadbrahmaṇaḥ sraṣṭṛtvaṃ taccharīrasyaiveti /
ataḥ sa svatantraḥ kartā san hitamevātmanaḥ saumanasyakaraṃ kuryānnāhitaṃ janmamaraṇajarārogādyanekānarthajālam /
nahi kaścidaparatantro bandhanāgāramātmanaḥ kṛtvānupraviśati /
naca svayamatyantanirmalaḥ sannatyantamalinaṃ dehamātmatvenopeyāt /
kṛtamapi kathañcidyadduḥkhakaraṃ tadicchayā jahyāt /
sukhakaraṃ copādadīta /
smarecca mayedaṃ jagadbimbaṃ vicitraṃ viracitamiti /
sarvo hi lokaḥ spaṣṭaṃ kāryaṃ kṛtvā smarati mayedaṃ kṛtamiti /
children.translated_text: For everyone in the world, having clearly accomplished a task, remembers: 'This was done by me.'

children.text: yathāca māyāvī svayaṃ prasāritāṃ māyāmicchayānāyāsenaivopasaṃharati, evaṃ śārīro 'pīmāṃ sṛṣṭimupasaṃharet /
children.translated_text: And just as a magician effortlessly withdraws by his will the <s>māyā</s> (illusion) he has himself projected, so too the embodied self should withdraw this creation.

children.text: svamapi tāvaccharīraṃ śārīro na śaknotyanāyāsenopasaṃhartum /
children.translated_text: But the embodied self is unable to withdraw effortlessly even its own body.

children.text: evaṃ hitakriyādyadarśanādanyāyyā cetamājjagatprakriyeti gamyate // 21 //
children.translated_text: Thus, because of the non-observation of acting for one's own benefit and such, it is understood that the creation of the world from a conscious [cause] is unreasonable. // 21 //

In yet another way, the doctrine of a conscious cause is challenged.
For when the creation of the world from a conscious [cause] is adopted, faults such as failure to act for one's own benefit and such arise.
Why?
Because of the designation of the other.
The <s>śruti</s> designates the other — the embodied self — as being of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>: 'That Self — thou art that, O <s>Śvetaketu</s>' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.7) — because it awakens [one to that identity].
Alternatively, [the <s>śruti</s>] also designates the other — <s>Brahman</s> — as being of the nature of the embodied self: 'Having created it, he entered into that very [creation]' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 2.6) — because it shows the embodied-selfhood of the creator, the unmodified <s>Brahman</s>, through entry into the effect.
And the supreme deity, designating the <s>jīva</s> with the word '<s>ātman</s>' (self) in 'Having entered with this living self (<s>jīva</s>), let me differentiate names and forms' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.3.2), shows that the embodied self is not different from <s>Brahman</s>.
Therefore, the creatorship that belongs to <s>Brahman</s> belongs to the embodied self too.
Hence, being an independent agent, it should do only what is beneficial for itself — what brings happiness — and not what is harmful: the web of manifold miseries such as birth, death, old age, disease, and the like.
For no one who is independent would build a prison for himself and enter it.
Nor would one who is himself supremely pure take on a supremely impure body as one's self.
Even if [the creation] were somehow already made, he would by his will abandon whatever causes suffering,
and would adopt whatever brings happiness.
And he would remember: 'This variegated image of the world was fashioned by me.'

children.text: adhikaṃ tu bhedanirdeśāt | BBs_2,1.22 |
children.translated_text: But [<s>Brahman</s>] is something more [than the <s>jīva</s>] — because of the designation of difference. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.22 |

children.text:
tuśabdaḥ pakṣaṃ vyāvartayati /
yatsarvajñaṃ sarvaśakti brahma nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaṃ śārīrādadhikamanyat, tadvayaṃ jagataḥ sraṣṭṛ brūmaḥ /
na tasminhitākaraṇādayo doṣāḥ prasajyante /
nahi tasya hitaṃ kiñcitkartavyamastyahitaṃ vā parihartavyaṃ, nityamuktasvabhāvāt /
naca tasya jñānapratibandhaḥ śaktipratibandho vā kvacidapyasti, sarvajñatvātsarvaśaktitvācca /
śārīrastvanevaṃvidhastasminprasajyante hitākaraṇādayo doṣāḥ /
natu taṃ vayaṃ jagataḥ sraṣṭāraṃ brūmaḥ /
kuta etat /
children.translated_text:
The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) turns aside the [prima facie] position.
That <s>Brahman</s> which is omniscient, omnipotent, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and free — which is something more than, something other than the embodied self — that we declare to be the creator of the world.
In that [<s>Brahman</s>], the faults of failure to act for one's own benefit and such do not arise.
For there is nothing beneficial that it needs to accomplish, nor anything harmful that it needs to avoid — because its nature is eternally free.
Nor is there any obstruction to its knowledge or obstruction to its power anywhere — because of its omniscience and omnipotence.
But the embodied self, which is not of such a nature — in its case, faults such as failure to act for one's own benefit and such do arise.
But we do not declare that [embodied self] to be the creator of the world.
How is this [established]?

children.text:
bhedanirdeśāt /
'ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ'' (bṛ. 2.4.5), 'so 'nveṣṭavyaḥ sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ' (chā. 8.7.1), 'satā somya tadā saṃpanno bhavati' (chā. 6.8.1) 'śārīra ātmā prājñenātmanānvārūḍhaḥ' (bṛ. 4.3.35) ityevañjātīyakaḥ kartṛkarmādibhedanirdeśo jīvādadhikaṃ brahma darśayati /
children.translated_text:
Because of the designation of difference.
'The Self, verily, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and deeply meditated upon' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 2.4.5), 'He is to be sought, he is to be inquired into' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 8.7.1), 'Having become united with the Existent, O dear one' (<s>Chāndogya</s> 6.8.1), 'The embodied self, mounted by the knowing self' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.3.35) — designations of difference of this kind — [involving] agent, object, and such — show that <s>Brahman</s> is something more than the <s>jīva</s>.

children.text:
nanvabhedanirdeśo 'pi darśitaḥ 'tattvamasi' ityevañjātīyakaḥ /
kathaṃ bhedābhedau viruddhau saṃbhaveyātām /
children.translated_text: Objection: But a designation of non-difference has also been shown — of the kind 'Thou art That.' How can [both] difference and non-difference, being contradictory, be possible?

children.text:
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
ākāśaghaṭākāśanyāyenobhayasaṃbhavasya tatra tatra pratiṣṭhapitatvāt /
apica yadā tattvamasītyevañjātīyakenābhedanirdeśenābhedaḥ pratibodhito bhavatyapagataṃ bhavati tadā jīvasya saṃsāritvaṃ brahmaṇaśca sraṣṭṛtvaṃ, samastasya mithyājñānavijṛmbhitasya bhedavyavahārasya samyagjñānena bādhitatvāt /
tatra kuta eva sṛṣṭiḥ kuto vā hitākaraṇādayo doṣāḥ /
children.translated_text: In that case, from where would creation [arise], and from where would faults such as failure to act for one's own benefit and such [arise]?

children.text: avidyāpratyupasthāpitanāmarūpakṛtakāryakaraṇasaṃghātopādhyavivekakṛtā hi bhrāntirhitākaraṇādilakṣaṇaḥ saṃsāro natu paramārthato 'stītyasakṛdavocāma /
children.translated_text: For the error characterized as <s>saṃsāra</s> — with its features of failure to act for one's own benefit and such — is caused by the non-discrimination of the limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) constituted by the aggregate of body and instruments, which are effects of name and form presented through <s>avidyā</s>; but it does not exist in ultimate reality — this we have stated repeatedly.

children.text: janmamaraṇacchedanabhedanādyabhimānavat /
children.translated_text: Just like the false identification with birth, death, cutting, splitting, and the like [attributed to the Self].

children.text: abādhite tu bhedavyavahāre 'se 'nveṣṭavyaḥ sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ' ityevañjātīyakena bhedanirdeśenāvagamyamānaṃ brahmaṇo 'dhikatvaṃ hitākaraṇādidoṣaprasaktiṃ niruṇaddhi // 22 //
children.translated_text: But when the conventional activity of difference is not yet sublated, the superiority of <s>Brahman</s> over [the <s>jīva</s>] — understood through designations of difference of the kind 'He is to be sought, he is to be inquired into' — blocks the consequence of the faults of failure to act for one's own benefit and such. // 22 //

This is not a fault.
Because the possibility of both has been established in each case, by the analogy of space and pot-space.
Moreover, when through a designation of non-difference of the kind 'Thou art That,' non-difference is awakened [in the mind], then the <s>jīva</s>'s state of being a transmigrant and <s>Brahman</s>'s state of being a creator both disappear — because the entirety of the conventional activity of difference, which is a manifestation of false knowledge, is sublated by right knowledge.

children.text: aśmādivac ca tadanupapattiḥ | BBs_2,1.23 |
children.translated_text: And the impossibility of those [faults is established] as in the case of stones and such. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.23 |

children.text:
yathā ca loke pṛthivītvasāmānyānvitānāmapyaśmanāṃ kecinmahārhā maṇayo vajravaiḍūryādayo 'nye madhyamavīryāḥ sūryakāntādayo 'nye prahīṇāḥ śvavāyasaprakṣepaṇārhāḥ pāṣāṇā ityanekavidhaṃ vaicitryaṃ dṛśyate /
yathā caikapṛthivīvyapāśrayāṇāmapi bījānāṃ bahuvidhaṃ patrapuṣpaphalagandharasādivaicitryaṃ candanakiṃpākādiṣūpalakṣyate /
yathā caikasyāpyannarasasya lohitādīni keśalomādīni ca vicitrāṇi kāryāṇi bhavanti /
children.translated_text: And just as from even a single food-essence, diverse effects such as blood, hair, body-hair, and the like come into being.

children.text: evamekasyāpi brahmaṇo jīvaprājñapṛthaktvaṃ kāryavaicitryaṃ copapadyata ityastadanupapattiḥ /
children.translated_text: Similarly, even from the one <s>Brahman</s>, the distinctness of the <s>jīva</s> and the omniscient [Lord], and the diversity of effects, is possible — thus those [alleged faults] are impossible.

children.text: paraparikalpitadoṣānupapattirtyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: the impossibility of the faults imagined by the opponent.

children.text: śruteśca prāmāṇyādvikārasya ca vācārambhaṇamātratvātsvapnadṛśyabhāvavaicitryavaccetyabhyuccayaḥ // 23 //
children.translated_text: And because of the authoritativeness of <s>śruti</s>, and because modification is a mere verbal handle (<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>), and as in the variety of things seen in dreams — this is an additional argument. // 23 //

Just as in the world, although stones all share the common nature of being earth, some are precious gems — diamonds, <s>vaiḍūrya</s> (cat's eye), and the like — of great value; others are of middling power — sunstones and the like; and others are worthless — mere rocks fit only for throwing at dogs and crows — thus manifold variety is seen.
And just as in seeds, all supported by the same earth, manifold variety of leaves, flowers, fruits, fragrances, flavors, and such is observed in sandalwood, <s>kiṃpāka</s> (poison fruit), and the like.

children.text: FN: kiṃpāko mahātālaphalam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Kiṃpāka</s>' is the great palm fruit.

children.text: 8 upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇam. sū. 24-25
children.translated_text: 8. The <s>Upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa</s> (Topic of the Observation of Assembling [Means]). <s>Sūtras</s> 24-25.

children.text: upasaṃhāradarśanān neti cen na kṣīravad dhi | BBs_2,1.24 |
children.translated_text: If [it be said that <s>Brahman</s> cannot be the cause] because of the observation of assembling [means] — [we say] no, because it is like milk. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.24 |

children.text:
cetanaṃ brahmaikamadvitīyaṃ jagataḥ kāraṇamiti yaduktaṃ tannopapadyate /
kasmāt /
upasaṃhāradarśanāt /
iha hi loke kulālādayo ghaṭapaṭādīnāṃ kartāro mṛddaṇḍacakrasūtrādyanekakārakopasaṃhāreṇa saṃgṛhītasādhanāḥ santastattatkāryaṃ kurvāṇā dṛśyante /
brahma cāsahāyaṃ tavābhipretaṃ tasya sādhanāntarānupasaṃgrahe sati kathaṃ sraṣṭṛtvamupapadyeta /
tasmānna brahma jagatkāraṇamiti cet /
children.translated_text:
The claim that conscious <s>Brahman</s>, one without a second, is the cause of the world — that is not tenable.
Why?
Because of the observation of assembling [means].
For in the world, makers of pots, cloth, and such — potters, weavers, and the like — are seen to accomplish their respective products only by assembling many instruments such as clay, sticks, wheels, threads, and the like.
But <s>Brahman</s>, as you conceive it, is without assistance — so in the absence of assembling other means, how could its creatorship be tenable?
Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is not the cause of the world — if this is the objection,

children.text:
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
yataḥ kṣīravaddravyasvabhāvaviśeṣādupapadyate /
yathā hi loke kṣīraṃ jalaṃ vā svayameva dadhihimabhāvena pariṇamate 'napekṣya bāhyaṃ sādhanaṃ tathehāpi bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text:
this is not a fault.
Because, like milk, it is possible due to the specific nature of the substance.
For just as in the world, milk or water transforms by itself into curds or ice, without depending on any external means — so too it will be here.

children.text: nanu kṣīrādyapi dadhyādibhāvena pariṇāmamānapekṣata eva bāhyaṃ sādhanamauṣṇyādikaṃ kathamucyate kṣīravaddhīti /
children.translated_text: Objection: But even milk, in transforming into curds and such, does depend on an external means such as heat and the like — how then can it be said 'like milk'?

children.text:
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
svayamapi hi kṣīraṃ yāṃ ca yāvatīṃ ca pariṇāmamātramanubhavati tāvatyeva tvāryate tvauṣṇyādinā dadhibhāvāya /
yadi ca svayaṃ dadhibhāvaśīlatā na syānnaivauṣṇyādināpi balāddadhibhāvamāpadyeta /
nahi vāyurākāśo vauṣṇyadinā balāddadhibhāvamāpadyate /
sādanasāmagryā ca tasya pūrṇatā saṃpādyate /
paripūrṇaśaktikaṃ tu brahma /
children.translated_text: But <s>Brahman</s> possesses complete power.

children.text: na tasyānyena kenacitpūrṇatā saṃpādayitavyā /
children.translated_text: Its completeness does not need to be brought about by anything else.

children.text: śrutiśca bhavati- 'na tasya kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ ca vidyate na tatsamaścābhyadhikaśca dṛśyate /
children.translated_text: And there is a <s>śruti</s>: 'No effect or instrument is known of It; none equal to or superior to It is seen.

children.text: parāsya śaktirvividhaiva śrūyate svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā ca //
children.translated_text: Its supreme power is heard to be of various kinds — knowledge, strength, and action are its inherent nature'

This is not a fault.
For whatever transformation milk undergoes by itself, and to whatever extent — to exactly that extent it is hastened by heat and such toward becoming curds.
And if it did not have the inherent tendency (<s>śīlatā</s>) to become curds by itself, it would not become curds even when forced by heat and such.
For air or space does not become curds when forced by heat and such.
And it is the completeness of the aggregate of means that is brought about [by the external agent].

children.text: ' (śve. 6.2) iti /
children.translated_text: (<s>Śvetāśvatara</s> 6.8).

children.text: tasmādekasyāpi brahmaṇo vicitraśaktiyogātkṣīrādivadvicitrapariṇāma upapadyate // 24 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, even from <s>Brahman</s> alone, because of its possession of manifold powers, a variegated transformation is possible, just as from milk and such. // 24 //

children.text:
FN: kārakāṇāmupasaṃhāro melanam /
tvāryate śaighryaṃ kāryate kṣīraṃ dadhibhāvamauṣṇyādinā /
children.translated_text:
Footnote: '<s>Kārakāṇām upasaṃhāra</s>' means the assembling of instruments.
'<s>Tvāryate</s>' means [the milk] is hastened — [i.e.,] the milk is hastened toward becoming curds by heat and such.

children.text: devādivad api loke | BBs_2,1.25 |
children.translated_text: And as in the case of gods and such, even in the world. | <s>BBs</s> 2,1.25 |

children.text:
syādetat /
upapadyate kṣīrādīnāmacetanānāmanapekṣyāpi bāhyaṃ sādhanaṃ dadhyādibhāvaḥ, dṛṣṭatvāt /
cetanāḥ punaḥ kulālādayaḥ sādhanasāmagrīmapekṣyaiva tasmai kāryāya pravartamānā dṛśyante /
kathaṃ brahma cetanaṃ sadasahāyaṃ pravarteteti /
devādivaditi brūmaḥ /
