children.translated_text: One might say: just as a certain person endowed with the capacity of vision but lacking the capacity of movement — a lame man — mounts upon another person endowed with the capacity of movement but lacking the capacity of vision — a blind man — and directs him; or just as a lodestone, itself unmoving, moves iron — so too <s>Puruṣa</s> will set <s>Pradhāna</s> in motion. This is a renewed objection based on the confidence of examples.

children.text:
atrocyate- tathāpi naiva doṣānnirmokṣo 'sti /
abhyupetahānaṃ tāvaddoṣa āpatati /
pradhānasya svatantrasya pravṛttyabhyupagamāt, puruṣasya na pravartakatvānabhyupagamāt /
kathaṃ codāsīnaḥ puruṣaḥ pradhānaṃ pravartayet /
paṅgurapi hyandhaṃ vāgādibhiḥ puruṣaṃ pravartayati /
naivaṃ puruṣasya kaścidapi pravartanavyāpāro 'sti, niṣkriyatvācca /
nāpyayaskāntavatsaṃnidhimātreṇa pravartayet /
saṃnidhinityatvena pravṛttinityatvaprasaṅgāt /
ayaskāntasya tvanityasaṃnidherasti svavyāpāraḥ saṃnidhiḥ, parimārjanādyapekṣā cāsyastītyanupanyāsaḥ puruṣāśmavaditi /
tathā pradhānasyācaitanyātpuruṣasya caudāsīnyāttṛtīyasya ca tayoḥ saṃbandhayiturabhāvātsaṃbandhānupapattiḥ /
children.translated_text: Similarly, since <s>Pradhāna</s> is insentient and <s>Puruṣa</s> is indifferent, and there is no third entity to bring them into relation, the relation [between them] is impossible.

children.text: yogyatānimitte ca saṃbandhe yogyatānucchedādanirmokṣaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: And if the relation is based on fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) as its ground, then since the fitness is never destroyed, there would be the contingency of no liberation.

children.text: pūrvavaccehāpyarthābhāvo vikalpayitavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here too, the absence of purpose should be considered as before.

children.text: paramātmanastu svarūpavyapāśrayamaudāsīnyaṃ māyāvyapāśrayaṃ ca pravartakatvamityastyatiśayaḥ // 7 //
children.translated_text: But for the Supreme Self, the indifference pertains to Its own essential nature, while the motive power pertains to <s>Māyā</s> — thus there is a [crucial] distinction. // 7 //

To this it is replied: even so, there is no liberation from the fault. First, the fault of abandoning one's own accepted position arises — because [you have already] accepted that <s>Pradhāna</s> acts independently, and [you have] not accepted that <s>Puruṣa</s> has any motive power. How would the indifferent <s>Puruṣa</s> set <s>Pradhāna</s> in motion? Even the lame man directs the blind man through speech and such. But <s>Puruṣa</s> has no operation of direction whatsoever, because of its absolute inactivity. Nor can it set [<s>Pradhāna</s>] in motion by mere proximity, as a lodestone does — because, since the proximity is permanent, the activity would also be permanent. But the lodestone, whose proximity is not permanent, has its own operation [that brings about] proximity — namely, rubbing and such.

children.text: aṅgitvānupapatteś ca | BBs_2,2.8 |
children.translated_text: And because of the impossibility of being a component (<s>aṅgin</s>). | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.8 |

children.text: itaśca na pradhānasya pravṛttiravalpate /
children.translated_text: For this further reason, the activity of <s>Pradhāna</s> is not justified.

children.text: yaddhi sattvarajastamasāmānyonyaguṇapradhānabhāvamutsṛjya sāmyena svarūpamātreṇāvasthānaṃ sā pradhānāvasthā /
children.translated_text: For the state in which <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, and <s>Tamas</s> — abandoning the relationship of being subordinate and principal to one another — abide in equilibrium, in their mere essential nature alone, that is the state of <s>Pradhāna</s>.

children.text: tasyāmavasthāyāmanapekṣasvarūpāṇāṃ svarūpapraṇāśabhayātparasparaṃ pratyaṅgibhāvānupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: In that state, since the <s>guṇas</s> — whose essential natures are independent [of each other] — cannot become subordinate components (<s>aṅga</s>) of one another, because of the fear of destroying their essential natures,

children.text: bāhyasya ca kasyacitkṣobhayiturabhāvādguṇavaiṣamyanimitto mahadādyutpādo na syāt // 8 //
children.translated_text: and since there is no external disturber, the origination of <s>Mahat</s> and such — which is caused by the disequilibrium of the <s>guṇas</s> — would not occur. // 8 //

children.text: anyathānumitau ca jñaśaktiviyogāt | BBs_2,2.9 |
children.translated_text: And if the inference is [made] otherwise, because of the absence of the capacity of knowledge. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.9 |

children.text:
athāpi syādanyathā vayamanumimīmahe yathā nāyamanantaro doṣaḥ prasajyeta /
nahyanapekṣasvabhāvāḥ kūṭasthāścāsmābhirguṇā abhyupagamyante pramāṇābhāvāt /
kāryavaśena tu guṇānāṃ svabhāvo 'bhyupagamyate /
children.translated_text: Even if one were to say: 'We infer otherwise, such that this immediately preceding fault would not arise — for we do not accept, for lack of evidence, that the <s>guṇas</s> have independent, immutable natures. Rather, the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> is accepted on the basis of their effects.'

children.text:
yathā yathā kāryotpāda upapadyate tathā tathaiṣāṃ svabhāvo 'bhyupagamyate /
calaṃ guṇavṛttamiti cāstyabhyupagamaḥ /
tasmātsāmyāvasthāyāmapi vaiṣamyopagamayogyā eva guṇā avatiṣṭhanta iti /
evamapi pradhānasya jñaśaktiviyogādracanānupapattyādayaḥ pūrvoktā doṣāstadavasthā eva /
jñaśaktimapi tvanumimānaḥ prativāditvānnivarteta /
children.translated_text: 'In whatever way the origination of effects is possible, in that very way the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> is accepted. And there is the accepted principle: "the functioning of the <s>guṇas</s> is dynamic." Therefore, even in the state of equilibrium, the <s>guṇas</s> abide as fit to enter disequilibrium' — even so, the faults previously stated — such as the impossibility of intelligent design — remain as they are, because of <s>Pradhāna</s>'s lack of the capacity of knowledge. And one who infers [for <s>Pradhāna</s>] even the capacity of knowledge would thereby cease to be an opponent —

children.text: cetanamekamanekaprapañcasya jagata upādānamiti brahmavādaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: because it would amount to the <s>Brahman</s> doctrine — that a single sentient entity is the material cause of the world with its manifold phenomenal expansion.

children.text: vaiṣamyopagamayogyā api guṇāḥ sāmyāvasthāyāṃ nimittābhāvānnaiva vaiṣamyaṃ bhajeran /
children.translated_text: And even though the <s>guṇas</s> are fit to enter disequilibrium, in the state of equilibrium they would never enter disequilibrium — because of the absence of an efficient cause.

children.text: bhajamānā vā nimittābhāvāviśeṣātsarvadaiva vaiṣamyaṃ bhajeranniti prasajyata evāyamanantaro 'pi doṣaḥ // 9 //
children.translated_text: Or if they were to enter [disequilibrium] — then because of the equal absence of an efficient cause [at all times], they would always be in disequilibrium. Thus this immediately preceding fault also follows. // 9 //

children.text: vipratiṣedhāc cāsamañjasam | BBs_2,2.10 |
children.translated_text: And because of [internal] contradictions, [the Sāṃkhya system] is inconsistent. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.10 |

children.text:
parasparaviruddhaścāyaṃ sāṃkhyānāmabhyupagamaḥ /
kvacitsaptendriyāṇyanukrāmanti, kvacidekādaśa /
tathā kvacinmahatastanmātrasargamupadiśanti, kvacidahaṅkīrāt /
tathā kvacittrīṇyantaḥkaraṇāni varṇayanti kvacidekamiti /
prasiddha eva tu śrutyeśvarakāraṇavādinyā virodhastadanuvartinyā ca smṛtyā /
tasmādapyasamañjasaṃ sāṃkhyānāṃ darśanamiti /
children.translated_text: The acceptance of the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> is also mutually contradictory. In some places they enumerate seven sense organs; in others, eleven. Similarly, in some places they teach the creation of the <s>tanmātras</s> from <s>Mahat</s>; in others, from <s>Ahaṃkāra</s>. Similarly, in some places they describe three internal organs (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>); in others, one. And the conflict with <s>śruti</s>, which teaches the Lord as the cause, and with <s>Smṛti</s> that follows [<s>śruti</s>], is already well established. Therefore, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine is also inconsistent.

children.text:
atrāha- nanvaupaniṣadānāmapyasamañjasameva darśanaṃ tapyatāpakayorjātyantarabhāvānabhyupagamāt /
ekaṃ hi brahma sarvātmakaṃ sarvasya prapañcasya kāraṇamabhyupagacchatāmekasyaivātmano viśeṣau tapyatāpakau na jātyantarabhūtāvityabhyupagantavyaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: Here the objection is raised: is not the doctrine of the <s>Upaniṣads</s> also inconsistent, because of not accepting a difference of kind between the one who is scorched and the one who scorches? For those who accept that one <s>Brahman</s> — the Self of all — is the cause of the entire phenomenal world, must accept that the scorched and the scorcher are [merely] modifications of one and the same Self, not of different kinds.

children.text:
yadi cetau tapyatāpakāvekasyātmano viśeṣau syātāṃ sa tābhyāṃ tapyatāpakābhyāṃ na nirmucyata iti tāpopaśāntaye samyagdarśanamupadiśacchāstramanarthakaṃ syāt /
nahyauṣṇyaprakāśadharmakasya pradīpasya tadavasthasyaiva tābhyāṃ nirmokṣa upapadyate /
yo 'pijalataraṅgavīcīphenādyupanyāsaḥ, tatrāpi jalātmana ekasya vīcyādanyo viśeṣā āvirbhāvatirobhāvarūpeṇa nityā eveti samāno jalātmano vīcyādibhiranirmokṣaḥ /
prasiddhaścāyaṃ tapyatāpakayorjātyantarabhāvo loke /
tathāhi- arthī cārthaścānyonyabhinnau labhyete /
yadyarthinaḥ svato 'nyor'tho na syāt, yasyārthino yadviṣayamarthitvaṃ sa tasyārtho nityasiddha eveti na tasya tadviṣayamarthitvaṃ syāt, yathā prakāśātmanaḥ pradīpasya prakāśākhyortho nityasiddha eveti na tasya tadviṣayamarthitvaṃ bhavati /
aprāpte hyarthe 'rthino 'rthitvaṃ syāditi /
tathārthāsyāpyarthatvaṃ na syāt /
yadi syātsvārthatvameva syāt /
nacaitadasti /
saṃbandhiśabdo hyetāvarthī cārthaśceti /
dvayośca saṃbandhinoḥ saṃbandhaḥ syānnaikasyaiva /
tasmādbhinnāvetāvarthārthinau /
tathānarthānarthināvapi /
arthino 'nukūlor'thaḥ pratikūlo 'narthastābhyāmekaparyāyeṇobhābhyāṃ saṃbadhyate /
tatrārthasyālpīyastvādbhūyastvāccānarthasyobhāvapyarthānarthāvanarthaṃ eveti tāpakaḥ sa ucyate /
tapyastu puruṣo ya ekaḥ paryāyeṇobhābhyāṃ saṃbadhyata iti tayostapyatāpakayorekātmatāyāṃ mokṣānupapattiḥ /
jātyantarabhāve tu tatsaṃyogahetuparihārātsyādapi kadācinmokṣopapattiriti /
children.translated_text: And if the scorched and the scorcher were modifications of one and the same Self, then that Self would not be liberated from those two — the scorched and the scorcher. And so the scripture that teaches right knowledge for the cessation of suffering would be purposeless. For a lamp possessing the properties of heat and light cannot be liberated from those [properties] while remaining in that very condition. And as for the illustration of water, waves, ripples, foam, and such — even there, the modifications such as waves are eternally present in the form of manifestation and de-manifestation for the one whose nature is water. So the one whose nature is water is equally unliberated from waves and such. And this difference of kind between the scorched and the scorcher is well established in the world. For instance, the one who desires and the object desired are apprehended as mutually different,

children.text:
atrocyate- na /
ekatvādeva tapyatāpakabhāvānupapatteḥ /
bhavedeṣa doṣo yadyekātmatāyāṃ tapyatāpakāvānyonyasya viṣayaviṣayibhāvaṃ pratipadyeyātām /
natvetadastyekatvādeva /
nahyagnirekaḥ sansvamātmānaṃ dahati prakāśayati vā satyapyauṣṇyaprakāśādidharmabhede pariṇāmitve ca /
kiṃ kūṭasthe brahmaṇyekasmiṃstapyatāpakabhāvaḥ saṃbhavet /
kva punarayaṃ tapyatāpakabhāvaḥ syāditi /
children.translated_text: To this it is replied: No. Because of the very oneness [of <s>Brahman</s>], the relationship of scorched and scorcher is impossible. This fault would arise if, despite the oneness of the Self, the scorched and the scorcher were to enter into the relationship of object and subject with each other. But this does not exist, precisely because of oneness. For fire, being one, does not burn or illumine itself — even though it has distinct properties of heat and illumination, and even though it undergoes transformation. How much less could the relationship of scorched and scorcher occur in the one, immutable <s>Brahman</s>? But then where does this relationship of scorched and scorcher exist?

children.text: ucyate- kiṃ na paśyasi karmabhūto jīvaddehastapyastāpakaḥ saviteti /
children.translated_text: It is replied: do you not see that the living body, which is the sphere of action, is the scorched and the sun is the scorcher?

children.text:
nanu taptirnāma duḥkhaṃ sā cetayiturnācetanasya dehasya /
yadi hi dehasyaiva taptiḥ syātsā dehanāśe svayameva naśyatīti tannāśāya sādhanaṃ naiṣitavyaṃ syāditi /
children.translated_text: But is not scorching by name suffering, and that belongs to the sentient one, not to the insentient body? For if the scorching belonged to the body alone, it would perish of its own accord with the destruction of the body, and no means would need to be sought for its destruction.

children.text:
ucyate- dehābhāve 'pi kevalasya cetanasya taptirna dṛṣṭā /
naca tvayāpi taptirnāma vikriyā cetayituḥ kevalasyeṣyate /
nāpi dehacetanayoḥ saṃhatatvamaśuddhyādidoṣaprasaṅgāt /
naca taptereva taptimabhyupagacchati /
children.translated_text: It is replied: even in the absence of the body, scorching of the sentient one alone [without a body] is not seen. Nor is scorching — which is a modification — accepted even by you as [belonging to] the sentient one in isolation. Nor is there a composite of body and sentient being — because of the contingency of faults such as impurity. Nor does one accept that scorching is scorched by itself [i.e., suffering is not self-referential].

children.text: kathaṃ tavāpi tapyatāpakabhāvaḥ sattvaṃ tapyaṃ tāpakaṃ raja iti cet /
children.translated_text: If you ask: 'How then is the relationship of scorched and scorcher [possible] in your own system — <s>Sattva</s> is the scorched and <s>Rajas</s> is the scorcher?' —

children.text:
na /
tābhyāṃ cetanasya saṃhatatvānupapatteḥ /
sattvānurodhitvāccetano 'pi tapyata iveti cet, paramārthatastarhi naiva tapyata ityāpatatīvaśabdaprayogāt /
na cettapyate nevaśabdo doṣāya /
nahi ḍuṇḍubhaḥ sarpaṃ ivetyetāvatā saviṣo bhavati /
sarpo vā ḍuṇḍubha ivetyetāvatā nirviṣo bhavati /
ataścāvidyākṛto 'yaṃ tapyatāpakabhāvo na pāramārthika ityabhyupagantavyamiti /
naivaṃ sati mamāpi kiñcidduṣyati /
atha pāramārthikameva cetanasya tapyatvamabhyupagacchasi tavaiva sutarāmanirmokṣaḥ prasajyeta , nityatvābhyupagamācca tāpakasya /
tapyatāpakaśaktyornityatve 'pi sanimittasaṃyogāpekṣatvāpatteḥ saṃyoganimittādarśananivṛttāvātyantikaḥ saṃyogoparamaḥ, tataścātyantiko mokṣa upapanna iti cet /
children.translated_text: No. Because for the conscious [Self], the state of being composite is untenable through those two [<s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s>]. [Objection:] Because the conscious [Self] conforms to <s>sattva</s>, it is as though it suffers — [Reply:] Then in ultimate reality it does not suffer at all — this follows from the use of the word 'as though' (<s>iva</s>). And if it does not [really] suffer, the word [<s>iva</s>] does not constitute a fault. For a <s>ḍuṇḍubha</s> (non-venomous snake) does not become venomous merely because one says 'like a snake' — nor does a snake become non-venomous merely because one says 'like a <s>ḍuṇḍubha</s>.' And therefore it must be accepted that this relation of heater and heated is created by <s>avidyā</s>, not ultimately real. And in that case, nothing of mine is compromised either. But if you accept that the suffering of the conscious [Self] is ultimately real, then for you especially, the impossibility of liberation would follow — and also because the heater [i.e., <s>Pradhāna</s>] is accepted as eternal. [Objection:] Even though the capacities of heater and heated are eternal, since the conjunction [of <s>Puruṣa</s> and <s>Prakṛti</s>] depends on a cause, when that cause — namely, non-discrimination — ceases, the conjunction ceases absolutely, and therefore absolute liberation is tenable —

children.text: na /
adarśanasya tamaso nityatvābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: Because darkness (<s>tamas</s>), which is non-discrimination, is accepted [by you] as eternal.

children.text: guṇānāṃ codbhāvābhibhavayoraniyatatvādaniyataḥ saṃyoganimittoparama iti viyogasyāpyaniyatatvātsāṃkhyasyaivānirmokṣo 'parihāryaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: And because the emergence and submergence of the <s>guṇas</s> are not fixed, the cessation of the cause of conjunction is also not fixed. Therefore, since disjunction too is not fixed, it is the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> [system] itself for which the impossibility of liberation is unavoidable.

children.text: aupaniṣadasya tvātmaikatvābhyupagamādekasya ca viṣayaviṣayibhāvānupapattervikārabhedasya ca vācārambhaṇamātratvaśravaṇādanirmokṣaśaṅkā svapne 'pi nopajāyate /
children.translated_text: But for the follower of the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, since the oneness of the Self is accepted, and since the relation of subject and object is untenable for one [non-dual Self], and since the differentiation of modifications is heard to be merely a verbal handle (<s>vācārambhaṇamātra</s>) — the doubt of impossibility of liberation does not arise even in dream.

children.text: vyavahāre tu yatra yathā dṛṣṭastapyatāpakabhāvastatra tathaiva sa iti na codayitavyaḥ parihartavyo vā bhavati // 10 //
children.translated_text: But in conventional activity, wherever and however the relation of heater and heated is observed, it is just so — and is not to be objected to or resolved. // 10 //
No.

children.text: FN: tvaḍyātrameva hi buddhīndriyamanekarūpādigrahaṇasamarthamekaṃ, sarmendriyāṇi pañca, saptamaṃ ca mana iti saptendriyāṇi /
children.translated_text: Footnote: For <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) alone is one [sense-organ] capable of grasping many forms and the like; the five sense-organs; and the mind as the seventh — thus seven sense-organs.

children.text: jñānendriyāṇi pañca karmendriyāṇi pañca manaścetyekādaśa /
children.translated_text: Five organs of knowledge, five organs of action, and mind — thus eleven.

children.text: buddhirahaṅkāro mana iti trāṇi /
children.translated_text: <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect), <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), and <s>manas</s> (mind) — three.

children.text: ekamiti buddhireva /
children.translated_text: 'One' means <s>buddhi</s> alone.

children.text: 2 mahaddīrghādhikaraṇam / sū. 11
children.translated_text: Section 2: <s>Mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa</s> / <s>Sūtra</s> 11

children.text:
pradhānakāraṇavādo nirākṛtaḥ /
paramāṇukāraṇavāda idānīṃ nirākartavyaḥ /
tatrādau tāvadyo 'ṇuvādinā brahmavādini doṣa utprekṣyate sa pratisamādhīyate /
tatrāyaṃ vaiśeṣikāṇāmabhyupagamaḥ - kāraṇadravyasamavāyino guṇāḥ kāryadravye samānajātīyaṃ guṇāntaramārabhante, śuklebhyastantubhyaḥ śuklasya paṭasya prasavadarśanāttadviparyayādarśanācca /
tasmāccetanasya brahmaṇo jagatkāraṇatve 'bhyupagamyamāne kārye 'pi jagati cetanyaṃ samaveyāt /
tadadarśanāttu na cetanaṃ brahma jagatkāraṇaṃ bhavitumarhatīti /
imamabhyupagamaṃ tadīyayaiva prakriyayā vyabhicārayati-
children.translated_text: The doctrine of <s>Pradhāna</s> as the cause has been refuted. The doctrine of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) as the cause is now to be refuted. Therein, first, the fault that the atomist imagines in the <s>Brahman</s>-doctrine is resolved. The position of the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> is as follows: the qualities inhering in the cause-substance produce a quality of the same class in the effect-substance — because the production of a white cloth from white threads is observed, and the contrary is not observed. Therefore, if the causality of the world by the conscious <s>Brahman</s> were accepted, consciousness would also inhere in the world as effect. But since that [universal consciousness in the world] is not observed, the conscious <s>Brahman</s> is not fit to be the cause of the world. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes this position by [showing] a deviation in their own procedure —

children.text: mahaddīrghavad vā hrasvaparimaṇḍalābhyām | BBs_2,2.11 |
children.translated_text: <s>Mahaddīrghavad vā hrasvaparimaṇḍalābhyām</s> — Or, [the production of what is] great and long from what is small and spherical [is analogous]. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.11 |

children.text:
eṣā teṣāṃ prakriyā- paramāṇavaḥ kila kañcitkālamanārabdhakāryā yathāyogaṃ rūpādimantaḥ pārimaṇḍalyaparimāṇaśca tiṣṭhanti /
te ca paścādadṛṣṭādipuraḥsarāḥ saṃyogasacivāśca santo dvyaṇukādikrameṇa kṛtsnaṃ kāryajātamārabhante /
kāraṇaguṇāśca kārye guṇāntaram /
yadā dvau paramāṇū dvyaṇukamārabhete tadā paramāṇugatā rūpādiguṇaviśeṣāḥ śuklādayo dvyaṇuke śaklādīnaparānārabhante /
paramāṇuguṇaviśeṣastu pārimāṇḍalyaṃ na dvyaṇuke pārimāṇḍalyamaparamārabhate, dvyaṇukasya parimāṇāntarayogābhyupagamāt /
aṇutvahrasvatve hi dvyamukavartinī parimāṇe varṇayanti /
yadāpi dve dvyaṇuke caturaṇukamārabhete tadāpi samānaṃ dvyaṇukasamavāyināṃ śuklādīnāmārambhakatvam /
aṇutvahrasvatve tu dvyaṇukasamavāyinī api naivārabhete, caturaṇukasya mahattvādīrghatvaparimāṇayogābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: This is their procedure: The atoms, they say, remain for some time without having produced any effect, possessing qualities such as color and the like as appropriate, and having the dimension of sphericality (<s>pārimaṇḍalya</s>). Subsequently, preceded by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) and the like, and assisted by conjunction, they produce the entire class of effects in the sequence of dyads and so forth. And the qualities of the cause [produce] another quality in the effect. When two atoms produce a dyad, the specific qualities such as whiteness and the like residing in the atoms produce other [qualities] — such as whiteness and the like — in the dyad. But the specific quality of atoms — sphericality — does not produce another sphericality in the dyad, because the dyad is accepted as possessing a different dimension. For they describe the dimensions present in the dyad as subtlety (<s>aṇutva</s>) and shortness (<s>hrasvatva</s>). And when two dyads produce a tetrad, likewise, the productive capacity of whiteness and the like inhering in the dyads is the same. But subtlety and shortness, even though inhering in the dyads, do not produce [themselves in the tetrad] — because the tetrad is accepted as possessing the dimensions of greatness (<s>mahattva</s>) and length (<s>dīrghatva</s>).

children.text:
yadāpi bahavaḥ paramāṇavo bahūni vā dvyaṇukāni dvyaṇukasahito vā paramāṇuḥ kāryamārabhate tadāpi samānaiṣā yojanā /
tadevaṃ yathā paramāṇoḥ parimaṇḍalātsato 'ṇu hrasvaṃ ca dvyaṇukaṃ jāyate mahaddīrghaṃ ca tryaṇukādi na parimaṇḍalam, yathā vā dvyaṇukādaṇorhrasvācca sato mahaddīrghaṃ ca tryaṇukaṃ jāyate nāṇu no hrasvam, evaṃ cetanādbrahmaṇo 'cetanaṃ jagajjaniṣyata ityabyupagame kiṃ tava cchinnam /
atha manyase virodhinā parimāṇāntareṇākrāntaṃ kāryadravyaṃ dvyaṇukādītyato nārambhakāṇi kāraṇagatāni pārimaṇḍalyādīnītyabhyupagacchāmi, natu cetanāvirodhinā guṇāntareṇa jagata ākrāntatvamasti, yena kāraṇagatā cetanā kārye cetanāntaraṃ nārabheta /
nahyacetanā nāma cetanāvirodhī kaścidguṇo 'sti, cetanāpratiṣedhamātratvāt /
tasmātpārimāṇḍalyādivaiṣamyātprāpnoti cetanāyā ārambhakatvamiti /
children.translated_text: And even when many atoms or many dyads, or an atom combined with a dyad, produce an effect — the same arrangement [applies]. Thus, just as from the spherical atom, a dyad arises that is subtle and short, and a triad and so forth that are great and long — not spherical; and just as from the subtle and short dyad, a triad arises that is great and long — not subtle and not short — so too, from the conscious <s>Brahman</s>, the insentient world will arise. What [argument] of yours is undermined by this acceptance? If you think: the effect-substance — the dyad and so forth — is pervaded by a contrary dimension, and therefore the sphericality and such residing in the cause are not productive — but the world is not pervaded by any quality contrary to consciousness, by which the consciousness residing in the cause would not produce another consciousness in the effect — [we reply:] For there is no quality called 'insentiency' that is contrary to consciousness, since it is merely the negation of consciousness. Therefore, by the analogy with the anomaly of sphericality and such, the non-productive character of consciousness is established.

children.text:
naivaṃ maṃsthāḥ /
yathā kāraṇe vidyamānānāmapi pārimāṇḍalyādināmanārambhakatvamevaṃ caitanyasyāpītyasyāṃśasya samānatvāt /
naca parimāṇāntarakrāntatvaṃ pārimāṇḍalyādīnāmārambhakatvopapatteḥ /
ārabdhamapi kāryadravyaṃ prāgguṇārambhātkṣaṇamātramaguṇaṃ tiṣṭhatītyabhyupagamāt /
naca parimāṇāntarārambhe vyagrāṇi pārimāṇḍalyādīnītyataḥ svasamānajātīyaṃ parimāṇāntaraṃ nārabhante parimāṇāntarasyānyahetutvābhyupagamāt /
'kāraṇabahutvātkāraṇamahatvātpracayaviśeṣācca mahat' (vai. sū. 7.1.9) 'tadviparītamaṇu' (7.1.10 ) 'etena dīrghatvahrasvatve vyākhyāte' (7.1.17) iti hi kāṇabhujāni sūtrāṇi /
naca saṃnidhānaviśeṣātkutaśctkāraṇabahutvādīnyevārabhante na pārimāṇḍalyādīnītyucyeta, dravyāntare guṇāntare vārabhyamāṇe sarveṣāmeva kāraṇaguṇānāṃ svāśrayasamavāyaviśeṣāt /
tasmātsvabhāvādeva pārimāṇḍalyādīnāmanārambhakatvaṃ, tathā cetanāyā apīti draṣṭavyam /
saṃyogācca dravyādīnāṃ vilakṣaṇānāmutpattidarśanātsamānajātīyotpattivyabhicāraḥ /
dravye prakṛte guṇodāharaṇamayuktamiti cet /
children.translated_text: You should not think so. Just as sphericality and such, even though present in the cause, are non-productive — so too consciousness [may be non-productive]: this part [of the argument] is common [to both sides]. And the non-productivity of sphericality and such is not [due to] being pervaded by a contrary dimension. Because it is accepted that even the produced effect-substance stands for a moment without qualities, prior to the production of qualities. And it is not the case that sphericality and such, being engaged in producing a contrary dimension, therefore do not produce a dimension of their own class — because a contrary dimension is accepted as having another cause. For the <s>sūtras</s> of <s>Kaṇāda</s> say: 'Greatness [arises] from the multiplicity of causes, from the greatness of causes, and from a special arrangement' (<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 7.1.9); 'The contrary is subtlety' (7.1.10); 'By this, length and shortness are explained' (7.1.17). And one should not say: because of a special proximity, only the multiplicity of causes and such are productive, not the sphericality and such — for when a new substance or quality is being produced, all the qualities of the cause have the same special relation of inherence in their substratum. Therefore, the non-productivity of sphericality and such is by nature itself — and so too should it be seen for consciousness. And from conjunction, the production of substances and such that are dissimilar [to their causes] is observed — hence there is a deviation from [the rule of] same-class production. [Objection:] When the subject is substance, an illustration from quality is inappropriate —

children.text:
na /
dṛṣṭāntena vilakṣaṇārambhamātrasya vivakṣitatvāt /
naca dravyasya dravyamevodāhartavyaṃ guṇasya vā guṇa eveti kaścinniyame heturasti /
sūtrakāro 'pi bhavatāṃ dravyasya guṇamudājahāra- 'pratyakṣāpratyakṣāṇāmapratyakṣatvātsaṃyogasya pañcātmakaṃ na vidyate' (vai. sū. 4.2.2) iti /
yathā pratyakṣāpratyakṣayorbhūmyākāśayoḥ samavayansaṃyogo 'pratyakṣa evaṃ pratyakṣāpratyakṣeṣu pañcasu bhūteṣu samavayaccharīramapratyakṣaṃ syāt /
pratyakṣaṃ hi śarīram /
tasmānna pāñcabhautikamiti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati- guṇaśca saṃyogo dravyaṃ śarīram /
'dṛśyate tu' (bra. sū. 2.1.6) iti cātrāpi vilakṣaṇotpattiḥ prapañcitā /
children.translated_text: No. Because only the production of what is dissimilar is intended by the illustration. And there is no reason for the rule that a substance must be illustrated only by a substance, or a quality only by a quality. Your own <s>sūtrakāra</s> [<s>Kaṇāda</s>] too illustrated a substance by a quality: 'Because conjunction — of the perceptible and the imperceptible — is imperceptible, there is no five-elemental [body]' (<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 4.2.2). Just as conjunction, inhering in the perceptible and imperceptible — earth and space — is itself imperceptible, so too the body, inhering in the five perceptible and imperceptible elements, should be imperceptible. But the body is perceptible. Therefore it is not composed of five elements — [this is the argument]. What is stated [here] amounts to this: conjunction is a quality, and the body is a substance [yet one is used to illustrate the other]. And in the [<s>sūtra</s>] 'But it is observed' (<s>BBs</s> 2.1.6), the production of what is dissimilar was elaborated upon in this context too.

children.text: nanvevaṃ sati tenaivaitadgatam /
children.translated_text: Objection: If so, that [point] was already covered by that [earlier <s>sūtra</s>].

children.text:
neti brūmaḥ /
tatsāṃkhyaṃ pratyuktam, etattu vaiśeṣikaṃ prati /
children.translated_text: We say: No. That was directed against the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>; but this is directed against the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>.

children.text: nanvatideśo 'pi samānanyāyatayā kṛtaḥ 'etena śiṣṭāparigrahā api vyākhyātāḥ' (bra.sū. 2.1.12) iti /
children.translated_text: Objection: But the extension too was made by virtue of the common reasoning: 'By this, those not accepted by the learned are also explained' (<s>BBs</s> 2.1.12).

children.text: satyametat /
children.translated_text: That is true.

children.text: tasyaiva tvayaṃ vaiśeṣikaprakriyārambhe tatprakriyānugatena nidarśanena prapañcaḥ kṛtaḥ // 11 //
children.translated_text: But this is an elaboration of that very [extension], at the commencement of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>-procedure, by means of an illustration that follows their own procedure. // 11 //

children.text: FN: paramāṇuḥ parimaṇḍalaḥ tadgataṃ parimāṇaṃ pārimāṇḍalyam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: An atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>) is spherical; the dimension residing in it is sphericality (<s>pārimaṇḍalya</s>).

children.text: dve dve iti paṭhitavyam /
children.translated_text: 'Two, two' — this is how it should be read.

children.text: 3 paramāṇujagadakāraṇatvādhikaraṇam / sū. 12-17
children.translated_text: Section 3: <s>Paramāṇujagadakāraṇatvādhikaraṇa</s> / <s>Sūtras</s> 12-17

children.text: ubhayathāpi na karmātastadabhāvaḥ | BBs_2,2.12 |
children.translated_text: <s>Ubhayathāpi na karmātas tadabhāvaḥ</s> — In either case, [the initial motion of atoms is] not from <s>karma</s>; therefore, that [production] does not exist. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.12 |

children.text:
idānīṃ paramāṇukāraṇavādaṃ nirākaroti /
sa ca vāda itthaṃ samuttiṣṭhata- paṭādīni hi loke sāvayavāni dravyāṇi svānugateraiva saṃyogasacivaistantvādibhirdravyairārabhyamāṇāni dṛṣṭāni /
tatsāmānyena yāvatkiñcitsāvayavaṃ tatsarvaṃ svānugateraiva saṃyogasacivaistairdravyairārabdhamiti gamyate /
sa cāyamavayavāvayavivibhāgo yato nivartate so 'pakarṣaparyantagataḥ paramāṇuḥ /
sarvaṃ cedaṃ jagadgirisamudrādikaṃ sāvayavaṃ, sāvayavatvāccādyantavat /
nacākāraṇena kāryeṇa bhavitavyamityataḥ paramāṇavo jagataḥ kāraṇamiti kaṇabhugabhiprāyaḥ /
tānīmāni catvāri bhūtāni bhūmyudakatejaḥpavanākhyāni sāvayavānyupalabhya caturvidhāḥ paramāṇavaḥ parikalpyante teṣāṃ cāpakarṣaparyantagatatvena parato vibhāgāsaṃbhavādvanaśyatāṃ pṛthivyādīnāṃ paramāṇuparyanto vibhāgo bhavati sa pralayakālaḥ /
tataḥ sargakāle ca vāyavīyeṣvaṇuṣvadṛṣṭāpekṣaṃ karmotpadyate tatkarma svāśrayamaṇumaṇvantareṇa saṃniyukti tato dvyaṇukādikrameṇa vāyurutpadyate /
evamagnirevamāpa evaṃ pṛthivī /
evameva śarīraṃ sendriyamiti /
evaṃ sarvamidaṃ jagadaṇubhyaḥ saṃbhavati /
aṇugatebhyaśca rūpādibhyo dvyaṇukādigatāni rūpādīni saṃbhavanti tantupaṭanyāyeneti kāṇādā manyante /
tatredamabhidhīyate- vibhāgāvasthānāṃ tāvadaṇūnāṃ saṃyogaḥ karmāpekṣo 'bhyupagantavyaḥ, karmavatāṃ tantvādīnāṃ saṃyogadarśanāt /
karmaṇaśca kāryatvānnimittaṃ kimapyabhyupagantavyam /
anabhyupagame nimittābhāvānnāṇuṣvādyaṃ karmasyāt /
abhyupagame 'pi yadi prayatno 'bhighātādirvā (athā)yathādṛṣṭaṃ kimapi karmaṇo nimittamabhyupagamyeta tasyāsaṃbhavānnaivāṇuṣvādyaṃ karma syāt /
nahi tasyāmavasthāyāmātmaguṇaḥ prayatnaḥ saṃbhavati śarīrābhāvāt /
śarīrapratiṣṭhe hi manasyātmanaḥ saṃyoge satyātmaguṇaḥ prayatno jāyate /
etenābhighātādyapi dṛṣṭaṃ nimittaṃ pratyākhyatavyam /
sargottarakālaṃ hi tatsarvaṃ nādyasya karmaṇo nimittaṃ saṃbhavati /
athādṛṣṭamādyasya karmaṇo nimittamityucyeta tatpunarātmasamavāyi vā syādaṇusamavāyi vā /
ubhayathāpi nādṛṣṭanimittamaṇuṣu karmāvakalpetādṛṣṭasyācetanatvāt /
nahyacetanaṃ cetanenānadhiṣṭhitaṃ svatantraṃ pravartate pravartayati veti sāṃkhyaprakriyāyāmabhihitam /
ātmanaścānutpannacaitanyasya tasyāmavasthāyāmacetanatvāt /
ātmasamavāyitvābhyupagamācca nādṛṣṭamaṇuṣu karmaṇo nimittaṃ syādasaṃbandhāt /
adṛṣṭavatā puruṣeṇāstyaṇūnāṃ saṃbandha iti cet, saṃbandhasātatyātpravṛttisātatyaprasaṅgo niyāmakāntarābhāvāt /
tadevaṃ niyatasya kasyacitkarmanimittasyābhāvānnāṇuṣvādyaṃ karma syāt /
karmābhāvāttanibandhanaḥ saṃyogo na syāt /
saṃyogābhāvācca tannibandhanaṃ dvyaṇukādi kāryajātaṃ na syāt /
saṃyogaścāṇoraṇvantareṇa sarvātmanā vā syādekadeśena vā /
sarvātmanā cedupacayānupapatteraṇumātratvaprasaṅgo dṛṣṭaviparyayaprasaṅgaśca /
pradeśavato dravyasya pradeśavatā dravyāntareṇa saṃyogasya dṛṣṭatvāt /
ekadeśena cetsāvayavatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
paramāṇūnāṃ kalpitāḥ pradeśāḥ syuriti cet /
kalpitānāmavastutvādavastveva saṃyoga iti vastunaḥ kāryasyāsamavāyikāraṇaṃ na syāt /
asati cāsamavāyikāraṇe dvyaṇukādikāryadravyaṃ notpadyeta /
yathācādisarge nimittābhāvātsaṃyogotpattyarthaṃ karma nāṇūnāṃ saṃbhavatyevaṃ mahāpralaye 'pi vibhāgotpattyarthaṃ karma naivāṇūnāṃ saṃbhavet /
nahi tatrāpi kiñcinniyataṃ tannimittaṃ dṛṣṭamasti /
children.translated_text: For there too, no determinate cause for that [action of separation] is observed.

children.text: adṛṣṭamapi bhogaprasiddhyarthaṃ na pralayaprasiddhyarthamityato nimittābhāvānna syādaṇūnāṃ saṃyogotpattyarthaṃ vibhāgotpattyarthaṃ vā karma /
children.translated_text: And <s>adṛṣṭa</s> too is [intended] for the accomplishment of experience (<s>bhoga</s>), not for the accomplishment of dissolution — therefore, because of the absence of a cause, there would be no action in the atoms for the purpose of producing either conjunction or separation.

children.text: ataśca saṃyogavibhāgābhāvāttadāyattayoḥ sargapralayayorabhāvaḥ prasajyeta /
children.translated_text: And therefore, because of the absence of conjunction and separation, the absence of creation and dissolution — which depend on them — would follow.

children.text: tasmādanupapanno 'yaṃ paramāṇukāraṇavādaḥ // 12 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, this doctrine of atomic causation is untenable. // 12 //

Now [the <s>sūtrakāra</s>] refutes the doctrine of atomic causation.
That doctrine arises thus: In the world, composite substances such as cloth and the like are seen to be produced by substances such as threads and the like, which are [themselves] conjoined with conjunction and related to their own [component parts].
By analogy, whatever is composite — all of it — is understood to be produced by substances conjoined with conjunction and related to their own [component parts].
And the limit of this division of parts and wholes — that to which it extends when taken to its ultimate reduction — is the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>).
And this entire world — mountains, oceans, and such — is composite; and being composite, it has a beginning and an end.
And since an effect must have a cause, the atoms are the cause of the world — such is the view of <s>Kaṇabhuj</s> (<s>Kaṇāda</s>).
Observing the four elements called earth, water, fire, and air to be composite, four kinds of atoms are postulated. And since, having reached the limit of ultimate reduction, further division is impossible — when earth and such are destroyed, division proceeds down to the atoms; that is the time of dissolution.
Then, at the time of creation, in the atoms of air, action arises dependent on <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit); that action conjoins its substratum atom with another atom; then, by the sequence of dyads and so forth, air is produced.
Likewise fire, likewise water, likewise earth.
And likewise the body with its sense-organs.
Thus this entire world arises from atoms.
And from the forms (color, etc.) residing in the atoms, the forms residing in dyads and so forth arise, by the analogy of threads and cloth — so the <s>Kaṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣikas) think.
To this we say: For atoms in the state of separation, conjunction must be accepted as dependent on action (<s>karma</s>), because conjunction is observed [to depend on action] in things possessing action, such as threads and the like.
And since action is an effect, some cause must also be accepted.
If no [cause] is accepted, then — due to the absence of a cause — the initial action would not arise in the atoms.
Even if [a cause is] accepted, if effort (<s>prayatna</s>), impact (<s>abhighāta</s>), or some other observed cause of action is accepted — [the initial action] would still not arise in the atoms, because of the impossibility of that [cause].
For in that state [prior to creation], effort — which is a quality of the self — is impossible, because there is no body.
For effort, which is a quality of the self, arises only when there is a conjunction of the self with the mind that is established in a body.
By this, impact and other observed causes too are to be rejected.
For all of those are possible only after creation, not as causes of the initial action.
If <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) is said to be the cause of the initial action — well, that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> would either inhere in the self or inhere in the atom.
In either case, the initial action in the atoms cannot be conceived as caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, because <s>adṛṣṭa</s> is insentient.
For an insentient thing, not superintended by a sentient [being], does not independently operate or cause [another] to operate — this was stated in the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> section.
And the self too, in that state, is insentient because consciousness has not yet arisen [in it].
And if <s>adṛṣṭa</s> is accepted as inhering in the self, it would not be the cause of action in the atoms — because there is no connection [between the self's <s>adṛṣṭa</s> and the atoms].
If it be said that the person possessing <s>adṛṣṭa</s> has a connection with the atoms — then, because of the continuity of the connection, the consequence of the continuity of activity [would follow], since there is no other restricting factor.
Thus, because of the absence of any determinate cause of the initial action, the initial action would not arise in the atoms.
In the absence of action, the conjunction dependent on it would not arise.
And in the absence of conjunction, the entire class of effects dependent on it — dyads and so forth — would not arise.
And the conjunction of one atom with another would be either with the atom's entire [being] or with one part of it.
If with the entire [being], then because increase in size would be impossible, the consequence would be that [the product] remains of atomic size — and this would contradict observation.
Because in the world, the conjunction of one substance having parts with another substance having parts is observed.
If with one part [of the atom], then the consequence of having parts [would follow for the atom].
If it be said that the atoms have imagined parts —
then, since imagined [parts] are unreal, the conjunction too would be unreal — and so it could not be the non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) of a real effect.
And in the absence of a non-inherent cause, the product substance — dyad and so forth — would not be produced.
And just as at the beginning of creation, action does not arise in the atoms for the purpose of producing conjunction because of the absence of a cause — so too at the time of great dissolution, action for the purpose of producing separation would likewise not arise in the atoms.

children.text:
FN: svānugataiḥ svasaṃbaddhaiḥ /
saṃbandhaścādhāryādhārabhūtaḥ pratyayahetuḥ samudāyaḥ /
children.translated_text:
Footnote: '<s>Svānugataiḥ</s>' means related to their own [components].
And the relation is the aggregate that serves as the basis for the cognition of container and contained.

children.text: samavāyābhyupagamāc ca sāmyād anavasthiteḥ | BBs_2,2.13 |
children.translated_text: And because of the acceptance of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) — [there would be] an infinite regress, due to the equal [applicability of the argument]. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.13 |

children.text:
samavāyābhyupagamācca tadabhāva iti prakṛtenāṇuvādanirākaraṇena saṃbadhyate /
dvābhyāṃ cāṇubhyāṃ dvyaṇukamutpadyamānamatyantabhinnamaṇubhyāmaṇvoḥ samavaitītyabhyupagamyate bhavatā /
nacaivamabhyupagacchatā śakyate 'ṇukāraṇatā samarthayitum /
kutaḥ /
sāmyādanavasthiteḥ /
yathaiva hyaṇubhyāmatyantabhinnaṃ sadvyaṇukaṃ samavāyalakṣaṇena saṃbandhena tābhyāṃ saṃbadhyata evaṃ samavāyo 'pi samavāyibhyo 'tyantabhinnaḥ sansamavāyalakṣaṇenānyenaiva saṃvandhena samavāyibhiḥ saṃbadhyetātyantabhedasāmyāt /
tataśca tasya tasyānyonyaḥ saṃbandhaḥ kalpayitavya ityanavasthaiva prasajyeta /
children.translated_text:
'And because of the acceptance of <s>samavāya</s>, there would be the absence of that [atomic causation]' — this connects with the ongoing refutation of the atomic doctrine.
When a dyad is produced from two atoms, it is accepted by you that [the dyad], being absolutely different from the atoms, inheres (<s>samavaiti</s>) in the atoms.
But one who accepts this cannot justify atomic causation.
Why?
Because of the equal [applicability of the argument], there would be an infinite regress.
For just as the dyad, being absolutely different from the atoms, is connected with them by a relation characterized as <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) — so too <s>samavāya</s> itself, being absolutely different from the things in which it inheres, should be connected with those things by yet another relation characterized as <s>samavāya</s> — because of the equal applicability [of the argument] of absolute difference.
And then, for each successive [relation], yet another mutual relation would have to be postulated — and so an infinite regress would follow.

children.text:
nanviha pratyayagrāhyaḥ samavāyo nityasaṃbaddha eva samavāyibhirgṛhyate nāsaṃbaddhaḥ saṃbandhāntarāpekṣo vā /
tataśca na tasyānyaḥ saṃbandhaḥ kalpayitavyo yenānavasthā prasajyeteti /
children.translated_text:
Objection: But <s>samavāya</s>, being apprehended through cognition, is always grasped as already connected with the things in which it inheres — never as unconnected or as requiring another relation.
Therefore, no other relation need be postulated for it, by which an infinite regress would follow.

children.text:
netyucyate /
saṃyogo 'pyevaṃ sati saṃyogibhirnityasaṃbaddha eveti samavāyavannānyaṃ saṃbandhamapekṣeta /
athārthāntaratvātsaṃyogaḥ saṃbandhāntaramapekṣeta, samavoyo 'pi tarhyarthāntaratvātsaṃbandhāntaramapekṣeta /
naca guṇatvātsaṃyogaḥ saṃbandhāntaramapekṣate na samavāyo 'guṇatvāditi yujyate vaktum /
apekṣākāraṇasya tulyatvāt /
guṇaparibhāṣāyāścātantratvāt /
children.translated_text: And because the definition of '<s>guṇa</s>' (quality) is not determinative [of this issue].

children.text: tasmādarthāntaraṃ samavāyamabhyupagacchataḥ prasajyetaivānavasthā /
children.translated_text: Therefore, for one who accepts <s>samavāya</s> as a separate category, an infinite regress would indeed follow.

children.text: prasajyamānāyāṃ cānavasthāyāmekāsiddhau sarvāsiddherdvābhyāmaṇubhyāṃ dvyaṇuka naivotpadyeta /
children.translated_text: And when an infinite regress follows, since the failure of one [step] entails the failure of all, the dyad would never be produced from two atoms.

children.text: tasmādapyanupapannaḥ paramāṇukāraṇavādaḥ // 13 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, for this reason too, the doctrine of atomic causation is untenable. // 13 //

This is not so, we reply.
If that were the case, conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) too would always be connected with the things conjoined — just like <s>samavāya</s> — and would not require another relation.
But if conjunction, being a different category, requires another relation, then <s>samavāya</s> too, being a different category, should require another relation.
Nor is it proper to say that conjunction, because it is a quality (<s>guṇa</s>), requires another relation, while <s>samavāya</s>, because it is not a quality, does not.
Because the ground for requiring [another relation] is the same [in both cases].

children.text: nityam eva ca bhāvāt | BBs_2,2.14 |
children.translated_text: [The atoms would be] eternally [active or inactive] — because of the permanent existence [of their nature]. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.14 |

children.text:
apicāṇavaḥ pravṛttisvabhāvā vā nivṛttisvabhāvā vobhayasvabhāvā vānubhayasvabhāvā vābhyupagamyante gatyantarābhāvāt /
caturdhāpi nopapadyate /
pravṛttisvabhāvatve nityameva pravṛtterbhāvātpralayābhāvaprasaṅgaḥ /
nivṛttisvabhāvatve 'pi nityameva nivṛtterbhāvātsargābhāvaprasaṅgaḥ /
ubhayasvabhāvatvaṃ ca virodhādasamañjasam /
children.translated_text: And having both natures would be inconsistent, because of their mutual contradiction.

children.text: anubhayasvabhāvatve tu nimittavaśātpravṛttinivṛttyorabhyupagamyamānayoradṛṣṭādernimittasya nityasaṃnidhānānnityapravṛttiprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: If they are of neither nature — and activity and cessation are accepted as arising from an external cause such as <s>adṛṣṭa</s> and the like — then, because that cause is permanently present, the consequence of perpetual activity [would follow].

children.text: atantratve 'pyadṛṣṭāderanityāpravṛttiprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: And if <s>adṛṣṭa</s> and the like are not determinative [i.e., not always operative], then the consequence of never having activity [would follow].

children.text: tasmādapyanupapannaḥ paramāṇukāraṇavādaḥ // 14 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, for this reason too, the doctrine of atomic causation is untenable. // 14 //

Moreover, the atoms are accepted as being either of the nature of activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), or of the nature of cessation (<s>nivṛtti</s>), or of both natures, or of neither nature — since there is no fifth alternative.
In all four cases, [the doctrine] is untenable.
If they are of the nature of activity, then — because activity would permanently exist — the consequence would be the absence of dissolution.
If they are of the nature of cessation, then — because cessation would permanently exist — the consequence would be the absence of creation.

children.text: rūpādimattvāc ca viparyayo darśanāt | BBs_2,2.15 |
children.translated_text: And because [the atoms] possess form (color, etc.), the reverse [of what is intended follows] — because it is so observed. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.15 |

children.text:
sāvayavānāṃ dravyāṇāmavayavavaśo vibhajyamānānāṃ yataḥ paro vibhāgo na saṃbhavati te caturvidhā rūpādimantaḥ paramāṇavaścaturvidhasya rūpādimato bhūtabhautikasyārambhakā nityāśceti yadvaiśeṣikā abhyupagacchanti sa teṣāmabhyupagamo nirālambana eva /
yato rūpādimattvātparamāṇūnāmaṇutvanityatvaviparyayaḥ prasajyeta /
paramakāraṇāpekṣayā sthūlatvamanityatvaṃ ca teṣāmabhipretaviparītamāpadyetetyarthaḥ /
kutaḥ /
evaṃ loke dṛṣṭatvāt /
yadi loke rūpādimadvastu tatsvakāraṇāpekṣayā sthūlamanityaṃ ca dṛṣṭam /
tadyathā paṭastantūnapekṣya sthūle 'nityaśca bhavati tantavaścaṃśūnapekṣya sthūlā anityāśca bhavanti, tathācāmī paramāṇavo rūpādimantastairabhyupagamyante, tasmātte 'pi kāraṇavantastadapekṣayā sthūlā anityāśca prāpnuvanti /
yacca nityatve kāraṇaṃ tairuktam- 'sadakāraṇavannityam' (vai. sū. 4.1.1) iti /
tadapyevaṃ satyaṇuṣu na saṃbhavati /
uktena prakāreṇāṇūnāmapi kāraṇavattvopapatteḥ /
yadapi nityatve dvitīyaṃ kāraṇamuktam- 'anityamiti ca viśeṣataḥ pratiṣedhābhāvaḥ' (vai. sū. 4.1.4) iti /
tadapi nāvaśyaṃ paramāṇūnāṃ nityatvaṃ sādhayati /
asati hi yasminkasmiṃścinnitye vastuni nityaśabdena nañaḥ samāso nopapadyate /
na punaḥ paramāṇunityatvamevāpekṣyate /
children.translated_text:
When composite substances are divided according to their parts, the four kinds of atoms — possessing form (color, etc.) — at which further division is impossible, are accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas as the originators of the four kinds of physical and derivative [substances] possessing form, and as eternal. That acceptance of theirs is without any foundation.
Because, from the atoms' possessing form and such, the reverse of their being atomic and eternal would follow.
The meaning is: With respect to the ultimate cause, grossness and impermanence — the opposite of what they intend — would befall [the atoms].
Why?
Because it is thus observed in the world.
In the world, whatever substance possesses form and such is observed to be gross and impermanent relative to its own cause.
Just as cloth, relative to threads, is gross and impermanent; and threads, relative to fibers, are gross and impermanent — so too these atoms are accepted by them as possessing form and such; therefore they too would have causes, and would be gross and impermanent relative to those [causes].
And the reason they give for eternality — 'What exists and is without a cause is eternal' (<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 4.1.1) —
that too, this being so, does not apply to the atoms.
Because, by the method stated, the atoms too are shown to have causes.
As for the second reason they give for eternality — 'And the absence of a [specific] negation establishes impermanence by [reference to] specific [causes only]' (<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 4.1.4) —
that too does not necessarily establish the eternality of atoms.
For if there were no eternal substance at all, the compound of the negative particle '<s>na</s>' with the word '<s>nitya</s>' (eternal) would not be possible.
But it is not the case that only the eternality of atoms is required [for this].

children.text:
taccāstyeva nityaṃ paramakāraṇaṃ brahma /
naca śabdārthavyavahāramātreṇa kasyacidarthasya prasiddhirbhavati, pramāṇāntarasiddhayoḥ śabdārthayorvyavahārāvatārāt /
yadapi nityatve tṛtīyaṃ kāraṇamuktam- 'avidyā ca' (vai. sū. 4.1.5) iti, tadyadyevaṃ vivrīyate satāṃ paridṛśyamānakāryāṇāṃ kāraṇānāṃ pratyakṣeṇāgrahaṇamavidyeti, tato dvyaṇukanityatāpyāpadyeta /
athādravyatve satīti viśeṣyeta tathāpyakāraṇavattvameva nityatānimittamādyeta /
tasya ca prāgevoktatvāt 'avidyā ca' iti punaruktaṃ syāt /
athāpi kāraṇavibhāgātkāraṇavināśāccanyasya tṛtīyasya vināśahetorasaṃbhavo 'vidyā sā paramāṇūnāṃ nityatvaṃ khyapayatīti vyākhyāyeta /
nāvaśyaṃ vinaśyadvastu dvābhyāmeva hetubhyāṃ vinaṣṭumarhatiti niyamo 'sti /
saṃyogasacive hyanekasmiṃśca dravye dravyāntarasyārambhake 'bhyupagamyamāna etadevaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: For this [rule] would hold only if a composite substance, in conjunction with many [component substances], were accepted as the originator of another substance.

children.text: yadā tvapāstaviśeṣaṃ sāmānyātmakaṃ kāraṇaṃ viśeṣavadavasthāntaramāpadyamānamārambhakamabhyupagamyate tadā ghṛtakāṭhinyavilayanavanmūrtyavasthāvilayanenāpi vināśa upapadyate /
children.translated_text: But when a cause — undifferentiated, of the nature of universality — is accepted as originating another state with specific properties, then destruction is possible even by the dissolution of the state of solidity — as in the melting and solidification of ghee.

children.text: tasmādrūpādimattvātsyādabhipretaviparyayaḥ paramāṇūnām /
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of possessing form and such, the reverse of what is intended would befall the atoms.

children.text: tasmādapyanupapannaḥ paramāṇukāraṇavādaḥ // 15 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, for this reason too, the doctrine of atomic causation is untenable. // 15 //

For there exists the eternal supreme cause — <s>Brahman</s>.
And the establishment of any meaning does not come about by mere verbal usage (<s>śabdārthavyavahāra</s>) alone, since verbal usage applies only to meanings already established by another means of knowledge.
As for the third reason they give for eternality — '<s>avidyā</s> ca' ('and ignorance') (<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 4.1.5) — if this is interpreted to mean that the non-apprehension by perception of the causes of things whose effects are visible is '<s>avidyā</s>' (ignorance, i.e., the absence of knowledge of a cause) — then the eternality of dyads too would follow [since their atomic causes are not perceptible].
If it were qualified by 'provided it is not a substance' — even then, only the absence of a cause would be inferred as the ground for eternality.
And since that has already been stated [in the first <s>sūtra</s>], '<s>avidyā ca</s>' would be a mere repetition.
Alternatively, if it is explained as: the impossibility of a third cause of destruction — other than the separation of the cause-parts and the destruction of the cause — is the '<s>avidyā</s>' that proclaims the eternality of atoms — even so, there is no rule that a destructible thing can be destroyed only by these two causes.

children.text: ubhayathā ca doṣāt | BBs_2,2.16 |
children.translated_text: And because of faults in either case. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.16 |

children.text:
gandharasarūpasparśaguṇā sthūlā pṛthivī, rūparasasparśaguṇāḥ sūkṣmā āpaḥ, rūpasparśaguṇaṃ sūkṣmataraṃ tejaḥ, sparśaguṇaḥ sūkṣmatamo vāyurityevametāni catvāri bhūtānyupacitāpacitaguṇāni sthūlasūkṣmatarasūkṣmatamatāratamyopetāni ca loke lakṣyante /
tadvatparamāṇavo 'pyupacitāpacitaguṇāḥ kalpyeranna vā /
ubhayathāpi ca doṣānuṣaṅgo 'parihārya eva syāt /
kalpyamāne tāvadupacitāpacitaguṇatva upacitaguṇānāṃ mūrtyupacayādaparamāṇutvaprasaṅgaḥ /
nacāntareṇāpi mūrtyupacayaṃ guṇopacayo bhavatītyucyate, kāryeṣu bhūteṣu guṇopacaye mūrtyupacayadarśanāt /
akalpyamāne tūpacitāpacitaguṇatve paramāṇutvasāmyaprasiddhaye yadi tāvatsarvaṃ ekaikaguṇā eva kalpyeraṃstatastejasi sparśasyopalabdhirna syāt, apsu rūpasparśayoḥ, pṛthivyāṃ ca rasarūpasparśānāṃ,
children.translated_text: Earth is gross, possessing the qualities of smell, taste, form, and touch; water is subtle, possessing the qualities of form, taste, and touch; fire is subtler still, possessing the qualities of form and touch; air is the subtlest, possessing the quality of touch alone — thus these four elements, with their increasing and decreasing qualities and their gradations of gross, subtle, subtler, and subtlest, are observed in the world. Correspondingly, the atoms too might or might not be imagined as having increasing and decreasing qualities. And in both cases, the consequence of a fault would be inescapable. If they are imagined as having increasing and decreasing qualities, then for those with more qualities, there would be the contingency of non-atomicity due to the increase in material bulk. And it cannot be said that qualities increase even without an increase in material bulk — because in the gross elements that are effects, when qualities increase, an increase in material bulk is observed. But if increasing and decreasing qualities are not imagined — then, to establish that all atoms are the same, if each were imagined as having only one quality, then in fire the perception of touch would not occur, in water the perception of form and touch [would not occur], and in earth the perception of taste, form, and touch [would not occur],

children.text: kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvātkāryaguṇānām /
children.translated_text: because the qualities of the effect are preceded by [and depend on] the qualities of the cause.

children.text: atha sarve caturguṇā eva kalpyetan, tato 'psvapi gandhasyopalabdhiḥ syāt, tejasi gandharasayoḥ, vāyau gandharūparasānām /
children.translated_text: And if all [atoms] were imagined as having four qualities each, then smell would be perceived even in water, smell and taste in fire, and smell, form, and taste in air.

children.text: nacaivaṃ dṛśyate /
children.translated_text: But this is not observed.

children.text: tasmādapyanupapannaḥ paramāṇukāraṇavādaḥ // 16 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the doctrine of atoms as the cause is untenable from this perspective as well. // 16 //

children.text: FN: mūrtyupacayāt sthaulyādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: NOTE: 'Because of the increase in material bulk' means because of grossness — this is the meaning.

children.text: aparigrahāc cātyantam anapekṣā | BBs_2,2.17 |
children.translated_text: And because of the complete non-acceptance [by learned authorities], [atoms] are to be utterly disregarded. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.17 |

children.text:
pradhānakāraṇavādo vedavidbhirapi kaiścinmanvādibhiḥ satkāryatvādyaṃśopajīvanābhiprāyeṇopanibaddhaḥ /
ayaṃ tu paramāṇukāraṇavādo na kaiścidapi śiṣṭaiḥ kenacidapyaṃśena parigṛhīta ityatyantamevānādaraṇīyo vedavādibhiḥ /
apica vaiśeṣikāstantrārthabhūtānṣaṭpadārthāndravyaguṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyākhyānatyantabhinnānbhinnalakṣaṇānabhyupagacchanti /
yathā manuṣyo 'śvaḥ śaśa iti /
tathātvaṃ cābhyupagamya tadviruddhaṃ dravyādhīnatvaṃ śeṣāṇamabhyupagacchanti /
tannopapadyate /
katham /
yathā hi loke śaśakuśapalāśaprabhṛtīnāmatyantabhinnānāṃ satāṃ netaretarādhīnatvaṃ bhavati, evaṃ dravyādīnāmatyantabhinnatvānnaiva dravyādhīnatvaṃ guṇādīnāṃ bhavitumarhati /
atha bhavati dravyādhīnatvaṃ guṇādīnāṃ tato dravyabhāve bhāvāddravyābhāve 'bhāvāddravyameva saṃsthānādibhedādanekaśabdapratyayabhāgbhavati /
yathā devadatta eka eva sannavasthāntarayogādanekaśabdapratyayabhāgbhavati tadvat /
tathā sati sāṃkhyasiddhāntaprasaṅgaḥ svasiddhāntavirodhaścāpadyeyātām /
children.translated_text: The doctrine of <s>Pradhāna</s> as the cause was adopted even by some knowers of the <s>Vedas</s> — <s>Manu</s> and others — with the intention of drawing upon certain aspects such as the pre-existence of the effect (<s>satkāryatva</s>) and the like. But this doctrine of atoms as the cause has not been accepted by any authoritative person in any aspect whatsoever — and therefore it is to be utterly disregarded by those who follow the <s>Veda</s>. Moreover, the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> accept six categories (<s>padārthas</s>) — called substance (<s>dravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), action (<s>karma</s>), universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) — which are the essential contents of their system, as being absolutely different [from each other], with distinct defining characteristics — like a human, a horse, and a hare. And having accepted such [absolute difference], they [then] accept the contradictory [position] that the remaining [categories] are dependent on substance. But this is untenable. How so? For just as in the world, things that are absolutely different — such as a hare, a blade of <s>kuśa</s> grass, and a <s>palāśa</s> leaf — are not dependent on each other, so too, since substance and the rest are absolutely different, the dependence of quality and the rest on substance should not be the case. And if quality and the rest are dependent on substance — existing when substance exists and not existing when substance does not exist — then substance itself, through the differences of configuration and the like, would be the referent of multiple words and concepts. Just as <s>Devadatta</s>, being one, becomes the referent of multiple words and concepts due to [assuming] different states — similarly. In that case, the contingency of [arriving at] the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> position and the contradiction of one's own position would arise.

children.text: nanvagneranyasyāpi sato dhūmasyāgnyadhīnatvaṃ dṛśyate /
children.translated_text: But is not the dependence of smoke — which exists as something other than fire — on fire also observed?

children.text:
satyaṃ dṛśyate /
bhedapratītestu tatrāgnidhūmayoranyatvaṃ niścīyate /
iha tu śuklaḥ kambalo rohiṇī dhenurnīlamutpalamiti dravyasyaiva tasya tasya tena tena viśeṣeṇa pratīyamānatvānnaiva dravyaguṇayoragnidhūmayoriva bhedapratītirasti /
tasmāddravyātmakatā guṇasya /
etena karmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyānāṃ dravyātmakatā vyākhyātā /
guṇā(dī)nāṃ dravyādhīnatvaṃ dravyaguṇayorayutasiddhatvāditi yaducyeta, tatpunarayutasiddhatvamapṛthagdeśatvaṃ vā syādapṛthakkālatvaṃ vāpṛthaksvabhāvatvaṃ vā /
sarvathāpi nopapadyate /
apṛthakagdeśatve tāvatsvābhyupagamo virudhyeta /
katham /
tantvārabdho hi paṭaṣṭantudeśo 'bhyupagamyate na paṭadeśaḥ /
paṭasya tu guṇāḥ śuklatvādayaḥ paṭadeśā abhyupagamyante na tantudeśāḥ /
tathācāhuḥ - 'dravyāṇi dravyāntaramārabhante guṇāśca guṇāntaram' (vai. sū. 1.1.10) iti /
tantavo hi kāraṇadravyāṇi kāryadravyaṃ paṭamārabhante /
tantugatāśca guṇāḥ śuklādayaḥ kāryadravye paṭe śuklādiguṇāntaramārabhanta iti hi te 'bhyupagacchanti /
so 'bhyupagamo dravyaguṇayorapṛthagdeśatve 'bhyupagamyamāne bādhyeta /
children.translated_text: True, it is observed. But the otherness of fire and smoke is determined there by the perception of difference. But here, since substance itself is perceived with this or that qualifier — 'a white blanket,' 'a tawny cow,' 'a blue lotus' — there is no perception of difference between substance and quality as there is between fire and smoke. Therefore, quality is of the nature of substance. By this, the nature-of-substance of action, universal, particular, and inherence is also explained. As for the statement that quality is dependent on substance because substance and quality are inseparably connected (<s>ayutasiddha</s>) — [we ask:] would that 'inseparable connection' be non-difference of place, non-difference of time, or non-difference of nature? In every case, it is untenable. First, if it is non-difference of place, [the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>'] own position would be contradicted. How? For a cloth produced from threads is accepted as existing in the location of the threads, not in the location of the cloth [as such]. But the qualities of the cloth — whiteness and the like — are accepted as existing in the location of the cloth, not in the location of the threads. And thus they say: 'Substances produce another substance; qualities produce another quality' (<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 1.1.10). For the threads, which are causal substances, produce the cloth, which is the effect-substance. And the qualities such as whiteness residing in the threads produce another [set of] qualities — whiteness and the like — in the effect-substance, the cloth: thus they accept. That acceptance would be contradicted if the non-difference of place of substance and quality were accepted.

children.text:
athāpṛthakkālatvamayutasiddatvamucyeta, savyadakṣiṇayorapi goviṣāṇayorayutasiddhatvaṃ prasajyeta /
tathāpṛthaksvabhāvatve tvayutasiddhatvena dravyaguṇayorātmabhedaḥ saṃbhavati, tasya tādātmyenaiva pratīyamānatvāt /
yutasiddhayoḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃyogo 'pyutasiddhayostu samavāya ityayamabhyupagamo mṛṣaiva teṣāṃ, prāksiddhasya kāryātkāraṇasyāyutasiddhatvānupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: And if non-difference of time were said to be inseparable connection, then even the left and right horns of a cow would turn out to be inseparably connected. And if non-difference of nature [were the definition], then inseparable connection, [far from proving] the difference of substance and quality, would be compatible with their identity — because [quality] is perceived as identical with [substance]. The position that [the relation] of things separately existing (<s>yutasiddha</s>) is conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), while [the relation] of inseparably existing things is inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) — this is a false [distinction], because it is impossible for the cause, which exists prior [to the effect], to be inseparably connected with its not-yet-existing effect.

children.text:
athānyatarāpekṣa evāyamabhyupagamaḥ syādayutasiddhasya kāryasya kāraṇena saṃbandhaḥ samavāya iti, evamapi prāgsiddhasyālabdhātmakasya kāryasya kāraṇena saṃbandho nopapadyate dvayāyattatvātsaṃbandhasya /
siddhaṃ bhūtvā saṃbadhyata iti cet, prākkāraṇasaṃbandhātkāryasya siddhāvabhyupagamyamānāyāmayutasiddhyabhāvātkāryakāraṇayoḥ saṃyogavibhāgau na vidyete itīdaṃ duruktaṃ syāt /
yathā cetpannamātrasyākriyasya kāryadravyasya vibhubhirākāśādibhirdravyāntaraiḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃyoga evābhyupagamyate na samavāya evaṃ kāraṇadravyeṇāpi saṃbandhaḥ saṃyoga eva syānna samavāyaḥ /
nāpi saṃyogasya samavāyasya vā saṃbandhavyatirekeṇāstitve kiñcitpramāṇamasti /
saṃbandhaśabdapratyayavyatirekeṇa saṃyogasamavāyaśabdapratyayadarśanāttayorastitvamiti cet /
children.translated_text: If this acceptance applies only from one direction — that the effect, being inseparably connected, is related to the cause by inherence — even so, the relation of the not-yet-existing, not-yet-constituted effect with the cause is untenable, because a relation requires two [relata]. If [you say] the effect first comes into being and then is related — then, since the effect is accepted as being established prior to [its] connection with the cause, the inseparable connection between cause and effect would be absent; and the statement that 'conjunction and disjunction do not exist [between cause and effect]' would be wrongly said. Moreover, if the relation of a newly arisen, actionless, effect-substance with other, all-pervading substances such as space and the like is accepted as conjunction rather than inherence, then its relation with the causal substance too should be conjunction, not inherence. And for the existence of either conjunction or inherence as something separate from mere relation, there is no evidence whatsoever. If [you say] the existence of [conjunction and inherence as separate entities] is known from the observation of distinct words and concepts for conjunction and inherence, apart from the word and concept of relation —

children.text:
na /
ekatve 'pi svarūpabāhyarūpāpekṣayānekaśabdapratyayadarśanāt /
yathaiko 'pi san devadatto loke svarūpaṃ saṃbandhirūpaṃ cāpekṣyānekaśabdapratyayabhāgbhavati, manuṣyo brāhmaṇaḥ śrotriyo vadānyo bālo yuvā sthaviraḥ pitā putraḥ pautro bhrātā jāmāteti, yathā caikāpi satī rekhā sthānānnyatvena niviśamānaikadaśaśatasahasrādiśabdapratyayabhedamanubhavati, tathāsaṃbandhinoreva saṃbandhaśabdapratyayavyatirekeṇa saṃyogasamavāyaśabdapratyayārhatvaṃ na vyatiriktavastvastitvena , ityupalabdilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdherabhāvo vastvantarasya /
nāpi saṃbandadhiviṣayatve saṃbandhaśabdapratyayayoḥ saṃtatabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ /
svarūpāhyarūpāpekṣayetyuktottaratvāt /
tathāṇvātmamanasāmapradeśatvānna saṃyogaḥ saṃbhavati, pradeśavato dravyasya pradeśavatā dravyāntareṇa saṃyogadarśanāt /
kalpitāḥ pradeśā aṇvātmamanasāṃ bhaviṣyantīti cet /
children.translated_text: No. Because even in the case of one [thing], multiple words and concepts are observed depending on the intrinsic form and the relational form. Just as <s>Devadatta</s>, even though one, becomes the referent of multiple words and concepts in the world depending on his intrinsic form and relational forms — human, <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, learned, generous, young, middle-aged, old, father, son, grandson, brother, son-in-law — and just as even a single line, by being placed in different positions, undergoes the distinctions of words and concepts such as one, ten, hundred, thousand, and so forth — so too, the worthiness of things that are [in fact] not related to receive the words and concepts of conjunction and inherence apart from the word and concept of relation is [merely] due to [viewing them from different angles], not because of the existence of a separate entity. And the absence of such a separate entity [follows] from the non-apprehension of what should be apprehended (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti</s>). Nor would there be the contingency of an infinite regress in the word and concept of 'relation' if relation itself is the referent [of those words] — because the answer has already been given that [multiple words and concepts arise] depending on the intrinsic form and extrinsic forms. Moreover, since atoms, selves, and minds are without parts, conjunction is not possible for them — because conjunction is observed only between a substance having spatial extent and another substance having spatial extent. If [you say] spatial parts are posited for atoms, selves, and minds —

children.text:
na /
avidyāmānārthakalpanāyāṃ sarvārthasiddhiprasaṅgāt /
iyānevāvidyamāno viruddho 'viruddho vārthaḥ kalpanīyo nāto 'dhika iti niyamahetvabhāvāt /
kalpanāyāśca svāyattatvātprabhūtatvasaṃbhavācca /
naca vaiśeṣikaiḥ kalpitebhyaḥ ṣaḍbhyaḥ padārthebhyo 'nye 'dhikāḥ śataṃ sahasraṃ vārthā na kalpayitavyā iti nivārako heturasti /
tasmādyasmai yasmai yadyadrocate tattatsiddhyet /
kaścitkṛpāluḥ prāṇināṃ duḥkhabahulaṃ saṃsāra eva mābhūditi kalpayet /
anyo vā vyasanī muktānāmapi punarutpattiṃ kalpayet /
kastayornivārakaḥ syāt /
kiñcānyat /
dvābhyāṃ paramāṇubhyāṃ niravayavābhyāṃ sāvayavasya dvyaṇukasyākāśeneva saṃśleṣānupapattiḥ /
nahyākāśasya pṛthivyādīnāṃ ca jatukāṣṭhavatsaṃśleṣo 'sti /
kāryakāraṇadravyayorāśritāśrayabhāvo 'nyathā nopapadyata ityavaśyaṃ kalpyaḥ samavāya iti cet /
children.translated_text: No. Because if one posits non-existent things, everything could be established. There is no limiting reason [to say] only this much of a non-existent, whether contradictory or non-contradictory, thing should be posited and no more — since positing is within one's own control and because an abundance [of positing] is possible. And the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> have no excluding reason why, beyond the six categories they have posited, a hundred or a thousand additional categories should not be posited. Therefore, whatever pleases whomever, that would be established for them. Some compassionate person might posit that <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is full of suffering for beings, should simply not exist. Or some mischievous person might posit that even the liberated are re-born. Who would refute either of them? Furthermore: from two partless atoms, the cohesion (<s>saṃśleṣa</s>) that produces a dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>) with parts is as untenable as cohesion with space. For there is no cohesion between space and earth and such, like [the cohesion of] lac and wood. If [you say] the relation of material-cause-and-effect between causal and effect-substances, in the form of substratum and superstratum, is impossible in any other way and therefore inherence must be posited —

children.text:
na /
itaretarāśrayatvāt /
kāryakāraṇayorhi bhedasiddhāvāśritāśrayabhāvasiddhirāśritāśrayabhāvasiddhau ca tayorbhedasiddhiḥ kuṇḍabadaravaditaretarāśrayatā syāt /
nahi kāryakāraṇayorbheda āśritāśrayabhāvo vā vedāntavādibhirabhyupagamyate, kāraṇasyaiva saṃsthānamātraṃ kāryamityabhyupagamāt /
kiñcānyat /
paramāṇūnāṃ paricchinnatvādyāvatyo diśaḥ ṣaḍaṣṭau daśa vā tāvadbhiravayavaiḥ sāvayavāste syuḥ sāvayavatvādanityāśceti nityatvaniravayavatvābhyupagamo bādhyeta /
children.translated_text: No. Because of mutual dependence. For the establishment of the difference between cause and effect [is needed] for the establishment of the substratum-superstratum relation, and the establishment of the substratum-superstratum relation [is needed] for the establishment of their difference — this would be a mutual dependence like the [proverbial] <s>kuṇḍa</s> (vessel) and <s>badara</s> (jujube fruit). For neither the difference of cause and effect nor the substratum-superstratum relation is accepted by the proponents of <s>Vedānta</s> — since they accept that the effect is merely a configuration of the cause. Furthermore: since atoms are finite, however many directions there are — six, eight, or ten — they would have that many parts, and being composite, they would be impermanent. Thus the acceptance of eternality and partlessness would be contradicted.

children.text: yāṃstvaṃ digbhedabhedino 'vayavānkalpayasi ta eva paramāṇava iti cet /
children.translated_text: If [you say]: those parts that you posit as distinguished by directional differences — those themselves are the atoms,

children.text:
na /
sthūlasūkṣmatāratamyakrameṇāparamakāraṇādvināśopapatteḥ /
yathā pṛthivī dvyaṇukādyapekṣayā sthūlatamā vastubhūtāpi vinaśyati, tataḥ sūkṣmaṃ sūkṣmataraṃ ca pṛthivyekajātīyakaṃ vinaśyati, tato dvyaṇukaṃ, tathā paramāṇavo 'pi pṛthivyekajātīyakatvādvinaśyeyuḥ /
children.translated_text: No. Because destruction of [everything] up to the ultimate cause is tenable through the progressive series of gross, subtle, subtler [modifications]. Just as earth — being the grossest substance relative to dyads and such — though a real entity, is destroyed; then what is subtle and subtler within the category of earth is destroyed; then the dyad — so too, even atoms, being of the same class as earth, would be destroyed.

children.text: vinaśyanto 'pyavayavavibhāgenaiva vinaśyantīti cet /
children.translated_text: If [you say]: what is destroyed is destroyed only through the separation of its parts,

children.text: nāyaṃ doṣaḥ /
yato ghṛtakāṭhinyavilayanavadapi vināśopapattimavocāma /
children.translated_text: Because we have stated that destruction is tenable even as the melting of the hardness of butter.

children.text: yathā hi ghṛtasuvarṇādīnāmavibhajyamānāvayavānāmapyagnisaṃyogāddravabhāvāpattyā kāṭhanyavināśo bhavati, evaṃ paramāṇūnāmapi paramakāraṇabhāvāpattyā mūrtyādivināśo bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: For just as for butter, gold, and such — even when their parts are not being separated — through contact with fire, destruction of hardness occurs by the attainment of a liquid state — so too, for atoms, destruction of materiality and such will occur through attaining the state of the ultimate cause.

children.text: tathā kāryarambho 'pi nāvayavasaṃyogenaiva kevalena bhavati, kṣīrajalādīnāmantareṇāpyavayavasaṃyogāntaraṃ dadhihimādikāryārambhadarśanāt /
children.translated_text: Likewise, the origination of effects too does not occur merely through the conjunction of parts alone — because in milk, water, and such, the origination of effects like curd, ice, and such is observed without any additional conjunction of parts.

children.text: tadevamasārataratarkasaṃdṛbdhatvādīśvarakāraṇaśrutiviruddhatvācchruti pravaṇaiśca śiṣṭairmanvādibhiraparigṛhītatvādatyantamevānapekṣāsminparamāṇukāraṇavāde kāryā śreyorthibhiriti vākyaśeṣaḥ // 17 //
children.translated_text: Thus, because this [doctrine of atoms] is woven together from extremely flimsy reasoning, because it contradicts the <s>śruti</s> on the Lord being the cause, and because it has not been accepted by learned authorities — <s>Manu</s> and others — who are inclined toward <s>śruti</s>, complete disregard for this doctrine of atoms as the cause should be exercised by those who seek the highest good — this is the remainder of the sentence. // 17 //
this is not a fault.

children.text: FN: tathātvamatyantabhinnatvam /
children.translated_text: NOTE: 'Such-ness' (<s>tathātva</s>) means absolute difference.

children.text:
sāṃkhyo 'travedāntī grāhyaḥ /
yadvā kāpilasyāpi tādātmyasiddhānta iti sāṃkhyagrahaṇam /
children.translated_text: '<s>Sāṅkhya</s>' here should be taken as [referring to] the <s>Vedāntin</s>. Alternatively, since even <s>Kapila</s>'s system has the doctrine of identity [of cause and effect], the reference to <s>Sāṅkhya</s> [is appropriate].

children.text: prabhūtatvasaṃbhavānniravadhitvasaṃbhavāt /
children.translated_text: 'Because of the possibility of abundance' means because of the possibility of unlimitedness.

children.text: saṃśleṣaḥ saṃgraha ekākarṣaṇenāparākarṣaṇaṃ tasyānupapattirityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Cohesion' (<s>saṃśleṣa</s>) means holding together — the drawing of one by means of another; its impossibility is the meaning.

children.text: 4 samudāyādhikaraṇam . sū. 18-27
children.translated_text: 4. The <s>Samudāyādhikaraṇa</s> (Topic of the Aggregate). <s>Sūtras</s> 18-27.

children.text: samudāya ubhayahetuke 'pi tadaprāptiḥ | BBs_2,2.18 |
children.translated_text: Even when the aggregate [is said to be] due to both [atoms and an unseen force], that [creation] is not attained. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.18 |

children.text:
vaiśeṣikarāddhānto duryuktiyogādvedavirodhācchiṣṭāparigrahācca nāpekṣitavya ityuktam /
sor'dhavaināśika iti vaināśikatvasāmyātsarvavaināśikarāddhānto natarāmapekṣitavya itīdamidānīmupapādayāmaḥ /
sa ca bahuprakāraḥ pratipattibhedādvineyabhedādvā /
tatraite trayo vādino bhavanti- kecitsarvāstitvavādinaḥ, kecidvijñānāstitvamātravādinaḥ, anye punaḥ sarvaśūnyatvavādina iti /
tatra te sarvāstitvavādino bāhyamāntaraṃ ca vastvabhyupagacchanti bhūtaṃ bhautikaṃ ca cittaṃ caittaṃ ca, tāṃstāvatpratibrūmaḥ /
tatra bhūtaṃ pṛthivīdhātvādayaḥ /
bhautikaṃ rūpādayaṣcakṣurādayaśca /
catuṣṭaye ca pṛthivyādiparamāṇavaḥ svarasnehoṣṇasvabhāvāste pṛthivyādibhāvena saṃhanyanta iti manyante /
tathā rūpavijñānavedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārasaṃjñakāḥ pañcaskandhāḥ /
te 'pyadhyātmaṃ sarvavyavahārāspadabhāvena saṃhanyanta iti manyante /
tatredamabhidhīyate- yo 'yamubhayahetuka ubhayaprakāraḥ samudāyaḥ pareṣāmabhipreto 'ṇuhetukaśca bhūtabhautikasaṃhatirūpaḥ skandhahetukaśca pañcaskandhīrūpaḥ tasminnubhayahetuke 'pi samudāye 'bhipreyamāṇe tadaprāptiḥ syātsamudāyāprāptiḥ /
samudāyabhāvānupapattirityarthaḥ /
kutaḥ /
samudāyināmacetanatvāt /
cittābhijjvalanasya ca samudāyasiddhyadhīnatvāt /
anyasya ca kasyaciccetanasya bhoktuḥ praśāsiturvā sthirasya saṃhanturanabhyupagamāt nirapekṣapravṛttyabhyupagame ca pravṛttyanuparamaprasaṅgāt /
āśayasyāpyanyatvānanyatvābhyāmanirūpyatvāt /
children.translated_text: And because the mental disposition (<s>āśaya</s>) too is indeterminable as either the same or different [from the aggregate].

children.text: kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamācca nirvyāpāratvātpravṛttyanupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: And because of the acceptance of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>), since [momentary entities] are devoid of operation, activity would be impossible.

children.text: tasmātsamudāyānupapattiḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the aggregate is impossible.

children.text: samudāyānupapattau ca tadāśrayā lokayātrā lupyeta // 18 //
children.translated_text: And if the aggregate is impossible, worldly transactions that depend on it would be destroyed. // 18 //

It has been stated that the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> doctrine should not be relied upon, because of its association with bad reasoning, because of its conflict with the <s>Veda</s>, and because of its non-acceptance by the learned. The <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) are half-<s>Vaināśika</s> (destructionists) — since they share the [doctrine of] destructionism, the entire <s>Vaināśika</s> doctrine should all the more not be relied upon. This we now demonstrate. And that [Buddhist system] is of many kinds, due to differences in understanding or differences among those to be instructed. Therein, there are three [types of] proponents: some are <s>Sarvāstivādins</s> (those who assert the existence of everything), some assert the existence of consciousness alone (<s>Vijñānavādins</s>), and others are proponents of universal emptiness (<s>Śūnyavādins</s>). Among these, the <s>Sarvāstivādins</s> accept both external and internal entities — material elements (<s>bhūta</s>), their derivatives (<s>bhautika</s>), mind (<s>citta</s>), and mental factors (<s>caitta</s>). We first address them. Among these, the material elements are the earth element and such. The derivatives are form (<s>rūpa</s>) and such, and the eye and other sense organs. And they hold that the atoms of the four elements — earth and such — whose natures are hardness, moisture, heat, and motion — combine into [gross] earth and such. Similarly, there are five aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>) designated as form, consciousness, feeling, perception, and volition. They hold that these too combine to serve as the basis for all transactions in the individual. Therein this is stated: this aggregate of both kinds — intended by the opponents, being caused by atoms in the form of the combination of elements and their derivatives, and caused by the <s>skandhas</s> in the form of the five aggregates — even when both kinds of aggregate are intended, the attainment of that [aggregate] would not be possible — i.e., the formation of the aggregate would be impossible. Why? Because the constituents of the aggregate are insentient. And because the manifestation of consciousness (<s>citta</s>) itself depends on the formation of the aggregate.
