And because no other sentient enjoyer or controller, who is permanent, is accepted as the one who effects the combination; and if independent activity is accepted [for the aggregates], there would be the contingency of unceasing activity.

children.text: FN: bhūte bhautikaṃ bāhyam, cittaṃ caittaṃ ca kāmādyantaramiti vibhāgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Footnote: Among the material elements, the derivatives are the external; mind and mental factors are the internal — this is the division.

children.text:
catuṣṭaye caturvidhāḥ /
svarāḥ kaṭhināḥ pārthivāḥ paramāṇavaḥ, snigdhā āpyāḥ, uṣṇastaijasāḥ, īraṇaṃ calanaṃ svabhāvo vāyavyānāmiti /
children.translated_text: The four kinds: hard atoms are earthy; moist [atoms are] watery; hot [atoms are] fiery; motion (<s>īraṇa</s>), i.e., movement, is the nature of the airy ones.

children.text: saviśeṣendriyāṇi rūpaskandhaḥ, ahamahamityālayavijñānapravāho vijñānaskandhaḥ, sukhādyanubhavo vedāntaskandhaḥ, gauraśva ityevaṃnāmaviśiṣṭasavikalpapratyayaḥ saṃjñāskandhaḥ, rāgadveṣamohadharmāḥ saṃskāraskandhaḥ /
children.translated_text: The sense organs with their specific [objects] are the <s>rūpa-skandha</s> (form-aggregate); the stream of <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> [characterized by] 'I, I' is the <s>vijñāna-skandha</s> (consciousness-aggregate); the experience of pleasure and such is the <s>vedanā-skandha</s> (feeling-aggregate); the conceptual cognition involving specific names such as 'cow,' 'horse' is the <s>saṃjñā-skandha</s> (perception-aggregate); the factors of desire, hatred, and delusion are the <s>saṃskāra-skandha</s> (volition-aggregate).

children.text: āśerate 'smin rāgādaya ityāśayaḥ saṃtānaḥ /
children.translated_text: '<s>Āśaya</s>' — that in which desire and such rest — is the continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>).

children.text: itaretarapratyayatvād iti cen notpattimātranimittatvāt | BBs_2,2.19 |
children.translated_text: If [one says] because of mutual causation — no, because [each is] merely an occasion for the origination [of the next]. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.19 |

children.text:
yadyapi bhoktā praśāsitā vā kaściccetanaḥ saṃhantā sthiro nābhyupagamyate tathāpyavidyādīnāmitaretarakāraṇatvādupapadyate lokayātrā /
tasyāṃ copapadyamānāyāṃ vā kiñcidaparamapekṣitavyamasti /
te cāvidyādayo 'vidyā saṃskāro vijñānaṃ nāma rūpaṃ ṣaḍāyatanaṃ sparśā vedanā tṛṣṇā upādānaṃ bhavo jātirjarā maraṇaṃ śokaḥ paridevanā duḥkhaṃ durmanastetyevañjātīyakā itaretarahetukāḥ saugate samaye kvacitsaṃkṣiptā nirdiṣṭāḥ kvacitprapañcitāḥ /
sarveṣāmapyayamavidyādikalāpo 'pratyākhyeyaḥ /
tadevamavidyādikalāpe parasparanimittanaimittikabhāvena ghaṭīyantravadaniśamāvartamāner'thākṣipta upapannaḥ saṃghāta iti cet /
children.translated_text: Even though no sentient enjoyer or controller who is permanent is accepted as effecting the combination, nevertheless — because of the mutual causation of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) and the others — worldly transactions are justified. And when they are justified, there is nothing else that needs to be additionally assumed. Those [factors] — ignorance, volitions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), name-and-form (<s>nāmarūpa</s>), the six sense-bases (<s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>), contact (<s>sparśa</s>), feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), grasping (<s>upādāna</s>), becoming (<s>bhava</s>), birth (<s>jāti</s>), old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and dejection — such items, being mutually causal, are enumerated sometimes concisely, sometimes elaborately, in the Buddhist system. This entire collection beginning with ignorance cannot be rejected. Thus, since this collection beginning with ignorance revolves ceaselessly like a waterwheel in the relationship of mutual cause and effect, the aggregate is established as implied by the purpose [it serves] — [is this the objection?]

children.text:
tanna /
kasmāt /
utpattimātranimittatvāt /
bhavedupapannaḥ saṃghāto yadi saṃghātasya kiñcinnimittamavagamyeta /
na tvavagamyate /
yata itaretarapratyayatve 'pyavidyādīnāṃ pūrvapūrvamuttarottarasyotpattimātranimittaṃ bhavedbhavenna tu saṃghātotpatteḥ kiñcinnimittaṃ saṃbhavati /
children.translated_text: This is not so. Why? Because [each is] merely an occasion for the origination [of the next]. The aggregate would be established if some cause for the aggregate were apprehended. But none is apprehended. For even though ignorance and the others are mutually causal, the preceding [member] is merely an occasion for the origination of the succeeding one — but there is no possible cause for the origination of the aggregate [as such].

children.text: nanvavidyādibhirarthādākṣipyate saṃghāta ityuktam /
children.translated_text: But it was said that the aggregate is implied by the purpose served by ignorance and the others.

children.text:
atrocyate- yadi tāvadayamabhiprāyo 'vidyādayaḥ saṃghātamantareṇātmānamalabhamānā apekṣante saṃghātamiti, tatastasya saṃghātasya nimittaṃ vaktavyam /
tacca nityeṣvapyaṇuṣvabhyupagamyamāneṣvāśrayāśrayibhūteṣu ca bhokteṣu satsu na saṃbhavatītyuktaṃ vaiśeṣikaparīkṣāyām /
kimaṅga punaḥ kṣaṇikeṣvapyaṇuṣu bhoktṛrahiteṣvāśrayiśūnyeṣu vābhyupagamyamāneṣu saṃbhavet /
athāyamabhiprāyo 'vidyādaya eva saṃghātasya nimittamiti, kathaṃ tamevāśrityātmānaṃ labhamānāstasyaiva nimittaṃ syuḥ /
atha manyase saṃghātā evānādau saṃsāre saṃtatyānuvartante tadāśrayāścāvidyādaya iti, tadapi saṃdhātātsaṃghātāntaramutpadyamānaṃ, niyamena vā sadṛśamevotpadyeta, aniyamena vā sadṛśaṃ visadṛśaṃ votpadyeta /
niyamābhyupagame manuṣyapudgalasya devatiryagyoninārakaprāptyabhāvaḥ prāpnuyāt /
aniyamābhyupagame 'pi manuṣyapudgalaḥ kadācitkṣaṇena hastī bhūtvā devo vā punarmanuṣyo vā bhavediti prāpnuyāt /
ubhayamapyabhyupagamaviruddham /
apica yadbhogārthaḥ saṃghātaḥ syātsa nāsti sthiro bhokteti tavābhyupagamaḥ /
tataśca bhogo bhogārtha eva sa nānyena prārthanīyaḥ /
tathā mokṣo mokṣārthaṃ eveti mumukṣuṇā nānyena bhavitavyam /
anyena cetprārthyetobhayaṃ bhogamokṣakālāvasthāyinā tena bhavitavyam /
children.translated_text: And if both [enjoyment and liberation] are to be sought by another, that [seeker] would have to endure through the times of enjoyment and liberation.

children.text: avasthāyitve kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamavirodhaḥ /
children.translated_text: But if it endures, that would contradict the acceptance of momentariness.

children.text: tasmāditaretarotpattimātranimittatvamavidyādīnāṃ yadi bhavedbhavatu nāma natu saṃghātaḥ siddhyet /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even if the mutual causation of origination among ignorance and the others exists, let it exist — but the aggregate is not thereby established.

children.text: bhoktrabhāvādityabhiprāyaḥ // 19 //
children.translated_text: The intent is: because of the absence of an enjoyer. // 19 //

To this it is replied: if the intention is that ignorance and the others, being unable to attain their own being without the aggregate, require the aggregate — then a cause for that aggregate must be stated. And it has been said in the examination of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system that such [a cause] is not possible even when atoms are accepted as eternal and when enjoyers serving as substrates exist. How much less would it be possible when atoms are accepted as momentary, devoid of an enjoyer, and devoid of a substrate? And if the intention is that ignorance and the others are themselves the cause of the aggregate — how could they, attaining their own being only in dependence on [the aggregate], be its cause? And if you think that aggregates have been continuing in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s> through succession, and that ignorance and the others depend on them — even so, the next aggregate arising from a [prior] aggregate would either necessarily produce a similar one, or without such necessity, produce either a similar or dissimilar one. If regularity is accepted, then a human individual (<s>pudgala</s>) could never obtain [rebirth as] a god, an animal, or a hell-being. If lack of regularity is accepted, then a human individual might in a single moment become an elephant, then a god, then a human again — and [such would be] the consequence. Both alternatives contradict [your own] accepted positions. Moreover, you accept that the aggregate would serve the purpose of enjoyment, and that there is no permanent enjoyer. In that case, enjoyment would be for its own sake and need not be sought by another. Similarly, liberation would be for its own sake, and there need be no one who desires liberation.

children.text: FN: kāryaṃ prati ayate gacchatīti pratyayaḥ kāraṇam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Pratyaya</s>' — that which goes toward (<s>ayate</s>) the effect — means a cause.

children.text: vijñānaṃ pṛthivyādicatuṣṭayaṃ rūpaṃ ceti ṣaḍāyatanāni yasyendriyajātasya tatṣaḍāyatanam /
children.translated_text: '<s>Ṣaḍāyatana</s>' — the sense-organ group whose six bases are consciousness, the four [elements] earth and such, and form.

children.text: tṛṣṇyā vākkāyaceṣṭopādānam /
children.translated_text: The grasping through speech and bodily effort motivated by craving is <s>upādāna</s>.

children.text: hā putra, tātetyādipralāpaḥ paridevanā /
children.translated_text: Lamentation (<s>parivedanā</s>) is wailing such as 'O son!' 'O father!' and such.

children.text: āśrayetyādi bhoktṛviśeṣaṇaṃ adṛṣṭāśrayeṣvityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Substrate' and such qualify the enjoyer — the meaning is: 'serving as substrates for unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>).'

children.text: uttarotpāde ca pūrvanirodhāt | BBs_2,2.20 |
children.translated_text: And because, upon the arising of the later [moment], the earlier ceases. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.20 |

children.text:
uktametadavidyādīnāmutpattimātranimittatvānna saṃghātasiddhirastīti /
tadapi tūtpattimātranimittatvaṃ na saṃbhavatītidamidānīmupapādyate /
kṣaṇabhaṅgavādino 'yamabhyupagama uttarasminkṣaṇa utpadyamāne pūrvaḥ kṣaṇo nirudhyata iti /
nacaivamabhyupagacchatā pūrvottarayoḥ kṣaṇayorhetuphalabhāvaḥ śakyate saṃpādayitum /
nirudhyamānasya niruddhasya vā pūrvakṣaṇasyābhāvagrastatvāduttarakṣaṇahetutvānupapatteḥ /
atha bhāvabhūtaḥ pariniṣpannāvasthaḥ pūrvakṣaṇa uttarakṣaṇasya heturityabhiprāyastathāpi nopapadyate /
bhāvabhūtasya punarvyāpārakalpanāyāṃ kṣaṇāntarasaṃbandhaprasaṅgāt /
atha bhāva evāsya vyāpāra ityabhiprāyastathāpi naivopapadyate /
hetusvabhāvānuparaktasya phalasyetpattyasaṃbhavāt /
svabhāvoparāgābhyupagame ca hetusvabhāvasya phalakālāvasthāyitve sati kṣaṇabhaṅgābhyupagamatyāgaprasaṅgaḥ /
vinaiva vā svabhāvoparāgeṇa hetu phalabhāvamabhyupagacchataḥ sarvatra tatprāpteratiprasaṅgaḥ /
apicotpādanirodhau nāma vastunaḥ svarūpameva vā syātāmavasthāntaraṃ vā vastvantarameva vā /
sarvathāpi nopapadyate /
yadi tāvadvastunaḥ svarūpamevotpādanirodhau syātāṃ tato vastuśabda utpādanirodhaśabdau ca paryāyāḥ prāpnuyuḥ /
asthāsti kaścidviśeṣa iti manyetotpādanirodhaśabdābhyāṃ madhyavartino vastuna ādyantākhye avasthe abhilapyete iti, evamapyādyāntamadhyakṣaṇatrayasaṃbandhitvādvastunaḥ kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamahāniḥ /
children.translated_text: If one thinks: 'There is some distinction — the words "origination" and "cessation" denote the initial and final states of an entity that exists in between' — even so, because the entity is connected with the three moments of beginning, end, and middle, the acceptance of momentariness is lost.

children.text: athātyantavyatiriktāvevotpādanirodhau vastunaḥ syātāmaśvamahiṣavat, tato vastu utpādanirodhābhyāmasaṃsṛṣṭamiti vastunaḥ śāśvatatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: And if origination and cessation were entirely distinct from the entity — as a horse is from a buffalo — then the entity, being unconnected with origination and cessation, would be permanent.

children.text: yadi ca darśanādarśane vastuna utpādanirodhau syātām, evamapi draṣṭṛdharmau tau na vastudharmāviti vastunaḥ śāśvatatvaprasaṅga eva /
children.translated_text: And if appearing and disappearing were the origination and cessation of the entity — even so, these two would be properties of the observer, not of the entity. Therefore, the permanence of the entity would follow.

children.text: tasmādapyasaṃgataṃ saugataṃ matam // 20 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the Buddhist doctrine is also inconsistent. // 20 //

It has been stated that because ignorance and the others are merely occasions for origination, the establishment of the aggregate is not possible. Now it is demonstrated that even this mutual occasioning of origination is not possible. This is the accepted position of the <s>Kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin</s> (proponent of momentary destruction): when the later moment arises, the earlier moment ceases. And one who accepts this cannot establish the causal relationship between the earlier and later moments. Because the earlier moment, being swallowed by cessation — whether it is ceasing or has ceased — cannot serve as the cause of the later moment, since it has fallen into non-existence. If the intention is that the earlier moment in its state of being, having reached full completion, is the cause of the later moment — even so, it is not possible. Because if a further operation is posited for [something] that has reached its state of being, there would be the contingency of connection with another moment. And if the intention is that its very being is its operation — even so, it is not possible. Because the origination of an effect not colored by the nature of the cause is impossible. And if the coloring by the cause's nature is accepted, then since the nature of the cause would endure during the time of the effect, there would be the contingency of abandoning the acceptance of momentariness. And if one accepts the causal relationship without any coloring by [the cause's] nature, there would be over-extension, since [the same relationship] would apply everywhere. Moreover, origination and cessation would be either the very nature of the entity, or a different state of the entity, or an entirely different entity.

children.text:
FN: nirudhyamānatvaṃ vināśakasāṃnidhyam /
niruddhatvamatītatvam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: 'Being in the state of ceasing' means the proximity of a destroyer. 'Having ceased' means having become past.

children.text: asati pratijñoparodho yaugapadyamanyathā | BBs_2,2.21 |
children.translated_text: If [the effect arises from] the non-existent [cause], the thesis would be contradicted; or [there would be] simultaneity — otherwise. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.21 |

children.text:
kṣaṇabhaṅgavāde pūrvakṣaṇo nirodhagrastatvānnottarasya kṣaṇasya heturbhavatītyuktam /
athāsatyeva hetau phalotpattiṃ brūyāt, tataḥ pratijñoparodhaḥ syāt /
caturvidhānhetūnpratītya cittacaittā utpadyanta itīyaṃ pratijñā hīyeta /
nirhetukāyāṃ cotpattāvapratibandhātsarvaṃ sarvatrotpadyeta /
children.translated_text: And if origination were without a cause, then since there would be no restriction, everything would arise everywhere.

children.text: athottarakṣaṇotpattiryāvattāvadavatiṣṭhate pūrvakṣaṇa iti brūyāttato yaugapadyaṃ hetuphalayoḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: And if one were to say that the earlier moment persists as long as the later moment is arising — then there would be simultaneity of cause and effect.

children.text: tathāpi pratijñoparodha eva syāt /
children.translated_text: Even so, the thesis would be contradicted.

children.text: kṣaṇikāḥ sarve saṃskārā itīyaṃ pratijñoparudhyeta // 21 //
children.translated_text: The thesis 'all conditioned things (<s>saṃskāra</s>) are momentary' would be contradicted. // 21 //

In the doctrine of momentary destruction, it has been stated that the earlier moment, being swallowed by cessation, cannot be the cause of the later moment. If one were to say that the effect arises even when the cause does not exist — then the thesis would be contradicted. The assertion that 'mind and mental factors arise depending on four kinds of causes' would be abandoned.

children.text: pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhāprāptir avicchedāt | BBs_2,2.22 |
children.translated_text: The two types of cessation — by deliberation and without deliberation — are unattainable, because of non-interruption. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.22 |

children.text:
apica vaināśikāḥ kalpayanti buddhibodhyaṃ trayādanyatsaṃskṛtaṃ kṣaṇikaṃ ceti /
tadapi ca kṣayaṃ pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhāyānirodhāvakāśaṃ cetyācakṣate /
trayamapi caitadavastvabhāvamātraṃ nirupākhyamiti manyante, buddhipūrvakaḥ kila vināśo bhāvānāṃ pratisaṃkhyānirodho nāma bhāṣyate, tadviparīto 'pratisaṃkhyānirodhaḥ āvaraṇabhāvamātramākāśamiti /
teṣāmākāśaṃ parastātpratyākhyāsyati /
nirodhadvayamidānīṃ pratyācaṣṭe /
pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhayoraprāptiḥ /
asaṃbhava ityarthaḥ /
kasmāt /
avicchedāt /
etau hi pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhau saṃtānagocarau vā syātāṃ bhāvagocarau vā /
na tāvatsaṃtānagocarau saṃbhavataḥ /
sarveṣvapi saṃtāneṣu saṃtānināmavicchinnena hetuphalabhāvena saṃtānavicchedasyāsaṃbhavāt /
nāpi bhāvagocarau saṃbhavataḥ /
children.translated_text: Nor can they apply to individual entities.

children.text: nahi bhāvānāṃ niranvayo nirupākhyo vināśaḥ saṃbhavati, sarvāsvapyavasthāsu pratyabhijñānabalenānvayyavicchedadarśanāt /
children.translated_text: For the destruction of entities — leaving no trace and being indeterminate — is not possible, because in all states, by the force of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>), the non-interruption of continuity is observed.

children.text: aspaṣṭapratyabhijñānāsvapyavasthāsu kvaciddṛṣṭenānvayyavicchedenānyatrāpi tadanumānāt /
children.translated_text: Even in states where recognition is unclear, from the non-interruption of continuity observed in some [cases], the same is inferred in others.

children.text: tasmātparaparikalpitasya nirodhadvayasyānupapattiḥ // 22 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the two types of cessation imagined by the opponents are impossible. // 22 //

Moreover, the <s>Vaināśikas</s> (Buddhists) posit that the conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) — which is other than the triad [of unconditioned dharmas] — is comprehensible by cognition and is momentary. And they declare that [the unconditioned] has three [aspects]: cessation, deliberate cessation (<s>pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>), non-deliberate cessation (<s>apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>), and space (<s>ākāśa</s>). And they consider all three of these to be mere non-entity (<s>avastu</s>), mere absence, indeterminate (<s>nirupākhya</s>). The deliberate destruction of entities is called <s>pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>; the opposite is <s>apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>; and space is mere obstruction-nature. Space will be rejected later on. The two types of cessation are now addressed. The attainment of deliberate cessation and non-deliberate cessation is impossible. The meaning is: [they are] impossible. Why? Because of non-interruption. For these two — deliberate cessation and non-deliberate cessation — would apply either to the continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>) or to individual entities (<s>bhāva</s>). They cannot apply to the continuum — because in all continua, since the members of the continuum stand in an uninterrupted relationship of cause and effect, the interruption of the continuum is impossible.

children.text: FN: nirupākhyaṃ niḥsvarūpam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Nirupākhya</s>' means 'devoid of [its own] nature.'

children.text: pratīpā pratukūlaḥ saṃkhyā santaṃ bhāvamasantaṃ karomītyevaṃrūpā buddhiḥ pratisaṃkhyā tayā nirodhaḥ /
children.translated_text: '<s>Pratīpā</s>' means opposed; '<s>pratisaṃkhyā</s>' is the understanding of the form 'I make the existing state non-existent' — cessation through such [deliberate understanding] is [<s>pratisaṃkhyānirodha</s>].

children.text: ubhayathā ca doṣāt | BBs_2,2.23 |
children.translated_text: And because of the fault in both ways. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.23 |

children.text: yo 'yamavidyādinirodhaḥ pratisaṃkhyānirodhāntaḥpātī paraparikalpitaḥ, sa samyagjñānādvā saparikarātsyātsvayameva vā /
children.translated_text: This cessation of <s>avidyā</s> and such, which falls under [either] <s>pratisaṃkhyānirodha</s> (deliberate cessation) [or <s>apratisaṃkhyānirodha</s> (spontaneous cessation)], as postulated by the opponent — would it arise from right knowledge together with its accessories, or would it arise by itself?

children.text: pūrvasminvikalpe nihartukavināśābhyupagamahāniprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the first alternative, there would be the consequence of abandoning the [Buddhist] acceptance that destruction is without a cause.

children.text: uttarasmiṃstu mārgopadeśānarthakyaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the second [alternative], there would be the consequence of the teaching of the path becoming purposeless.

children.text: evamubhayathāpi doṣaprasaṅgādasamañjasamidaṃ darśanam // 23 //
children.translated_text: Thus, because of the consequence of faults in both ways, this doctrine is inconsistent. // 23 //

children.text: FN: parikarā yamaniyamādayastatsahitāt /
children.translated_text: Footnote: 'Accessories' (<s>parikara</s>) are <s>Yama</s>, <s>Niyama</s>, and such — [cessation would arise] from [right knowledge] endowed with those.

children.text: sarvaṃ duḥkhaṃ kṣaṇikamiti bhāvanopadeśo mārgopadeśaḥ /
children.translated_text: The teaching of the path is the instruction in the contemplation that 'everything is suffering, everything is momentary.'

children.text: ākāśe cāviśeṣāt | BBs_2,2.24 |
children.translated_text: And regarding space (<s>ākāśa</s>), because of no distinction. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.24 |

children.text:
yacca teṣāmevābhipretaṃ nirodhadvayamākāśaṃ ca nirupākhyamiti, tatra nirodhadvayasya nirupākhyatvaṃ purastānnirākṛtam /
ākāśasyedānīṃ nirākriyate /
ākāśe cāyukto nirupākhyatvābhyupagamaḥ /
pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhayoriva vastutvapratipatteraviśeṣāt /
āgamaprāmāṇyāttāvat 'ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ' (tai. 2.1) ityādiśrutibhya ākāśasya ca vastutvaprāptiḥ /
vipratipannānprati tu śabdaguṇānumeyatvaṃ vaktavyaṃ, gandhādīnāṃ guṇānāṃ pṛthivyādivastvāśrayatvadarśanāt /
api cāvaraṇābhāvamātramākāśamicchatāmekasminsuparṇe patatyāvaraṇasya vidyamānatvātsuparṇāntarasyotpitsato 'navakāśatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: And as for what is accepted by those very [Buddhists] — that the two types of cessation and space are indeterminate (<s>nirupākhya</s>) [i.e., non-entities] — therein, the indeterminate nature of the two types of cessation was refuted earlier. The [indeterminate nature] of space is now being refuted. Regarding space, the acceptance of its being indeterminate is unjustified — because of no distinction from the two types of cessation, in which real-entity-status (<s>vastutva</s>) was apprehended. First, from the authority of scripture, from <s>śrutis</s> such as 'From the Self, space was born' (<s>Taittirīya</s> 2.1), space too attains real-entity-status. And to those who hold a different view, it should be said that [space] is inferable from its quality of sound — because qualities such as smell and the like are seen to have real substances like earth and the like as their substrates. Moreover, for those who hold that space is merely the absence of obstruction — since when one bird is occupying [a space], the obstruction is present, there would be the consequence that another bird wishing to fly up would have no space.

children.text: yatrāvaraṇābhāvastatra patiṣyatīti cet /
children.translated_text: If [one says] that [the bird] will fly where obstruction is absent —

children.text:
yenāvaraṇabhāvo viśeṣyate tattarhi vastubhūtamevākāśaṃ manyamānasya saugatasya svābhyupagamavirodhaḥ prasajyeta /
saugate hi samaye 'pṛthivī bhagavaḥ kiṃsaṃniścayā' ityasminprativacanapravāhe pṛthivyādīnāmante vāyuḥ 'kiṃsaṃniścayaḥ' ityasya praśnasya prativacanaṃ bhavati 'vāyurākāśasaṃniścayaḥ' iti /
tadākāśasyāvastutve na samañjasaṃ syāt /
tasmādapyayuktamākāśasyāvastutvam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, from this standpoint too, the non-entity-status of space is unjustified.

children.text: apica nirodhadvayamākāśaṃ ca trayamapyetannirūpākhyamavastu nityaṃ ceti vipratiṣiddham /
children.translated_text: Moreover, [to say] that all three — the two types of cessation and space — are indeterminate (<s>nirupākhya</s>), non-entities, and yet eternal — is self-contradictory.

children.text: nahyavastuno nityatvamanityatvaṃ vā saṃbhavati, vastvāśrayatvāddharmadharmivyavahārasya /
children.translated_text: For neither eternality nor non-eternality is possible for a non-entity, because the transaction involving properties and their substrates is grounded in real entities.

children.text: dharmadharmibhāve hi ghaṭādivadvastutvameva syānna nirupākhyatvam // 24 //
children.translated_text: For if there were the relation of property and substrate, then [that substrate] would be a real entity, like a pot and such — not indeterminate. // 24 //

then that by which the absence of obstruction is qualified [i.e., the positive locus] — the Buddhist who regards that as a real entity called 'space' would face a contradiction with his own accepted position. For in the Buddhist system, in the course of answering the question 'What is the basis of earth, O Lord?', [we find that] at the end [of the series] of earth and such, air is [said to be] 'based on space' — this being the answer to the question 'What is the basis of air?' If space were not a real entity, that would not be consistent.

children.text:
FN: patiṣyati saṃcariṣyatītyarthaḥ /
kiṃ samyak niścaya āśrayo 'syā iti kiṃ saṃniścayā /
children.translated_text:
Footnote: '<s>Patiṣyati</s>' means 'will move' — this is the meaning.
'<s>Kiṃsaṃniścayā</s>' — what is its basis (<s>saṃniścaya</s>)? — [means] what is its support?

children.text: anusmṛteś ca | BBs_2,2.25 |
children.translated_text: And because of recollection (<s>anusmṛti</s>). | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.25 |

children.text:
apica vaināśikaḥ sarvasya vastunaḥ kṣaṇikatāmabhyupayannupalabdhurapi kṣaṇikatāmabhyupeyāt /
naca sā saṃbhavati /
anusmṛteḥ anubhavamupalabdhimanūtpadyamānaṃ smaraṇamevānusmṛtiḥ /
sā copalabdhyekakartṛkā satī saṃbhavati /
puruṣāntaropalabdhiviṣaye puruṣāntarasya smṛtyadarśanāt /
kathaṃ hyahamado 'drākṣamidaṃ paśyāmīti ca pūrvottaradarśinyekasminnasati pratyayaḥ syāt /
apica darśanasmaraṇayoḥ kartaryekasminpratyakṣaḥ pratyabhijñāpratyayaḥ sarvasya lokasya prasiddho 'hamado 'drākṣamidaṃ paśyāmīti /
yadi hi tayorbhinnaḥ kartā syāttato 'haṃ smārāmyadrākṣīdanya iti pratīyāt /
natvevaṃ pratyeti kaścit /
yatraivaṃ pratyayastatra darśanasmaraṇayorbhinnameva kartāraṃ sarvaloko 'vagacchati, smarāmyahamasāvado 'drākṣīditi /
iha tvahamado 'drākṣamiti darśanasmaraṇayorvināśiko 'pyātmānamevaikaṃ kartāramavagacchati /
na nāhamityātmano darśanaṃ nirvṛttaṃ nihnute yathāgniranuṣṇo 'prakāśa iti vā /
tatraivaṃ satyekasya darśanasmaraṇalakṣaṇadvayasaṃbandhe kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamahāniraparihāryā vaināśikasya syāt /
tathānantaramanantarāmātmana eva pratipattiṃ pratyabhijānannekakartṛkāmottamāducchvāsādatītāśca pratipattīrā janmana ātmaikakartṛkāḥ pratisaṃdadhānaḥ kathaṃ kṣaṇabhaṅgavādī vaināśiko nāpapeta sa yadi brūyātsādṛśyādetatsamapatsyata iti /
taṃ pratibrūyāt /
tenedaṃ sadṛśamiti dvayāyattatvātsādṛśyasya, kṣaṇabhaṅgavādinaḥ sadṛśayordvayorvastunorgrahīturekasyābhāvāt, sādṛśyanimittaṃ pratisaṃdhānamiti mithyāpralāpa eva syāt /
syāccetpūrvottarayoḥ kṣaṇayoḥ sādṛśyasya grahītaikaḥ, tathāsatyekasya kṣaṇadvayāvastha4nātkṣaṇikatvapratijñā pīḍyeta /
tenedaṃ sadṛśamiti pratyayāntaramevedaṃ na pūrvottarakṣaṇadvayagrahaṇanimittamiticet /
children.translated_text: Moreover, the <s>Vaināśika</s> (proponent of destruction / momentariness), who accepts the momentariness of all entities, would have to accept the momentariness of the perceiver too. But this is not possible — because of recollection. Recollection (<s>anusmṛti</s>) is memory that arises following a [prior] experience, i.e., perception. And such [memory] is possible only when the agent of perception and the agent of memory are one and the same — because memory pertaining to what was perceived by one person is not seen in another person. For how could the cognition 'I saw that, I now see this' arise without a single [persisting subject] who was the seer in both the earlier and later instances? Moreover, when the agent of seeing and remembering is one, the recognition-cognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) 'I saw that, I now see this' is a well-known, directly evident [experience] for all people. For if the agent of the two [acts] were different, then one would have the cognition 'I remember — it was someone else who saw.' But no one has such a cognition. Where such a cognition does arise, there the whole world understands that the agent of seeing and remembering is indeed different: 'I remember — it was he who saw that.' But here, 'I saw that' — even a proponent of destruction recognizes a single agent for both seeing and remembering. He does not deny the Self's [past] perception, saying 'not I' — just as one would not say 'fire is not hot, not luminous.' This being so, the connection of one [and the same subject] with two characteristics — seeing and remembering — would inevitably force the <s>Vaināśika</s> to abandon his acceptance of momentariness. Similarly, when one recognizes one cognition after another as one's own — 'each successive cognition is mine' — [and] connects the cognitions from one's latest breath back to all past cognitions since birth as having one and the same agent — how could the <s>Vaināśika</s>, the proponent of momentary destruction, not be refuted? If he were to say 'this could be explained by similarity' — we would reply to him: since similarity depends on two [things] ('this is similar to that'), and since for a proponent of momentary destruction there is no single perceiver who grasps both similar entities, the claim that 'recognition is based on similarity' would be mere idle talk. And if there were a single perceiver grasping both the earlier and later moments as similar, then the claim of momentariness would be undermined, since one [entity] persists through two moments. If [one says] 'this is similar to that' is itself just another cognition, not caused by the grasping of two moments —

children.text:
na /
tenedamiti /
bhinnapadārthopādānāt /
pratyayāntarameva cetsādṛśyaviṣayaṃ syāttenedaṃ sadṛśamiti vākyaprayogo 'narthakaḥ syāt /
sādṛśyamityeva prayogaḥ prāpnuyāt /
yadā hi lokaprasiddhaḥ padārthaḥ parīkṣakairna parigṛhyate tadā svapakṣasiddhiḥ parapakṣadoṣo vobhayamapyucyamānaṃ parīkṣakāṇāmātmanaśca yathārthatvena na buddhisaṃtānamārohati /
evamevaiṣor'tha iti niścitaṃ yattadeva vaktavyam /
tato 'nyaducyamānaṃ bahupralāpitvamātmanaḥ kevalaṃ prakhyāpayet /
nacāyaṃ sādṛśyātsaṃvyavahāro yuktaḥ /
tadbhāvāvagamāttatsadṛśabhāvānavagamācca /
bhavedapi kadācidbāhyavastuni vipralambhasaṃbhavāttadevedaṃ syāttatsadṛśaṃ veti saṃdehaḥ /
children.translated_text: There might sometimes be a doubt regarding an external object — because deception is possible — [the doubt being:] 'Is this the same [thing], or is it similar to that?'

children.text: upalabdhari tu saṃdeho 'pi na kadācidbhavati sa evāhaṃ syāṃ tatsadṛśo veti /
children.translated_text: But regarding the perceiver, there is never even a doubt: 'Am I the same [person], or [merely] similar to that [earlier person]?'

children.text: ya evāhaṃpūrvedyuradrākṣaṃ sa evāhamadya smarāmīti niścitatadbhāvopalambhāt /
children.translated_text: Because there is the ascertained apprehension of identity: 'The very same I who saw yesterday, that same I now remember.'

children.text: tasmādapyanupapanno vaināśikasamayaḥ // 25 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, from this standpoint too, the <s>Vaināśika</s> doctrine is untenable. // 25 //

No. [The expression] 'this is [similar] to that' involves the use of distinct referents [in two different words]. And if [the cognition of] similarity were merely another [independent] cognition, then the verbal usage 'this is similar to that' would be meaningless — one would expect merely the usage 'similarity' [without relata]. When a universally accepted [concept] is not accepted by examiners, then neither the establishment of one's own position nor the demonstration of faults in the opposing position — both of which are being stated — ascends to the intellect of the examiners themselves as being truthful. [Rather, the examiner should declare:] 'This is precisely the meaning' — whatever is ascertained, that alone should be stated. Stating anything else would merely proclaim one's own excessive talkativeness. And this transactional usage is not justified by similarity — because what is apprehended is the [identity of the] entity itself, and the similar-entity-status is not apprehended.

children.text: nāsato 'dṛṣṭatvāt | BBs_2,2.26 |
children.translated_text: Not from non-being, because it is not observed. | <s>BBs</s> 2.2.26 |

children.text:
itaścānupapanno vaināśikasamayaḥ, yataḥ sthiramanuyāyikāraṇamanabhyupagacchatāmabhāvādbhāvotpattirityetadāpadyate /
darśayanti cābhāvādbhāvotpattim- 'nānupamṛdya prādurbhāvāt' iti /
vinaṣṭāddhi kila bījādaṅ kura utpadyate, tathā vinaṣṭātkṣīrāddadhi, mṛtpiṇḍācca ghaṭaḥ /
kūṭastāccetkāraṇātkāryamutpadyetāviśeṣātsarvaṃ sarvata utpadyeta /
tasmādabhāvagrastebhyo bījādibhyo 'ṅ kurādīnāmutpadyamānatvādabhāvādbhāvotpattiriti manyante /
children.translated_text: For this further reason the <s>Vaināśika</s> doctrine is untenable: because those who do not accept a stable, persisting cause would be committed to the origination of being from non-being. And they do demonstrate the origination of being from non-being: 'not without the destruction [of the cause does the effect] come into being.' For indeed, it is held that a sprout arises from a seed that has been destroyed, curds from milk that has been destroyed, and a pot from a lump of clay [that has been destroyed]. And if the effect were to arise from an immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>) cause, then because of the absence of any distinction, everything would arise from everything. Therefore, because sprouts and such are seen to arise from seeds and such that have been consumed by non-being, the origination of being from non-being [is their view].

children.text:
tatredamucyate- 'nāsato 'dṛṣṭatvāt' iti /
nābhāvādbhāva utpadyate /
yadyabhāvādbhāva utpadyetābhāvatvāviśeṣātkāraṇaviśeṣābhyupagamo 'narthakaḥ syāt /
nahi bījādīnāmupamṛditānāṃ yo 'bhāvastasyābhāvasya śaśaviṣāṇādīnāṃ ca niḥsvabhāvatvāviśeṣādabhāvatve kaścidviśeṣo 'sti, yena bījādevāṅ kuro jāyate kṣīrādeva dadhītyevañjātīyakaḥ kāraṇiśeṣaṇādibhyupagamor'thavānsyāt /
nirviśeṣasya tvabhāvasya kāraṇatvābhyupagame śaśaviṣāṇādibhyo 'pyaṅ kurādayo jāyeran /
nacaivaṃ dṛśyate /
yadi punarabhāvasyāpi viśeṣo 'bhyupagamyetotpalādīnāmiva nīlatvādistato viśeṣavattvādevābhāvasya bhāvatvamutpalādivatprasajyeta /
nāpyabhāvaḥ kasyacidutpattihetuḥ syāt, abhāvatvādeva, śaśaviṣāṇādivat /
ābhāvācca bhāvotpattāvabhāvānvitameva sarvaṃ kāryaṃ syāt /
nacaivaṃ dṛśyate /
sarvasya ca vastunaḥ svena svena rūpeṇa bhāvātmanaivopalabhyamānatvāt /
naca mṛdānvitāḥ śarāvādayo bhāvastantvādivikārāḥ kenacidabhyupagamyante /
mṛdvikārāneva tu mṛdānvitānbhāvāṃllokaḥ pratyeti /
yattūktaṃ svarūpopamardamantareṇa kasyacitkūṭasthasya vastunaḥ kāraṇatvāmupapatterabhāvādbhāvotpattirbhavitumarhatīti /
tadduruktam /
sthirasvabhāvānāmeva suvarṇādīnāṃ pratyabhijñāyamānānāṃ rucakādikāryakāraṇabhāvadarśanāt /
children.translated_text: Because the cause-effect relation is observed precisely in entities with stable natures — such as gold and such — which are recognized [as persisting through their modifications, such as] bracelets and the like.

children.text: yeṣvapi bījādiṣu svarūpopamarde lakṣyate teṣvarapi nāsāvupamṛdyamānā pūrvāvasthottarāvasthāyāḥ kāraṇamabhyupagamyate, anupamṛdyamānāmevānuyāyināṃ bījādyavayavānāmaṅ kurādikāraṇabhāvābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: Even in seeds and such, where destruction of the [prior] form is observed, that destroyed prior state is not accepted as the cause of the subsequent state. Rather, the enduring component parts of the seed and such, which are not destroyed, are accepted as the cause of the sprout and such.

children.text: tasmādasadbhyaḥ śaśaviṣāṇādibhyaḥ sadutpattyadarśanātsadbhyaśca suvarṇādibhyaḥ sadutpattidarśanādanupapanno 'yamabhāvādbhāvotpattyabhyupagamaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, since the origination of being from non-entities such as a hare's horn is not observed, and since the origination of being from real entities such as gold is observed — this acceptance of the origination of being from non-being is untenable.

children.text: apica caturbhiścittacaittā utpadyante, paramāṇubhyaśca bhūtabhautikalakṣaṇaḥ samudāya utpadyata ityabhyupagamya punarabhāvādbhāvotpattiṃ kalpayadbhirabhyupagatamapahnuvānairvaināśikaiḥ sarvo loka ākulīkriyate // 26 //
children.translated_text: Moreover, having accepted that mind and mental factors arise from the four [causes], and that the aggregate characterized as elements and their derivatives arises from atoms — the <s>Vaināśikas</s>, who then further postulate the origination of being from non-being, thereby deny what they themselves have accepted, and thus confuse the entire world. // 26 //

To this it is said: 'Not from non-being, because it is not observed.' Being does not arise from non-being. If being were to arise from non-being, then because of the absence of any distinction in non-being-ness, the acceptance of specific causes would be purposeless. For there is no distinction in non-being between the non-being of destroyed seeds and such, and the non-being of a hare's horn and such — since both are equally devoid of any intrinsic nature. Therefore, [a distinction] such that a sprout arises only from a seed, and curds only from milk — such acceptance of a specific cause would have no purpose. But if the non-being — being without distinctions — were accepted as the cause, then sprouts and such would arise even from a hare's horn and such. But this is not observed. If, on the other hand, one were to accept that even non-being has distinctions — like blueness and such in a lotus and such — then, precisely because of having distinctions, non-being would become being, like a lotus and such. Nor could non-being be the cause of anything's origination — precisely because of being non-being, like a hare's horn and such. And if being were to originate from non-being, then every effect would be pervaded by non-being. But this is not observed — because every entity is apprehended only in its own form, as having the nature of being. And no one accepts that pots and such that are pervaded by clay are [at the same time] modifications of threads and such. Rather, the world understands them to be modifications of clay pervaded by clay. As for the claim that because the intrinsic form of an immutable entity cannot be the cause [since it would yield no distinctions], the origination of being from non-being must be accepted — that is poorly stated.

children.text: udāsīnānām api caivaṃ siddhiḥ | BBs_2,2.27 |

yadi cābhāvādbhāvotpattirabhyupagamyeta, evaṃsatyudāsīnānāmanīhamānānāṃpi janānāmabhimatasiddhiḥ syāt /

children.translated_text: And no one would make any effort whatsoever for heaven or liberation.

children.text: tasmādapyanupapanno 'yamabhāvādbhāvotpattyabhyupagamaḥ // 27 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, from this standpoint too, the acceptance of the origination of being from non-being is untenable. // 27 //

And if the origination of being from non-being were accepted, then in that case, even for indifferent people who make no effort, the attainment of what they desire would result — because non-being is easily available. A farmer, even without exerting effort in the cultivation of his field, would obtain a harvest. And a potter, even without exerting effort in preparing the clay, would obtain a vessel.

children.text:
evaṃ bāhyārtavādamāśritya samudāyāprāptyādiṣu dūṣaṇeṣūdbhāviteṣu vijñānavādī bauddha idānīṃ pratyavatiṣṭhite /
keṣāñcitkila bāhye vastunyabhiniveśamālakṣya tadanurodhena bāhyārthavādaprakriyeyaṃ virocitā /
nāsau sugatābhiprāyaḥ /
tasya tu vijñānaikaskandhavāda evābhipretaḥ /

satyapi bāhyerthe buddhyārohamantareṇa pramāṇaprameyaphalavyavahārānavatārāt /
kathaṃ punaravagamyate 'ntastha evāyaṃ sarvavyavahāro na vijñānavyatirikto bāhyor'tho 'stīti /
tadasaṃbhavādityāha /
sa hi bāhyortho 'bhyupagamyamānaḥ paramāṇavo vā syustatsamūhā vā stambhādayaḥ syuḥ /
tatra na tāvatparamāṇavaḥ stambhādipratyayaparicchedyā bhavitumarhanti (paramāṇvābhāsajñānānutpatteḥ) /
nāpi tatsamūhāḥ stambhādayaḥ, teṣāṃ paramāṇubhyo 'nyatvānanyatvābhyāṃ nirūpayitumaśakyatvāt /

aṅgīkṛte ca tasminviṣayākārasya jñānenaivāvaruddhatvādapārthikā bāhyārthasadbhāvakalpanā /

svapnādivaccedaṃ draṣṭavyam /
yathāhi svapnamāyāmarīcyudakagandharvanagarādipratyayā vinaiva bāhyenārthena grāhyagrāhakākārā bhavanti, evaṃ jāgaritagocarā api stambhādipratyayā bhavitumarhantītyavagamyate /
pratyayatvāviśeṣāt /
kathaṃ punarasati bāhyārthe pratyayavaicitryamupapadyate /
vāsanāvaicitryādityāha /
anādau hi saṃsāre bījāṅ kuravadvijñānānāṃ vāsanānāṃ cānyonyanimittanaimittikabhāvena vaicitryaṃ na vipratiṣidhyate /
apicānvayavyatirekābhyāṃ vāsanānimittameva jñānavaicitryamityavagamyate /
svapnādiṣvantareṇāpyarthaṃ vāsanānimittasya jñānavaicitryasyobhābhyāmapyāvābhyāmabhyupagamyamānatvāt /
antareṇa tu vāsanāmarthanimittasya jñānavaicitryasya mayānabhyupagamyamānatvāt /
tasmādapyabhāvo bāhyārthasyeti /
children.translated_text: Thus, when the faults such as the impossibility of aggregation and the like were raised against the doctrine of external objects, the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (idealist) <s>Bauddha</s> now takes his stand. For some, observing a certain attachment to external objects, devised this procedure of the external-object doctrine in accordance with that [attachment]. But that is not the intention of the <s>Sugata</s> (the Buddha). His intended doctrine is that of consciousness as the sole aggregate (<s>vijñānaikaskandhavāda</s>). And in that <s>Vijñānavāda</s>, all conventional transactions of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge are established as being entirely internal — in the form that has ascended to awareness. For even when external objects exist, the conventional transactions of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and results do not proceed without ascending to awareness. But how is it known that all this conventional activity is internal alone, and that no external object apart from consciousness exists? 'Because of its impossibility,' he says. For that external object, if accepted, would either be atoms or aggregates of them — such as pillars and the like. Therein, first, atoms cannot be the content delimited by the cognition of pillars and such — because no cognition having the appearance of atoms arises. Nor can their aggregates — pillars and the like — [be the external objects], because they cannot be determined as either different from or non-different from the atoms. Similarly, universals (<s>jāti</s>) and the like are also undermined. Moreover, cognition — being of a common nature — arises merely as experience; the fact that there is a bias toward each particular object — 'this is the cognition of a pillar,' 'this is the cognition of a wall,' 'this is the cognition of a pot,' 'this is the cognition of a cloth' — cannot be explained without a distinguishing feature belonging to the cognition itself. Therefore, the conformity of cognition to its object must necessarily be accepted. And once that is accepted — since the form of the object is exhausted within the cognition itself — the supposition that external objects exist is purposeless. Moreover, from the invariable rule of simultaneous apprehension, the non-difference of object and cognition follows. For neither of the two is apprehended without the other being apprehended. And this [non-difference] is not tenable even if their natures were actually distinct, because there is no obstructing cause. Therefore, from this too, the non-existence of the object [follows]. This should be viewed like dream and the like. For just as dream-cognitions, illusions, mirage-water, and cities of the <s>Gandharvas</s> have the forms of the grasped and the grasper without any external object — so too the cognitions of waking life concerning pillars and the like can [occur without external objects]. Because there is no distinction in being cognitions. But how, in the absence of external objects, is the variety of cognitions explained? 'From the variety of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>),' he says. For in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, like seed and sprout, the mutual causation of cognitions and latent impressions in their variety is not contradicted. Moreover, from positive and negative correlation, it is understood that the variety of cognitions is caused by latent impressions alone — because in dream and the like, the variety of cognition caused by latent impressions, even without objects, is accepted by both of us. But the variety of cognition caused by objects without latent impressions is not accepted by me. Therefore too, external objects do not exist.

children.text:
evaṃ prāpte brūmaḥ - 'nābhāva upalabdheḥ' iti /
na khalvabhāvo bāhyasyārthasyādhyavasātuṃ śakyate /
kasmāt /
upalabdheḥ /
upalabhyate hi pratipratyayaṃ bāhyor'thaḥ stambhaḥ kuḍyaṃ ghaṭaḥ paṭa iti /
nacopalabhyamānasyaivābhāvo bhavitumarhati /
yathā hi kaścidbhuñjāno bhujitasādhyāyāṃ tṛptau svayamanubhūyamānāyāmevaṃ brūyānnāhaṃ bhuñje na vā tṛpyāmīti, tadvadindriyasaṃnikarṣeṇa svayamupalabhamāna eva bāhyamarthaṃ nāhamupalabhe naca so 'stīti bruvankathamupādeyavacanaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: Having reached this position, we say: 'There is no non-existence [of external objects], because of apprehension.' The non-existence of external objects certainly cannot be ascertained. Why? Because of apprehension. For with every cognition, an external object is apprehended — pillar, wall, pot, cloth. And what is being apprehended cannot be non-existent. Just as someone who is eating, with the satisfaction — which is accomplished through eating — being experienced by himself, were to say 'I am not eating, nor am I satisfied' — similarly, one who is himself apprehending an external object through sense-contact, and yet says 'I do not apprehend, nor does it exist' — how could his word be worthy of acceptance?

children.text:
nanu nāhamahaṃ bravīmi na kañcidarthamupalabha iti kiṃ tūpalabdhivyatiriktaṃ nopalabha iti bravīmi /
bāḍhamevaṃ bravīṣi niraṅ kuśatvātte tuṇḍasya /
natu yaktyupetaṃ bravīṣi /
yata upalabdhivyatireko 'pi balādarthasyābhyupagantavya upalabdhereva /
nahi kaścidupalabdhimeva stambhaḥ kuḍyaṃ cetyupalabhate /
upalabdhiviṣayatvenaiva tu stambhakuḍyādīnsarve laukikā upalabhante yatpratyācakṣāṇā api bāhyārthameva vyācakṣate yadantarjñeyarūpaṃ tadbahirvadavabhāsata iti /
te 'pi sarvalokaprasiddhāṃ bahiravabhāsamānāṃ saṃvidaṃ pratilabhamānāḥ pratyākhyātukāmāśca bāhyamarthaṃ bahirvadati vatkāraṃ kurvanti /
itarathā hi kasmādbahirvadati brūyuḥ /
nahi viṣṇumitro vandhyāputravadavabhāsata iti kaścidācakṣīta /
tasmādyathānubhavaṃ tattvamabhyupagacchadbhirbahirevāvabhāsata iti yuktamabhyupagantuṃ natu bahirvadavabhāsata iti /
children.translated_text: Objection: I am not saying 'I do not apprehend any object at all.' Rather, I am saying 'I do not apprehend [anything] apart from apprehension.' Very well — you do say this, because your tongue is unbridled. But you do not say it with reason. For the separateness of the object from apprehension must forcefully be accepted precisely because of apprehension. For no one apprehends mere apprehension as 'this is a pillar' or 'this is a wall.' Rather, all worldly people apprehend pillars, walls, and such as objects of apprehension. That is why even those who deny external objects describe an external object when they say: 'What is the internal cognizable form appears as though external.' They too, receiving a cognition that appears as external and is well-known to all people, and yet wishing to deny external objects, resort to the expression 'as though external' (<s>bahirvat</s>). Otherwise, why would they say 'as though external'? For no one says '<s>Viṣṇumitra</s> appears like the son of a barren woman.' Therefore, for those who accept reality as it is experienced, it is proper to accept that [the object] appears externally indeed — not 'as though externally.'

children.text:
nanu bāhyārthasyāsaṃbhavādbahirvadavabhāsata ityadhyavasitam /
nāyaṃ sādhuradhyavasāyo yataḥ pramāṇapravṛttyapravṛttipūrvakau saṃbavāsaṃbhavāvavadhāryete na punaḥ saṃbhavāsaṃbhavapūrvike pramāṇapravṛttyapravṛttī /
yaddhi pratyakṣādīnāmanyatamenāpi pramāṇenopalabhyate tatsaṃbhavati /
yattu na kenacidapi pramāṇenopalabhyate tanna saṃbhavati /
iha tu yathāsvaṃ sarvaireva pramāṇairbāhyor'tha upalabhyamānaḥ kathaṃ vyatirekāvyatirekādivikalpairna saṃbhavatītyucyetopalabdhereva /
naca jñānasya viṣayasārūpyādviṣayanāśo bhavati, asati viṣaye viṣayasārūpyānupapatteḥ, bahirupalabdheśca viṣayasya /
ata eva sahopalambhaniyamo 'pi pratyayaviṣayayorupāyopeyabhāvahetuko nābhedahetuka ityabyupagantavyam /
apica ghaṭajñānaṃ paṭajñānamiti viśeṣaṇayoreva ghaṭapaṭayorbhedo na viśeṣyasya jñānasya /
dvābhyāṃ ca bheda etasya siddho bhavatyekasmācca dvayoḥ /
tasmādarthajñānayorbhedaḥ /
tathā ghaṭadarśanaṃ ghaṭasmaraṇamityatrāpi pratipattavyam /
atrāpi hi viśeṣyayoreva darśanasmaraṇayorbhedo na viśeṣaṇas ghaṭasya /
yathā kṣīragandhaḥ kṣīrarasa iti viśeṣyayoreva gandharasayorbhedo na viśeṣaṇasya kṣīrasya tadvat /
apica dvayorvijñānayoḥ pūrvottarakālayoḥ svasaṃvedanenaivopakṣīṇayoritaretaragrāhyagrāhakatvānupapattiḥ /
tataśca vijñānabhedapratijñā kṣaṇikatvādidharmapratijñā svalakṣaṇasāmānyalakṣaṇavāsyavāsakatvāvidyopaplavasadasaddharmabandhamokṣādipratijñāśca svaśāstragatāstā hīyeran /
kiñcānyat /
vijñānaṃ vijñānamityabhyupagacchatā bāhyorthaḥ stambhaḥ kuḍyamityevañjātīyakaḥ tasmānnābhyupagamyata eveti yuktamabhyupagantum /
atha vijñānaṃ prakāśātmakatvātpradīpavatsvayamevānubhūyate na tathā bāhyo 'pyartha iti cet /
children.translated_text: Objection: Because external objects are impossible, it was ascertained that [things] 'appear as though external.' [Reply:] This is not a good ascertainment. Because possibility and impossibility are determined on the basis of whether valid means of knowledge operate or not — and not conversely, that the operation or non-operation of valid means of knowledge is based on possibility or impossibility. For what is apprehended by any one of the valid means of knowledge — perception and the like — that is possible. And what is not apprehended by any valid means of knowledge — that is not possible. But here, since the external object is apprehended by all the valid means of knowledge, each in its own way — how can it be said, merely on the basis of alternatives like non-distinctness and distinctness, that it is impossible — when it is being apprehended? And the conformity of cognition to its object does not destroy the object — because in the absence of the object, conformity to the object is impossible, and because the object is apprehended externally. For this very reason, the invariable rule of simultaneous apprehension too must be accepted as being due to the relation of means and end between cognition and object — not as a basis for non-difference. Moreover, in 'pot-cognition' and 'cloth-cognition,' the difference belongs to the qualifiers — pot and cloth — not to the qualified, namely cognition. And the difference of this [cognition] from those two is established, and [the difference] of the two from the one [cognition is also established]. Therefore, object and cognition are different. Similarly, in 'seeing a pot' and 'remembering a pot,' one should understand that the difference belongs to the qualifieds — seeing and remembering — not to the qualifier, the pot. Just as in 'the smell of milk' and 'the taste of milk,' the difference belongs to the qualifieds — smell and taste — not to the qualifier, milk. Moreover, it is untenable that two cognitions — which belong to successive moments — and which have perished through self-awareness — could grasp each other as grasped and grasper. And consequently, the assertions found in their own scripture — concerning the plurality of cognitions, the assertion of properties like momentariness, the assertion of particular characteristics and universal characteristics, the assertion of latent impressions and their impressors, the assertion of <s>avidyā</s>-defilement and real-and-unreal properties, and the assertion of bondage and liberation — all these would be undermined. What more? By one who accepts 'consciousness, consciousness,' it is proper to accept that an external object of this kind — pillar, wall, and such — is simply not accepted [by you]. But if you say: consciousness, being of the nature of illumination, is itself experienced like a lamp, but the external object is not similarly [self-illuminating] —

children.text: atyantaviruddhāṃ svātmani kriyāmabhyupagacchasyagnirātmānaṃ dahatītivat, aviruddhaṃ tu lokaprasiddhaṃ svātmavyatiriktena vijñānena bāhyor'thonubhūyata iti necchāsyaho pāṇḍityaṃ mahaddarśitam /
children.translated_text: You are accepting an utterly self-contradictory action in the self — like saying 'fire burns itself.' But the non-contradictory, well-known-in-the-world [position] — that the external object is experienced by a cognition other than itself — you do not wish [to accept]. Ah, what great learning has been displayed!

children.text: nacārthāvyatiriktamapi vijñānaṃ svayamevānubhūyate, svātmani kriyāvirodhādeva /
children.translated_text: And cognition, even if non-different from the object, is not itself experienced by itself — because of the very contradiction of action in the self.

children.text:
nanu vijñānasya svarūpavyatiriktagrāhyatve tadapyanena grāhyaṃ tadapyanyenetyanavasthā prāpnoti /
apica pradīpavadavabhāsātmakatvājjñānasya jñānāntaraṃ kalpayataḥ samatvādavabhāsyāvabhāsakabhāvānupapatteḥ kalpanānarthakyamiti /
tadubhayamapyasat /
vijñānagtahaṇamātra eva vijñānasākṣiṇo grahaṇākāṅkṣānutpādādānavastāśaṅkānupapatteḥ /
sākṣipratyayayośca svabhāvavaiṣamyādupalabdhrupalabhyabhāvopapatteḥ /
svayaṃsiddhasya ca sākṣiṇo 'pratyākhyeyatvāt /
kiñcānyat /
pradīpavadvijñānamavabhāsakāntaranirapekṣaṃ svayameva prathata iti bruvatāpramāṇagamyaṃ vijñānamanavagantṛkamityuktaṃ syāt /
śilāghanamadhyasthapradīpasahasraprathanavat /
children.translated_text: Objection: If cognition must be grasped by something other than its own nature, then that [grasper] too must be grasped by another, and that by yet another — and an infinite regress would follow. Moreover, since cognition is of the nature of illumination like a lamp, for one who posits another cognition [to grasp it], because of parity [of reasoning], and because the relation of illuminated and illuminator is untenable [between two things of the same nature], the positing would be purposeless. [Reply:] Both [objections] are untenable. Because upon the mere grasping of a cognition, no desire for a further grasping of the witness arises — and therefore the apprehension of an infinite regress is untenable. And because of the natural difference between the witness-awareness and ordinary cognition, the relation of apprehender and apprehended is tenable. And because the self-established witness cannot be denied. What more? By one who says 'cognition shines by itself, independent of another illuminator, like a lamp' — what is being said is that cognition is not accessible to any valid means of knowledge and has no knower. Like the shining of a thousand lamps in the interior of a solid rock.

children.text: bāḍhamevam, anubhavarūpatvāttu vijñānasyeṣṭo naḥ pakṣastvayānujñāyata iti cet /
children.translated_text: Objection: Very well — but since cognition is of the nature of experience, the position desired by us is thereby granted by you.

children.text:
na /
anyasyāvagantuścakṣuḥsādhanasya pradīpādiprathanadarśanāt /
ato vijñānasyāpyavabhāsyatvāviśeṣātsatyevānyasminnavagantari prathanaṃ pradīpavadityavagamyate /
sākṣiṇo 'vagantuḥ svayaṃsiddhatāmupakṣipatā svayaṃ prathate vijñānamityeṣa eva mama pakṣastvayā vācoyuktyantareṇāśrita iti cet /
children.translated_text: Objection: By conceding the self-established nature of the witness-knower, you have adopted my very position under a different verbal formulation — that cognition shines by itself.

children.text: na /
children.translated_text: No.

children.text: vijñānasyotpattipradhvaṃsānekatvādiviśeṣavattvābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: Because [you] accept that cognition possesses distinguishing properties such as origination, destruction, plurality, and the like.

children.text: ataḥ pradīpavadvijñānasyāpi vyatiriktāvagamyatvamasmābhiḥ prasādhitam // 28 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, we have established that cognition too, like a lamp, is knowable by something other [than itself]. // 28 //

No. Because it is observed that the shining of a lamp and such requires another knower possessing the instrument of the eye. Therefore, since cognition too does not differ [from a lamp] in being something that is illuminated, it is understood that it shines — like a lamp — only when there is another knower.

avidyopaplavo 'vidyāsaṃsargaḥ /

yaduktaṃ bāhyārthapalāyinā svapnādipratyayavajijāgaritagocarā api stambhādipratyayā vinaiva bāhyenārthena bhaveyuḥ pratyayatvāviśeṣāditi /

children.translated_text: What was said by the denier of external objects — that waking-state cognitions of pillars and the like too could occur without any external object, just like dream-cognitions, because there is no distinction in being cognitions — that is to be refuted.

kiṃ punarvaidharmyam /
bādhābādhāviti brūmaḥ /
bādhyate hi svapnopalabdhaṃ vastu pratibuddhasya mithyā mayopalabdho mahājanasamāgama iti, nahyasti mama mahājanasamāgamo nidrālagnaṃ tu me mano babhūva tenaiṣā bhrāntirudbabhūveti /
evaṃ māyādiṣvapi bhavati yatāvidhaṃ bādhaḥ /
naivaṃ jāgaritopalabdhaṃ vastu stambhādikaṃ kasyāñcidapyavasthāyāṃ bādhyate /
apica samṛtireṣā yatsvapnadarśanam /
upalabdhistu jāgaritadarśanam /
smṛtyupalabdhayośca pratyakṣamantaraṃ svayamanubhūyater'thaviprayogasaṃyogātmakamiṣṭaṃ putraṃ smarāmi nopalabha upalabdhumicchāmīti /
tatraivaṃsati na śakyate vaktuṃ mithyā jāgaritopalabdhirūpalabdhitvātsvapnopalabdhivadityubhayorantaraṃ svayamanubhavatā /
naca svānubhavāpalāpaḥ prājñamānibhiryuktaḥ kartum /
apicānubhavavirodhaprasaṅgājjāgaritapratyayānāṃ svato nirālambanatāṃ vaktumaśaknuvatā svapnapratyayasādharmyādvaktumiṣyate /
children.translated_text: Moreover, being unable to assert the objectlessness of waking cognitions on their own account — because of the consequent contradiction with experience — [the idealist] wishes to assert it on the basis of similarity with dream-cognition.

children.text: naca yo yasya svato dharmo na saṃbhavati so 'nyasya sādharmyāttasya saṃbhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: But a property that does not belong to something on its own account will not come to belong to it on account of similarity with something else.

children.text: nahyagniruṣṇo 'nubhūyamāna udakasādharmyācchīto bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: For fire, experienced as hot, will not become cold because of similarity with water.

children.text: darśitaṃ tu vaidharmyaṃ svapnajāgaritayoḥ // 29 //
children.translated_text: And the dissimilarity between dream and waking has been demonstrated. // 29 //

Here it is said: Waking cognitions cannot be like dream-cognitions. Why? Because of dissimilarity. For there is dissimilarity between dream and waking. What dissimilarity? We say: sublation and non-sublation. For what is apprehended in dream is sublated by the awakened person — 'Falsely did I apprehend a great gathering of people; there is no great gathering for me; my mind was overcome by sleep, and hence this delusion arose.' Similarly, in illusion and the like too, sublation occurs in its own way. But the objects apprehended in waking — such as pillars and the like — are never sublated in any state whatsoever. Moreover, dream-seeing is a form of memory, while waking-seeing is [direct] apprehension. And between memory and apprehension, the difference is directly experienced by oneself — having the nature of disconnection from and connection with the object: 'I remember my dear son but do not apprehend him; I wish to apprehend him.' This being so, one who himself experiences the difference between the two cannot say 'waking apprehension is false because it is an apprehension, like dream-apprehension.' And the denial of one's own experience is not proper for those who consider themselves wise.

children.text:
FN: nidrālagnimiti karaṇadoṣābhidhānam /
saṃskāramātrajaṃ hi vijñānaṃ samṛtiḥ /
pramāṇajo 'nubhava upalabdhiḥ /
children.translated_text:
Footnote: '<s>Nidrālagni</s>' (sluggish from sleep) is a reference to defects of the sense-organs.
For cognition produced merely from impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is memory.
Experience produced from a means of knowledge is perception (<s>upalabdhi</s>).

children.text: na bhāvo 'nupalabdheḥ | BBs_2,2.30 |
children.translated_text: There is no existence [of <s>vāsanās</s>] — because of the non-apprehension [of external objects]. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.30 |

children.text:
yadapyuktaṃ vināpyarthena jñānavaicitryaṃ vāsanāvaicitryādevāvakalpyata iti /
tatprativaktavyam /
atrocyate- nabhāvo vāsanānāmupapadyeta tvatpakṣe 'nupalabdherbāhyānāmarthānām /
arthopalabdhinimittā hi pratyarthaṃ nānārūpā vāsanā bhavanti /
children.translated_text:
As for the claim that even without [external] objects, the variety of cognitions is accounted for by the variety of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) alone —
that must be answered.
Here we say: The existence of <s>vāsanās</s> would not be possible in your position, because external objects are not apprehended [in your system].
For <s>vāsanās</s> of diverse forms arise for each object from the apprehension of [external] objects.

children.text:
anupalabhyamāneṣu tvartheṣu kiṃnimittā vicitrā vāsanā bhaveyuḥ /
anāditve 'pyandhaparaṃparānyāyenāpratiṣṭhaivānavasthā vyavahāralopinī syānnābhiprāyasiddhiḥ /
yāvapyanyavyatirekāvarthāpalāpinopanyastau vāsanānimittamevedaṃ jñānajātaṃ nārthanimittamiti, tāvapyevaṃsati pratyuktau draṣṭavyau /
vinār'thopalabdhyā vāsanānupapatteḥ /
apica vināpi vāsanābhirarthopalabdhyupagamādvinā tvarthopalabdhyā vāsanotpattyanabhyupagamādarthasadbhāvamevānvayavyatirekāvapi pratiṣṭhāpayataḥ /
apica vāsanā nāma saṃskāraviśeṣāḥ /
children.translated_text: Moreover, <s>vāsanās</s> are specific types of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>).

children.text: saṃskārāśca nāśrayamantareṇāvakalpyante /
children.translated_text: And impressions cannot be conceived without a substratum.

children.text: evaṃ loke dṛṣṭatvāt /
children.translated_text: Because this is observed in the world.

children.text: naca tava vāsanāśrayaḥ kaścidasti pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ // 30 //
children.translated_text: And in your [system], there is no substratum for <s>vāsanās</s>, because nothing [permanent] is apprehended by any means of knowledge. // 30 //

But when objects are not apprehended, what would be the cause of diverse <s>vāsanās</s>?
Even if [they are claimed to be] beginningless, by the principle of an unbroken chain of blind men, there would be mere groundlessness — an infinite regress that destroys all conventional activity — not the achievement of the intended purpose.
As for the two [arguments] of positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s>) adduced by the denier of [external] objects — [claiming that] this entire class of cognitions is caused by <s>vāsanās</s> alone and not by objects — even those two should be understood as already answered, given the circumstances.
Because <s>vāsanās</s> are impossible without the apprehension of objects.
Moreover, since the apprehension of objects is accepted even without <s>vāsanās</s>, but since the arising of <s>vāsanās</s> without the apprehension of objects is not accepted — the [arguments of] positive and negative concomitance actually establish the existence of [external] objects.

children.text: FN: bhāva utpattiḥ sattā vā /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Bhāva</s>' means origination or existence.

children.text: kṣaṇikatvāc ca | BBs_2,2.31 |
children.translated_text: And because of momentariness. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.31 |

children.text:
yadapyālayavijñānaṃ nāma vāsanāśrayatvena parikalpitaṃ tadapi kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamādanavasthitasvarūpaṃ satpravṛttivijñānavanna vāsanānāmadhikaraṇaṃ bhavitumarhati /
nahi kālatrayasaṃbandhinyekasminnanvayinyasati kūṭasthe vā sarvārthadarśini /
deśakālanimittāpekṣavāsanādhānasmṛtipratisaṃdhānādivyavahāraḥ saṃbhavati /
sthirasvarūpatve tvālayavijñānasya siddhāntahāniḥ /
apica vijñānavāde 'pi kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamasya samānatvādyāni bāhyārthavāde kṣaṇikatvanibandhanāni dūṣaṇānyudbhāvitāni 'uttarotpāde ca pūrvanirodhāt' ityevamādīni tānīhāpyanusaṃdhātavyāni /
children.translated_text:
As for the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> (storehouse consciousness) that has been postulated as the substratum of <s>vāsanās</s> — that too, because of the acceptance of momentariness, being of unstable nature, like the active consciousness (<s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>), cannot serve as the locus of <s>vāsanās</s>.
For unless there exists a single, continuous entity that is connected to all three times — either immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>) or all-perceiving —
the conventional activity of depositing <s>vāsanās</s>, memory, recognition, and such — which depend on place, time, and occasion — is not possible.
But if the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> were of stable nature, it would contradict the [Buddhist's own] established doctrine [of momentariness].
Moreover, since the acceptance of momentariness is the same even in the Vijñānavāda (consciousness-only doctrine), the objections raised against the Bāhyārthavāda (external-object doctrine) on the basis of momentariness — 'and because of the cessation of the prior [moment] when the subsequent one arises' and such — those should be applied here as well.

children.text: evametau dvāvapi vaināśikapakṣau nirākṛtau bāhyārthavādipakṣo vijñānavādipakṣaśca /
children.translated_text: Thus both these Vaināśika (Buddhist) positions have been refuted — the Bāhyārthavāda (external-object doctrine) and the Vijñānavāda (consciousness-only doctrine).

children.text: śūnyavādipakṣastu sarvapramāṇavipratiṣiddha iti tannirākaraṇāya nādaraḥ kriyate /
children.translated_text: As for the Śūnyavāda (voidist position), since it is contradicted by all means of knowledge, no effort is made to refute it [separately].

children.text: nahyayaṃ sarvapramāṇaprasiddho lokavyavahāro 'nyattattvamanadhigamya śakyate 'pahnotumapavādābhāva utsargaprasiddheḥ // 31 //
children.translated_text: For this conventional activity of the world — established by all means of knowledge — cannot be denied without attaining another reality. In the absence of a superseding cognition, the general rule (<s>utsarga</s>) prevails. // 31 //

children.text: FN: nādaraḥ kriyate sūtrāntarāṇi na racyanta etānyevāvṛttyā yojayante /
children.translated_text: Footnote: 'No effort is made' — [i.e.,] separate <s>sūtras</s> are not composed; these very [sūtras] are applied repeatedly.

children.text: sarvathānupapatteś ca | BBs_2,2.32 |
children.translated_text: And because of the impossibility in every respect. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.32 |

children.text:
kiṃ bahunā /
sarvaprakāreṇa yathāyathāyaṃ vaināśikasamaya upapattimattvāya parīkṣyate tathātathā sikatākūpavadvidīryata eva /
na kāñcidapyatropapattiṃ paśyāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: We see no coherence in it whatsoever.

children.text: ataścānupapanno vaināśikatantravyavahāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the system of the Vaināśika school is untenable.

children.text: apica bāhyārthavijñānaśūnyavādatrayamitaretaraviruddhamupadiśatā sugatena spaṣṭīkṛtamātmano 'saṃbaddhapralāpitvaṃ, pradveṣo vā prajāsu viruddhārthapratipattyā vimuhyeyurimāḥ prajā iti /
children.translated_text: Moreover, by teaching three mutually contradictory [doctrines] — externalism (<s>bāhyārthavāda</s>), consciousness-only (<s>vijñānavāda</s>), and voidism (<s>śūnyavāda</s>) — <s>Sugata</s> (the Buddha) has clearly demonstrated his own nature as one who speaks incoherently — or his hostility toward all beings, [thinking:] 'By apprehending contradictory meanings, these beings will become confused.'

children.text: sarvathāpyanādaraṇīyo 'yaṃ sugatasamayaḥ śreyaskāmairityabhiprāyaḥ // 32 //
children.translated_text: The purport is: This doctrine of <s>Sugata</s> should in every way be disregarded by those who seek the highest good. // 32 //

What more is there to say?
In whatever manner this Vaināśika (Buddhist) doctrine is examined for coherence, in every such manner it crumbles — like a well dug in sand.

children.text: FN: vedabāhyā atra prajā grāhyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Footnote: '<s>Vedabāhyā</s>' (those outside the <s>Veda</s>) — these should be understood as the people referred to here.

children.text: 6 ekasminnasaṃbhavādhikaraṇam / sū. 33-36
children.translated_text: 6. The <s>Ekasminn Asaṃbhavādhikaraṇa</s> (Topic of the Impossibility in One [Substratum]). <s>Sūtras</s> 33-36.

children.text: naikasminn asaṃbhavāt | BBs_2,2.33 |
children.translated_text: Not [tenable] — because of the impossibility [of contradictory properties] in one [substratum]. | <s>BBs</s> 2,2.33 |

children.text:
nirastaḥ sugatasamayaḥ /
vivasanasamaya idānīṃ nirasyate /
sapta caiṣāṃ padārthāḥ saṃmatā jīvājīvāsravasaṃvaranirjarabandhamokṣā nāma /
saṃkṣepatastu dvāveva padārthau jīvājīvākhyau /
yathāyogaṃ tayorevetarāntarbhāvāditi manyante /
tayorimamaparaṃ prapañcamācakṣate pañcāstikāyā nāma- jīvāstikāyaḥ pudgalāstikāyo dharmāstikāyo 'dharmāstikāya ākāśāstikāyaśceti /
sarveṣāmapyeṣāmavāntaraprabhedānbahuvidhānsvasamayaparikalpitānvarṇayanti /
sarvatra cemaṃ saptabhaṅgīnayaṃ nāma nyāyamavatārayanti /
syādasti, syānnāsti, syādasti ca nāsti ca, syādavaktavyaḥ, syādasti cāvaktavyaśca, syānnāsti cāvaktavyaśca, syādasti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaśceti /
evamevaikatvanityatvādiṣvapīmaṃ saptabhaṅgīnayaṃ yojayanti /
atrācakṣmahe- nāyamabhyupagamo yukta iti kutaḥ /
ekasminnasaṃbhavāt /
nahyekasmindharmiṇi yugapatsadasattvādiviruddhadharmasamāveśaḥ saṃbhavati śītoṣṇavat /
ya ete saptapadārthā nirdhāritā etāvanta evaṃrūpāśceti te tathaiva vā syurnaiva vā tathā syuḥ /
itarathā hi tathā vā syuratathā vetyanirdhāritarūpaṃ jñānaṃ saṃśayajñānavadapramāṇameva syāt /
children.translated_text:
The doctrine of <s>Sugata</s> has been set aside.
Now the doctrine of the <s>Digambaras</s> (Jainas) is being refuted.
Their seven categories are accepted as: <s>jīva</s> (soul), <s>ajīva</s> (non-soul), <s>āsrava</s> (influx of <s>karma</s>), <s>saṃvara</s> (stoppage), <s>nirjara</s> (wearing off), <s>bandha</s> (bondage), and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
But in brief, there are only two categories — called <s>jīva</s> and <s>ajīva</s>.
Because the others are included in one or the other of these two, as the case may be — so they think.
Of these two, they state the following further elaboration: five <s>astikāyas</s> (extended substances), namely — <s>jīvāstikāya</s> (the soul-substance), <s>pudgalāstikāya</s> (the matter-substance), <s>dharmāstikāya</s> (the substance of motion), <s>adharmāstikāya</s> (the substance of rest), and <s>ākāśāstikāya</s> (the space-substance).
Of all of these, they describe manifold sub-divisions postulated within their own system.
And everywhere they apply this principle called the '<s>saptabhaṅgī</s> method' (seven-fold predication):
'Perhaps it exists' (<s>syād asti</s>); 'perhaps it does not exist' (<s>syān nāsti</s>); 'perhaps it both exists and does not exist' (<s>syād asti ca nāsti ca</s>); 'perhaps it is inexpressible' (<s>syād avaktavyaḥ</s>); 'perhaps it exists and is inexpressible' (<s>syād asti cāvaktavyaś ca</s>); 'perhaps it does not exist and is inexpressible' (<s>syān nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca</s>); 'perhaps it exists, does not exist, and is inexpressible' (<s>syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca</s>).
Thus they apply this <s>saptabhaṅgī</s> method even to [properties like] oneness, eternality, and such.
To this we say: This acceptance is not proper. Why?
Because of the impossibility in one [substratum].
For the accommodation of mutually contradictory properties — such as existence and non-existence — in one and the same substratum simultaneously is not possible, like heat and cold.
These seven categories that have been determined — 'they are exactly this many and of this nature' — either they are truly so, or they are not truly so.
Otherwise, knowledge whose form is undetermined — 'they may be so, or they may not be so' — like doubtful knowledge, would not be a valid means of knowledge at all.

children.text: nanvanekātmakaṃ vastviti nirdhāritarūpameva jñānamutpadyamānaṃ saṃśayajñānavannāpramāṇaṃ bhavitumarhati /
children.translated_text: Objection: Since the thing has many aspects, the knowledge that arises — having a determined form — 'the thing has many aspects' — should not be invalid like doubtful knowledge.

children.text:
neti brūmaḥ /
niraṅ kuśaṃ hyanekāntatvaṃ sarvavastuṣu pratijānānasya nirdhāraṇasyāpi vastutvaviśeṣātsyāditi syānavnāstītyādivikalpopanipātādinirdhāraṇātmakataiva syāt /
evaṃ nirdhārayiturnirdhāraṇaphalasya ca syātpakṣe 'stitā syācca pakṣe nāstīti /
evaṃsati kathaṃ pramāṇabhūtaḥ saṃstīrthakaraḥ pramāṇaprameyapramātṛpramitaṣvanirdhāritāsūpadeṣṭuṃ śaknuyāt /
kathaṃ vā tadabhiprāyānusāriṇastadupadiṣṭer'the 'nirdhāritarūpe pravarteran /
aikāntikaphalatvanirdhāraṇe hi sati tatsādhanānuṣṭhānāya sarvo loko 'nākulaḥ pravartate nānyathā /
ataścānirdhārtārthaṃ śāstraṃ praṇayanmattonmattavadanupādeyavacanaḥ syāt /
tathā pañcānāmastikāyānāṃ pañcatvasaṃkhyāsti vā nāsti veti vikalpyamānā syāttāvadekasminpakṣe, pakṣāntare tu na syādityato nyūnasaṃkhyātvamadhikasaṃkhyātvaṃ vā prāpnuyāt /
nacaiṣāṃ padārthānāmavaktavyatvaṃ saṃbhavati /
children.translated_text:
No, we say.
For one who proclaims unrestricted indeterminacy (<s>anekāntatva</s>) regarding all things, even the determination [itself] — because of being a particular thing — would be subject to 'perhaps it exists' and 'perhaps it does not exist' and such alternatives. And thus the determination would be [merely] of the nature of [non-determination].
Likewise, for the determiner and the result of the determination, in one alternative there would be existence, and in another there would be non-existence.
This being so, how could the authoritative <s>Tīrthaṅkara</s> (ford-maker), [supposedly] authoritative as a means of knowledge, be able to teach when the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the knower, and the known are all undetermined?
And how would his followers, following his intention, engage in a teaching whose object is of undetermined nature?
For only when the result is determined to be single-pointed do all people engage without confusion in the practice of means to attain that — not otherwise.
Therefore, one who composes a scripture with undetermined content would, like a drunkard or a madman, be one whose words deserve no regard.
Furthermore, the number five of the five <s>astikāyas</s> — when subjected to the alternatives 'perhaps it exists' and 'perhaps it does not exist' — in one alternative [the number] would exist, and in the other it would not — and thus a lesser or greater number would result.
Nor can the <s>padārthas</s> (categories) be [truly] inexpressible.

children.text:
avaktavyāścennocyeran /
ucyante cāvaktavyāśceti vipratiṣiddham /
ucyamānāśca tathaivāvadhāryante nāvadhāryanta iti ca /
tathā tadavadhāraṇaphalaṃ samyagdarśanamasti vā nāsti vā, evaṃ tadviparītamasamyagdarśanamapyasti vā nāsti veti pralapanmattonmattapakṣasyaiva syānna pratyāyitavyapakṣasya /
svargāpavargayośca pakṣe bhāvaḥ pakṣe cābhāvastathā pakṣe nityatā pakṣe cānityatetyanavadhāraṇāyāṃ pravṛttyanupapattiḥ /
anādisiddhajīvaprabhṛtīnāṃ ca svaśāstrāvadhṛtasvabhāvānāmayathāvadhṛtasvabhāvatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: And regarding the <s>jīva</s> and other [categories], which are established from beginningless time and whose natures have been determined in their own scripture — the consequence would arise that their natures are not as determined.

children.text: evaṃ jīvādiṣu padārtheṣvekasmindharmiṇi sattvāsattvayorviruddhayordharmayorasaṃbhavātsattve caikasmindharme 'sattvasya dharmāntarasyāsaṃbhavādasattve caivaṃ sattvasyāsaṃbhavādasaṃgatamidamārhataṃ matam /
children.translated_text: Thus, because in the <s>jīva</s> and other categories — in one substratum — the accommodation of the contradictory properties of existence and non-existence is impossible; and because in one property — existence — the accommodation of the other property — non-existence — is impossible; and because in non-existence likewise the accommodation of existence is impossible — this Jaina doctrine is incoherent.

children.text: etenaikānekanityānityavyatiriktāvyatiriktādyanekāntābhyupagamā nirākṛtā mantavyāḥ /
children.translated_text: By this, the acceptance of indeterminacy (<s>anekānta</s>) regarding one and many, eternal and non-eternal, distinct and non-distinct, and such [pairs] should also be considered refuted.

children.text: yattu pudgalasaṃjñakebhyo 'ṇubhyaḥ saṃgātāḥ saṃbhavantīti kalpayanti tatpūrveṇaivāṇuvādanirākaraṇena nirākṛtaṃ bhavatītyato na pṛthaktannirākaraṇāya prayatyate // 33 //
children.translated_text: As for their postulation that aggregates arise from atoms called <s>pudgala</s> — that is already refuted by the earlier refutation of the atomic doctrine, and therefore no separate effort is made to refute it. // 33 //

If they were inexpressible, they should not be spoken of.
But they are spoken of and [yet called] inexpressible — this is self-contradictory.
And things that are spoken of are apprehended as such — and are not [truly] unapprehended.
Likewise, the fruit of that apprehension — right vision (<s>samyagdarśana</s>) — either exists or does not exist; and similarly its opposite — wrong vision — either exists or does not exist. Such babbling would belong to the position of a drunkard or madman — not to the position of one who seeks to instruct.
And regarding heaven and final liberation: in one alternative they exist, in another they do not; likewise in one alternative they are permanent, in another impermanent — and because of such non-determination, engagement [in practice] would be impossible.

children.text: FN: jīvājīvau bhoktṛbhogyau, viṣayābhimukhyenenidriyāṇāṃ pravṛttirāsravaḥ, tāṃ saṃvṛṇotīti saṃvaro yamaniyamādiḥ, nirjarayati nāśayati kalmaṣamiti nirjarastaptaśilārohaṇādiḥ, bandhaḥ karma, mokṣaḥ karmapāśanāśe satyalokākāśapraviṣṭasya satatordhvagamanam /
children.translated_text: Footnote: <s>Jīva</s> and <s>ajīva</s> are the experiencer and the experienced. The turning of the sense-organs toward their objects is <s>āsrava</s> (influx). That which obstructs it is <s>saṃvara</s> (stoppage) — restraints, observances, and the like. That which wears away, i.e., destroys, impurity is <s>nirjara</s> — walking on heated stones, and the like. <s>Bandha</s> (bondage) is <s>karma</s>. <s>Mokṣa</s> (liberation) is, when the bonds of <s>karma</s> are destroyed, the perpetual upward movement of [the soul] that has entered the space above the world.

children.text:
astikāyaśabdaḥ sāṃketikaḥ padārthavācī /
jīvaścāsāvastikāyaśceti vigrahaḥ /
children.translated_text:
The word '<s>astikāya</s>' is a technical term meaning 'category.'
The grammatical analysis is: '<s>jīvaś cāsāv astikāyaś ca</s>' (it is a <s>jīva</s> and it is a substance).

children.text: pūryante gantīti pudgalāḥ paramāṇusaṃghāḥ kāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: '<s>Pudgalāḥ</s>' — those that are filled or those that go — are aggregates of atoms, [i.e.,] bodies.

children.text: saptānāṃstitvādīnāṃ bhaṅgānāṃ samāhāraḥ saptabhaṅgī tasyā nayo nyāyaḥ /
children.translated_text: The aggregate of the seven predications (<s>bhaṅgas</s>) — existence and so forth — is the <s>saptabhaṅgī</s>; its method (<s>naya</s>) is the principle (<s>nyāya</s>).
